selection_reason: With no prior experiments, the most informative first step is to establish a well-balanced multimodal baseline that uses standard, reasonable choices across all design dimensions (multiprofile for data richness, scgpt as a pretrained domain-specific RNA encoder, resnet50 as a standard image encoder, avgpool as a simple robust aggregation, and concat as the simplest fusion). This anchors the search: subsequent experiments can isolate the effect of each component (e.g., swapping to imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, or comparing to image-only/RNA-only baselines) against this reference. It avoids overcommitting to a complex or unusual configuration while still exercising the full multimodal pipeline, making it the highest-information first experiment under a limited budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_013: multimodal, scgpt+resnet50, avgpool, concat → 51.2% acc), the most fundamental uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion is actually contributing value over a single modality. config_022 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) uses the identical RNA encoder (scgpt) and aggregation (avgpool) as config_013, differing only in the absence of the image branch. This makes it a clean single-variable comparison that isolates the contribution of the image modality. If RNA alone matches or exceeds 51.2%, it signals that the current image encoder/fusion is not adding signal and we should pivot to improving the RNA representation or trying a stronger image encoder. If RNA alone is substantially lower, it confirms the image modality is contributing and justifies further multimodal exploration. Under a limited budget, establishing this baseline before testing more complex fusion/aggregation variants is the highest-information-per-experiment choice.

Evidence: config_022 (rna_only, scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) achieves 0.530 acc / 0.515 F1, while config_013 (multimodal, scgpt, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) achieves only 0.512 acc / 0.477 F1. The ~1.8% accuracy and ~3.8% F1 gap suggests the image modality, as currently fused, is degrading performance rather than contributing useful signal. Question tested: config_010 changes exactly one variable from config_013—fusion from concat to weighted—while keeping scgpt, resnet50, multiprofile, and avgpool fixed. This isolates whether the concat fusion (which implicitly treats both modalities symmetrically) is the bottleneck, or whether the image encoder/aggregation itself is the problem. Why this is the best next experiment: it is the most parsimonious single-variable intervention most likely to close the gap if fusion is the culprit, since weighted fusion can learn to downweight the weaker image stream in favor of the stronger RNA signal. If it improves performance, we gain a promising direction to exploit; if it does not, we cleanly rule out fusion as the primary issue and can redirect to testing the image encoder (config_017) or aggregation (config_006) next, having eliminated one confound.

The key surprise in the completed experiments is that RNA-only (config_022, acc=0.5305) outperforms both multimodal configs using scgpt+resnet50 (config_013 acc=0.5121, config_010 acc=0.5251). This suggests the image modality may be adding noise rather than signal. The most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality has any standalone predictive value at all. config_003 (image_only, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool) is a clean ablation: it uses the same image encoder and aggregation as the multimodal runs but removes the RNA branch entirely. If image-only accuracy is very low, it confirms the image is a noise source and future budget should focus on RNA-only variants (e.g., transformer aggregation, different RNA encoders). If image-only is moderate, the problem lies in fusion, and we should explore alternative fusion/aggregation strategies. This single experiment resolves the dominant uncertainty and directly guides where to allocate the remaining limited budget, making it the highest-information next step.

Evidence: config_022 (rna_only, scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) is the current best at 0.5305 acc / 0.5152 F1, outperforming both multimodal+resnet50 configs (0.5121 concat, 0.5251 weighted). This strongly suggests RNA carries the dominant signal and resnet50 image features add noise. However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (scgpt), so it is unclear whether the performance is driven by the learned scgpt representation or simply by the informativeness of the RNA data. Question: config_034 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) changes only the RNA encoder from scgpt to PCA while holding all other settings identical to config_022, cleanly isolating the RNA encoder effect. If PCA performs comparably to scgpt, the RNA signal is captured by linear structure and encoder choice is less critical; if PCA is substantially worse, scgpt's learned representation is essential. Why best next: This single-variable comparison resolves the most important open uncertainty (is scgpt special or is RNA just informative?) before investing budget in more complex multimodal or aggregation variants. The answer directly informs which RNA encoder to pair with image in future multimodal experiments, making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_034 (RNA-only, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved the best result so far (acc=0.591, F1=0.573), substantially outperforming scgpt-based RNA-only (0.530) and all multimodal scgpt+resnet50 configs (0.512–0.525). This suggests the RNA encoder choice is the dominant factor, and image modality with scgpt actually hurt performance. Uncertainty: We have no data on whether image modality helps when paired with the stronger pca_n2000 encoder. Question tested: config_014 (multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is a single-variable extension of config_034—adding only the image branch with the simplest fusion (concat). This directly isolates whether image information provides any incremental value on top of the best RNA representation. Why this is the best next experiment: It is the most informative single test under budget constraints. If it exceeds 0.591, multimodal fusion with pca_n2000 is a promising direction to exploit. If it does not, we can confidently deprioritize multimodal configurations and focus remaining budget on RNA-only variants (e.g., transformer aggregation, singleprofile) or scvi_n200 encoders, avoiding costly exploration of a likely unproductive branch.

Evidence: config_014 (pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.619 acc, and the only image encoder tested so far is resnet50, which alone achieved only 0.328 acc (config_003). The multimodal gain over RNA-only was modest (+0.028). Uncertainty: we do not know whether a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) can meaningfully increase the image modality's contribution or whether resnet50 is already near the ceiling for what image features can add. This experiment (config_002) is a clean single-variable swap from config_014—only the image encoder changes from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l—so any performance difference isolates the effect of image representation quality. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it tests a fundamental, unexplored design axis (image encoder capacity) that could either open a high-performing direction (if ViT-L substantially improves fusion) or confirm that image features are a minor contributor (allowing us to focus remaining budget on aggregation, fusion, or profile settings with the best RNA encoder).

Evidence: The best-performing configuration so far is config_002 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat, acc=0.629), and all completed experiments use avgpool aggregation—no transformer aggregation has been tested. This is a major unexplored design axis. Question: Does transformer-based aggregation improve over simple avgpool when combined with the strongest known encoders (PCA + ViT)? config_042 changes exactly one variable (avgpool → transformer) relative to config_002, cleanly isolating the aggregation effect. Why best next: With a limited budget, testing a single high-impact unexplored dimension on the current best backbone maximizes information gain. A positive result identifies a new best configuration and confirms aggregation matters; a null result rules out an entire family of transformer-aggregation variants, saving future experiments. This is more informative than testing fusion (weighted vs. concat) because we already have weak evidence that fusion differences are small (~1-2%), whereas aggregation is completely untested and could have a larger architectural impact.

The current best configuration (config_002: pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieves 0.629 accuracy, and the evidence strongly points to PCA + ViT + avgpool as the right backbone. The key remaining uncertainty within this top setup is the fusion strategy: concat vs. weighted. With scGPT+ResNet50, weighted fusion was modestly better than concat (0.525 vs 0.512), but that was under a weaker encoder pair. Config_009 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted while holding pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, and multiprofile constant, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_002. If weighted fusion helps, we identify a new best; if not, we confirm concat is optimal for this architecture and can redirect budget toward other open questions (e.g., singleprofile or scvi_n200). This is the highest-information, lowest-risk next step under the limited budget.

1) Evidence: The strongest signal across all 9 completed experiments is the RNA encoder choice — pca_n2000 outperforms scgpt by ~0.06 in rna_only and ~0.10 in multimodal settings. The current best (config_009: pca_n2000 + ViT + avgpool + weighted, acc 0.635) is built on PCA, but scvi_n200 has not been tested at all, leaving a critical gap in our understanding of which RNA representation is optimal. 2) Question: config_045 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) isolates the effect of the RNA encoder by holding every other design choice at its best-known value (ViT image encoder, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion, multiprofile). This gives a clean single-variable comparison against config_009. 3) Why this is the best use of the next experiment: The RNA representation is the highest-impact design axis (the pca-vs-scgpt gap was the largest single effect observed), and we have zero data on scvi_n200. If scvi_n200 matches or beats PCA, it opens a new promising direction; if it falls well short, it confirms PCA's dominance and lets us focus remaining budget on fusion/aggregation refinements. Either outcome substantially reduces uncertainty on the most important design decision, making this the highest-information experiment available.

With no completed experiments, the highest-priority uncertainty is establishing a performance baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, fastest-to-train configuration in the space, using a standard, well-understood encoder (PCA) with no image processing, no multiprofile aggregation, and no fusion. It answers the fundamental question: 'What is the achievable performance with a minimal RNA-only model?' This baseline is essential before interpreting any gains from adding image modality, switching to multiprofile, using learned encoders (scGPT, scVI), or varying fusion/aggregation. It also serves as a clear reference point for all subsequent single-variable comparisons (e.g., adding image, changing encoder, switching to multiprofile). Running the cheapest, most interpretable configuration first maximizes information per experiment under a limited budget.

Evidence: Only one experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) has been completed, yielding ~48.5% accuracy. This establishes a baseline for the RNA modality but leaves the central question unanswered: does adding the image modality improve performance? Uncertainty: We have no information about whether image features carry complementary signal, whether they help or hurt, or which image encoder is effective. This experiment (config_027: multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, None, concat) directly tests the effect of adding a strong image encoder (ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L) to the exact same RNA setup as config_001, keeping profile setting (singleprofile) and RNA encoder (pca_n2000) constant. The only change is the addition of the image modality with a simple concat fusion, making this a clean single-factor comparison. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly addresses the most important design decision for a multimodal study—whether the image modality adds value at all—while minimizing confounds. The result will either validate the multimodal direction (justifying further investment in image encoders, fusion, and aggregation) or show that images do not help (redirecting effort toward RNA encoder or profile choices). This is the highest-information experiment available given the current sparse evidence.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, pca, single) achieved 0.485 acc and config_027 (multimodal, pca, ViT-L, concat, single) achieved 0.535 acc, a +5-point gain from adding image. However, we have no image-only baseline, so we cannot determine whether this gain comes from the image modality alone, from a synergistic interaction, or from the specific fusion. Question: config_024 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) isolates the image contribution using the same encoder and profile setting as config_027, directly answering how much of the multimodal improvement is attributable to the image alone. Why this is the best next step: Without this baseline, subsequent experiments (e.g., testing better RNA encoders, multiprofile, or alternative fusion) lack a reference for attributing gains to the correct modality. Establishing the image-only floor is the highest-information experiment under the current sparse evidence, and it is a clean single-variable comparison (remove RNA) rather than a multi-factor change.

Evidence: config_027 (multimodal, pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieves 0.535 acc, a modest +5pt gain over RNA-only (0.485), while image alone is very weak (0.227). This suggests the image signal is noisy and its contribution may be suboptimal under simple concatenation. Question: Does weighted fusion (config_032) improve over concat by appropriately downweighting the weak image modality? This is a clean single-variable comparison against config_027—only the fusion method changes. Why best next: Under a limited budget, isolating the fusion mechanism is the highest-information experiment because it directly informs whether the image modality's value is being properly extracted. If weighted > concat, it confirms the image adds useful but noisy signal and guides all future multimodal designs; if equal, concat suffices and we can redirect budget toward RNA encoder or multiprofile questions. No other single experiment reduces uncertainty about this critical design axis as efficiently.

Evidence: Our best result (config_027, 53.5% acc) uses PCA n2000 for RNA + ViT-L for image with concat fusion in a single-profile setting. RNA alone (48.5%) far outperforms image alone (22.7%), indicating RNA is the dominant signal and the image provides a modest complementary boost. We have only tested one RNA encoder (PCA, a linear method) and one image encoder (ViT-L). Uncertainty: Whether a learned nonlinear RNA representation (scvi_n200) captures biological structure that PCA misses, potentially improving both the RNA baseline and the multimodal ceiling. Question tested: config_021 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA n2000 to scvi_n200 while holding image encoder (ViT-L), fusion (concat), and profile setting (single) identical to config_027, cleanly isolating the RNA representation effect. Why this is the best next experiment: RNA is the stronger modality, so improving its representation is the highest-leverage single change. A direct A/B comparison against config_027 tells us whether to invest further in learned RNA encoders (scgpt, multiprofile) or whether PCA already captures most of the useful signal—critical information before committing budget to more complex multiprofile/aggregation configurations.

Evidence: Our best result is config_027 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat) at 0.535 acc. We've established that concat≈weighted fusion and pca≈scvi RNA encoder (differences <0.5%), and that image alone is weak (0.227) but adds ~5% in multimodal. The entire multiprofile dimension remains completely untested—this is the largest source of uncertainty. Question: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile (with avgpool aggregation) improve over the best singleprofile result, holding RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion constant? config_049 is the minimal, direct extension of config_027 into multiprofile space (same pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat; only profile setting and aggregation change, and aggregation is a necessary consequence of multiprofile). Why best use of budget: It isolates the single most important unexplored design axis (multiprofile vs singleprofile) with the simplest aggregation, avoiding confounds from simultaneously changing encoder or fusion. A positive result would justify further investment in multiprofile variants (transformer aggregation, other encoders); a negative result would redirect budget toward other axes (image encoder choice, scgpt).

The strongest evidence so far is the large jump from singleprofile (config_027, acc=0.535) to multiprofile with avgpool (config_049, acc=0.629), indicating that multi-profile aggregation is the most impactful design axis. However, we have only one multiprofile data point, so we cannot yet tell whether avgpool is the best aggregation strategy or whether a more expressive method like transformer could further improve performance by capturing inter-profile relationships. Config_004 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding everything else constant (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat, multiprofile), directly isolating the effect of aggregation architecture. This is the highest-information single-variable test: if transformer outperforms avgpool, it opens a promising new direction; if it does not, it confirms avgpool sufficiency and lets us redirect budget toward RNA encoder or fusion choices in the multiprofile regime.

The best result so far is config_049 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.629 acc. The only fusion comparison we have (singleprofile: concat 0.535 vs weighted 0.532) showed a negligible difference, but that was in a lower-performing regime. Config_013 changes only the fusion method (concat → weighted) while keeping all other settings identical to config_049, giving a clean single-variable test of whether weighted fusion helps when multiple profiles are aggregated via avgpool. This is the most direct exploitation of the current best configuration: if weighted improves performance, it opens a productive direction; if not, we confirm concat is optimal for this architecture and can confidently pivot to testing RNA encoder or image encoder variations next.

The current best configuration (config_013: pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.635 acc / 0.618 F1. We have strong evidence that multiprofile + avgpool + weighted is the right structural backbone, and that in singleprofile settings pca_n2000 and scvi_n200 performed nearly identically (0.535 vs 0.532). However, scgpt has never been tested in any completed experiment, leaving a critical uncertainty about whether a more expressive RNA encoder can further improve the multiprofile pipeline. config_020 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) is a clean single-variable change from config_013, isolating the RNA encoder effect in the best-performing structural context. This is the best use of the next budget slot because: (1) it tests the most uncertain and potentially high-impact remaining design axis (RNA encoder quality in multiprofile), (2) it directly exploits the proven best aggregation/fusion combination, and (3) the result will either open a new promising direction or confirm that pca_n2000 is sufficient, reducing uncertainty about whether further encoder exploration is warranted.

Evidence: The current best config (config_013: multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.635) establishes that multiprofile + avgpool + weighted fusion is the strongest combination tested. However, the image encoder axis is completely untested — all 9 completed experiments use imagenet_vit_l. Uncertainty: We do not know whether the large ViT-L representation is essential or whether a ResNet50 backbone would perform comparably in the multimodal multiprofile setting. This question has high leverage: the answer determines whether ~15+ resnet50 configurations are worth pursuing or can be eliminated. Question tested: config_009 changes only the image encoder (resnet50 vs imagenet_vit_l) relative to config_013, cleanly isolating the effect of image representation quality while holding RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation, and fusion constant. Why this is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, resolving a binary, high-impact design axis (image encoder architecture) with a single-variable comparison is more informative than incremental tweaks to aggregation or RNA encoder, both of which already have partial evidence (avgpool > transformer; pca_n2000 >> scgpt in multiprofile). The result will either confirm imagenet_vit_l is necessary (focusing the search) or reveal resnet50 is competitive (opening a broader, potentially more efficient design space).

With no prior experiments, the most critical uncertainty is whether each modality individually carries sufficient signal for the classification task, and what performance floor we should expect. Config_005 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) is the simplest, cleanest baseline: it uses a well-established RNA encoder (scgpt), the simplest profile setting, and no image processing or fusion. Establishing the RNA-only performance first provides an essential reference point against which all subsequent image-only and multimodal results can be meaningfully compared. Without this baseline, a multimodal result would be uninterpretable—we could not tell whether fusion is adding value or merely matching a strong single-modality model. This experiment is also computationally lightweight, conserving budget for the multimodal experiments that follow.

We have a single baseline (config_005: rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt → acc 0.411, F1 0.378), leaving major uncertainty about whether the image modality contributes any predictive signal. config_027 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, no aggregation, concat fusion) is the minimal structural change from config_005: it keeps the same RNA encoder (scgpt), the same profile setting (singleprofile), and adds only the image branch with a simple concat fusion (which is structurally necessary once a second modality is present). This directly isolates the effect of adding image information. If config_027 substantially exceeds 0.411, image adds value and we can then explore which image encoder, aggregation, or fusion strategy matters most. If it performs similarly or worse, we learn that the image modality (at least with this encoder/fusion) is not helping, redirecting budget toward RNA-side improvements (e.g., multiprofile, alternative encoders). Under a tight budget, resolving whether the second modality is worth pursuing is the highest-value uncertainty to reduce before committing experiments to finer-grained design choices.

Evidence: config_027 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieves 0.4348 acc / 0.4234 F1, outperforming config_005 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) at 0.4106 acc / 0.3785 F1, indicating that adding image features with concat fusion is beneficial. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the fusion mechanism itself (concat vs. weighted) is a meaningful design choice, or whether the gain is purely from the additional modality. This experiment (config_051) is a clean single-variable change from config_027—only the fusion type shifts from concat to weighted—while holding RNA encoder (scgpt), image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), profile setting (singleprofile), and aggregation (None) constant. If weighted fusion improves performance, it reveals that modality weighting matters and guides future multiprofile/aggregation experiments; if it does not, concat is confirmed as sufficient and we can redirect budget toward testing aggregation or profile settings. This is the most informative next step under a limited budget because it isolates one important design axis from the current best configuration with minimal confounding.

Evidence: config_027 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, concat, singleprofile) is the best result so far (acc=0.4348, F1=0.4234), modestly outperforming RNA-only scgpt (config_005, acc=0.4106) and weighted-fusion multimodal (config_051, acc=0.4224). However, all three experiments used scgpt as the RNA encoder, so we have zero information about whether the RNA representation choice is a meaningful design axis. Question: config_021 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, concat, singleprofile) is a single-variable controlled comparison to config_027—only the RNA encoder changes from scgpt to scvi_n200. This isolates the effect of the RNA encoder while holding image encoder, fusion, and profile setting constant. Why this is the best next experiment: Under a tight budget, the RNA encoder is a fundamental design decision that could account for substantial performance variance. If scvi_n200 matches scgpt, we learn the RNA representation is not a bottleneck and can focus budget on other axes (aggregation, multiprofile, image encoder). If it differs substantially, we gain a critical design insight that reshapes the remaining search. This is more informative than, e.g., testing an image-only baseline or jumping to multiprofile, because it directly extends the strongest evidence we currently have with a minimal, interpretable change.

Evidence: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l with concat fusion (config_021) achieved the best result so far (acc 0.532, F1 0.517), dramatically outperforming scgpt-based configs (~0.41–0.43). For scgpt, concat (0.435) slightly beat weighted (0.422), but the difference was small and the base performance was much lower. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether concat or weighted fusion is optimal when paired with the stronger scvi_n200 encoder—the fusion interaction may differ at higher representation quality. This experiment (config_006) tests exactly that: it changes only the fusion method (concat→weighted) while holding scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, and singleprofile fixed, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_021. It is the best next use of budget because it is a low-risk, high-information exploitation step: if weighted matches or beats concat, it opens a new fusion direction; if concat remains superior, we confirm the best singleprofile multimodal recipe and can confidently move to testing multiprofile or alternative image encoders next.

All five completed experiments are singleprofile, so we have zero evidence on whether multiprofile (with aggregation) improves performance. The strongest finding is that scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l substantially outperforms scgpt-based configs (~0.53 vs ~0.42-0.43), and weighted fusion marginally edges concat for scvi_n200 (0.5375 vs 0.5321). Config_046 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is the most direct multiprofile extension of our best singleprofile config (config_006), changing only the profile setting and adding the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates the effect of multiprofile while holding the RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion strategy constant. It is the highest-value next experiment because profile setting is the largest unexplored design axis, and knowing whether multiple profiles add signal (or just noise/complexity) will strongly guide all subsequent experiments involving aggregation and fusion.

Evidence: config_046 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) achieved the best accuracy (0.7062), a massive jump over the best singleprofile result (config_006, 0.5375). This confirms multiprofile is the dominant design lever. However, we have only one multiprofile data point, using avgpool aggregation. The key uncertainty is whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) can further improve over simple average pooling when combining multiple profiles. Question: config_042 (transformer, weighted) isolates the aggregation method by changing only avgpool→transformer relative to config_046, keeping RNA encoder, image encoder, profile setting, and fusion all identical. Why this is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, understanding whether aggregation architecture matters is more informative than re-testing fusion (which showed negligible differences in singleprofile: config_006 vs config_021). If transformer aggregation yields a meaningful gain, it identifies a new optimization axis; if it does not, we can confidently conclude avgpool is sufficient and redirect budget toward other untested dimensions (e.g., image encoder choice or RNA encoder alternatives in the multiprofile setting).

Evidence: The current best configuration is config_042 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1. In singleprofile settings, weighted fusion marginally outperformed concat (0.537 vs 0.532), but that difference was small. In the multiprofile regime—where performance gains are largest—we have only tested weighted fusion (config_042, config_046). The effect of fusion strategy in multiprofile is therefore untested. Question: config_013 is identical to config_042 except fusion changes from weighted to concat, isolating the fusion effect under the strongest-performing multiprofile + transformer aggregation setup. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison against the current best, directly testing whether the fusion choice that showed only a marginal edge in singleprofile also matters (or even reverses) when multiprofile + transformer aggregation is in play. If concat matches or beats weighted, it broadens the design space at no cost; if weighted clearly wins, we confirm the fusion choice and can confidently move budget toward testing alternative RNA encoders or image encoders in the multiprofile setting. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best (config_042, acc=0.725) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l with transformer aggregation and weighted fusion in the multiprofile setting. All completed multimodal experiments have exclusively used imagenet_vit_l as the image encoder, so the effect of the image encoder choice in the high-performing multiprofile regime is completely untested. Question: config_049 (scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) changes only the image encoder from imagenet_vit_l to resnet50, making it a clean single-variable comparison against config_042. This isolates whether the ViT-L backbone is essential or whether a simpler CNN (resnet50) could match or exceed it. Why this is the best use of the next budget: The image encoder is a major architectural decision that has been held constant across all 8 experiments. Under a limited budget, resolving whether this choice matters (and in which direction) is more informative than, e.g., re-testing fusion (weighted vs concat showed only ~0.004 difference) or testing a clearly inferior RNA encoder (scgpt was ~0.10 worse than scvi_n200 in singleprofile). A large gap would confirm imagenet_vit_l is critical; a small gap would free the search to focus on other axes.

Evidence: scvi_n200 clearly outperforms scgpt in singleprofile multimodal settings (~0.53 vs ~0.43 accuracy), and multiprofile + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion is the strongest configuration (config_042: 0.725 acc). However, all multiprofile experiments so far use scvi_n200; we have zero data on how scgpt performs in the multiprofile regime. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether the aggregation step (transformer over multiple profiles) compensates for a weaker per-profile RNA representation, potentially narrowing or eliminating the scvi_n200 advantage. This experiment (config_001: scgpt, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) changes only the RNA encoder relative to config_042, cleanly isolating the RNA encoder effect in the multiprofile regime. If scgpt is close to scvi_n200 here, it reveals that profile-level aggregation mitigates representation quality and opens a cheaper design space; if it is substantially worse, it confirms scvi_n200 is essential and we can focus remaining budget on image encoder and fusion refinements. This single-variable comparison is the highest-information experiment available under the limited budget.

With no prior experiments, the highest-priority question is establishing a strong multimodal singleprofile baseline to anchor all subsequent comparisons. config_009 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, concat fusion, singleprofile) is chosen because: (1) it pairs a learned RNA embedding (scvi_n200) with a strong pretrained image encoder (ViT-L), representing a well-motivated 'default strong' multimodal setup; (2) concat fusion is the simplest fusion strategy, avoiding confounding from learned weighting; (3) singleprofile keeps the experiment focused on the core question of whether the two modalities, when simply combined, provide a useful signal. This baseline will serve as the reference point for all follow-up experiments testing whether removing a modality (image_only/rna_only), changing the RNA encoder, switching to multiprofile+aggregation, or altering fusion actually improves or degrades performance. Under a limited budget, anchoring the search around a clear, interpretable multimodal reference is more informative than starting with a unimodal baseline (which would leave the multimodal ceiling unknown) or a complex multiprofile configuration (which would conflate multiple design choices).

With only one completed experiment (config_009: multimodal, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, singleprofile, concat fusion, acc≈0.53), the most critical uncertainty is whether the multimodal fusion is actually adding value over a single-modality baseline. config_002 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is the cleanest controlled comparison: it removes the RNA modality while keeping the identical image encoder, profile setting, and overall architecture, isolating the contribution of RNA and the fusion mechanism. If image-only approaches or exceeds 0.53, the multimodal premise is questionable and budget should shift toward single-modality optimization; if it is substantially lower, it validates the multimodal direction and justifies further investment in fusion/aggregation/profile design. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the foundational design decision (is multimodal worth the complexity?) before committing budget to finer-grained comparisons like encoder choice, aggregation, or multiprofile settings.

We have two data points: multimodal (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, concat) at 0.532 acc and image-only (ViT-L) at 0.227 acc. The critical missing piece is the RNA-only baseline with the same scvi_n200 encoder and singleprofile setting. Config_003 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) completes the modality ablation: if RNA-only approaches 0.532, the image modality adds little and future effort should focus on RNA representation; if it is substantially lower, fusion is genuinely beneficial and we should invest in better fusion/aggregation. This single experiment resolves the most important uncertainty—whether the multimodal gain is driven by RNA alone or by true cross-modal synergy—before spending budget on more complex multiprofile or fusion variants.

Evidence: config_009 (multimodal, scvi_n200, vit_l, concat) achieves 0.532 acc, only ~1.2% above RNA-only (config_003, 0.520), while image-only (config_002) is very weak at 0.227. This suggests the image modality contributes a small signal that may be underutilized by the current concat fusion. Question: config_024 is identical to config_009 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, providing a clean single-variable A/B test of whether the fusion strategy can amplify the image contribution. Why this is the best next experiment: it isolates the fusion effect without confounding changes to encoder, profile setting, or aggregation. If weighted fusion meaningfully improves accuracy, it reveals that fusion design is a lever worth further exploration (and justifies testing other fusion variants). If it does not, it strengthens the hypothesis that the image signal is inherently limited under singleprofile, redirecting effort toward multiprofile or alternative encoders. Under a limited budget, this minimal-change comparison maximizes information per experiment about a key design decision.

All four completed experiments use singleprofile; the multiprofile dimension (and its associated aggregation choice) is entirely unexplored, representing the largest source of uncertainty. The best-performing config so far is config_024 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted; acc 0.5375). config_017 is the most direct extension of that configuration: it changes only the profile setting to multiprofile and adds avgpool aggregation, while keeping the same RNA encoder, image encoder, and weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of multiprofile + simple aggregation. If it improves over 0.5375, multiprofile is a promising direction to further explore (e.g., transformer aggregation); if it degrades, we learn that the single-profile scvi representation is already sufficient and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder or image encoder variants. Under a limited budget, testing the simplest multiprofile variant first is more informative than jumping to a complex transformer aggregation, because it establishes a clean baseline for the aggregation axis.

Evidence: config_017 (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) achieved 0.706 acc, a dramatic jump over all singleprofile configs (~0.53). The key untested question is whether avgpool is specifically important or whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) could further improve performance. config_025 is a clean single-variable comparison to config_017, changing only aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, and weighted fusion constant. This is the best next experiment because: (1) it isolates the aggregation mechanism that appears to drive the largest performance gain observed so far, (2) the prior singleprofile data (config_009 vs config_024) showed fusion method has only marginal effect (~0.005), suggesting aggregation is the more impactful design axis to probe, and (3) the result generalizes—if transformer outperforms avgpool here, it likely does so across other encoder combinations, guiding all subsequent multiprofile experiments efficiently under the limited budget.

Evidence: The jump from singleprofile (~0.53) to multiprofile+transformer+weighted (0.725, config_025) is dramatic, but we cannot yet attribute this improvement to the image modality versus the multiprofile RNA representation alone. RNA singleprofile alone achieved 0.520, and multimodal singleprofile only reached 0.532, suggesting the image contributes very little in singleprofile mode. Question: config_013 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) isolates whether the multiprofile+transformer RNA pipeline alone can approach 0.725, or whether the image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) is providing a meaningful complementary signal in the multiprofile setting. Why this is the best next experiment: It changes only one factor (removing the image) from the current best configuration, cleanly separating the contribution of the image modality from the profile/aggregation gains. If rna_only multiprofile+transformer approaches 0.72, the image is unnecessary and we should focus budget on RNA encoder and profile choices; if it falls well short, the multimodal fusion is justified and we should exploit that direction. This single experiment resolves the most fundamental design uncertainty before spending further budget on encoder or fusion variations.

The strongest evidence so far shows that multiprofile + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion with scvi_n200 and imagenet_vit_l achieves the best performance (config_025: 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1), and that multiprofile is the dominant design lever (~0.18 gain over singleprofile). However, the RNA encoder choice is the largest untested dimension—we have only ever used scvi_n200. Config_019 is a clean single-variable swap (scvi_n200 → pca_n2000) within the best-performing multiprofile/transformer/weighted/imagenet_vit_l setup. This directly tests whether a learned RNA representation (scvi) adds meaningful value over a simple linear one (PCA-2000) in the regime where the model is already strong. If pca_n2000 matches scvi_n200, it tells us the RNA encoder is not a bottleneck and we can redirect budget toward image encoder or fusion; if it degrades substantially, it confirms the learned encoder's importance and justifies further investment in scgpt or other learned encoders. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice because it isolates one critical, completely unexplored variable in the most promising configuration.

Evidence: The multiprofile + transformer + weighted fusion + imagenet_vit_l pipeline is clearly the strongest architecture (config_025: 0.725 acc vs 0.537 for single-profile). Within that pipeline, scvi_n200 substantially outperforms pca_n2000 (0.725 vs 0.586), showing the RNA encoder is a critical design axis. However, scgpt has never been tested, leaving a major uncertainty about whether it could surpass scvi_n200 or underperform like pca_n2000. Question: config_011 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, multiprofile) is identical to the best-performing config_025 except for the RNA encoder, cleanly isolating the encoder effect. Why best next experiment: The RNA encoder is the most consequential unexplored variable—two of three encoders have been tested and showed a ~0.14 acc gap, so the third could shift the ranking meaningfully. Resolving this now prevents wasting future budget on suboptimal encoders in downstream combinations (e.g., with resnet50 or different fusion). It is a single-variable change from the current best, maximizing information per experiment.

The current best configuration (config_025: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, multiprofile; acc=0.725) has been validated across RNA encoder (scvi_n200 >> pca_n2000 > scgpt) and aggregation (transformer > avgpool) choices. However, the image encoder effect has never been isolated in the multiprofile setting—all completed multiprofile experiments use imagenet_vit_l. Config_034 changes only the image encoder to resnet50 while keeping scvi_n200, transformer, weighted, and multiprofile fixed, providing a clean single-variable comparison against config_025. This is the highest-value next experiment because: (1) it resolves the largest remaining uncertainty about a core design axis, (2) if resnet50 is competitive it broadens the feasible design space, and (3) if it underperforms significantly it confirms imagenet_vit_l as a necessary component, preventing wasted budget on resnet50-based variants. No other single experiment reduces as much uncertainty about the optimal architecture under the limited budget.

With zero completed experiments, all design choices are uncertain. The most informative first experiment is a standard, moderate multimodal baseline that anchors the design space for all future comparisons. config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) uses well-understood, standard components at each dimension: PCA for RNA (simple, fast, no training), ResNet-50 for image (standard pretrained backbone), avgpool for aggregation (simple, interpretable), and concat for fusion (simple, no learned weights). This places it near the center of the configuration space, so every subsequent experiment—varying RNA encoder (scvi/scgpt), image encoder (ViT-L), aggregation (transformer), fusion (weighted), profile setting (singleprofile), or modality (rna_only/image_only)—constitutes a clean single-variable comparison against this baseline. Starting with the simplest reasonable multimodal pipeline also lets us determine whether the basic architecture is functional before investing budget in more complex encoders or fusion strategies, maximizing the information gained per experiment under the limited budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_004: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat → 61.9% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality actually contributes meaningful signal over RNA alone. config_029 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is the cleanest single-variable comparison to config_004: the RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation are all identical; only the image modality is removed. If RNA alone achieves comparable accuracy, it would collapse the search space by eliminating the need to optimize image encoders, fusion strategies, and cross-modal aggregation—saving many experiments. If RNA alone is substantially worse, it confirms multimodal fusion is essential and justifies investing subsequent experiments in encoder and fusion choices. Establishing this modality-level baseline before exploring encoder variants (scvi, scgpt, ViT-L) or fusion strategies (weighted, transformer) is the highest-information use of the next budget slot.

We have a multimodal baseline (config_004: pca_n2000+resnet50+avgpool+concat, acc=0.619) and an RNA-only baseline (config_029: pca_n2000+avgpool, acc=0.591), showing a ~2.8% accuracy gain from adding image. However, we lack an image-only baseline to decompose the contribution of each modality. config_039 (image_only, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool) is the cleanest complement: it shares the same image encoder (resnet50), profile setting (multiprofile), and aggregation (avgpool) as the two completed experiments. This lets us isolate whether the image modality contributes independently or whether the multimodal gain is synergistic. Understanding this is critical before investing further experiments in more complex multimodal variants (different encoders, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion), as it tells us whether the image signal is a meaningful additive component or a minor correction. Under a limited budget, completing the modality decomposition (RNA-only, image-only, multimodal) with matched hyperparameters is the highest-information next step.

Evidence: config_004 (multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieves 0.6186 acc, while config_029 (RNA-only, same pca_n2000) achieves 0.5907 and config_039 (image-only, resnet50) only 0.3275. RNA is clearly the dominant signal, and the multimodal gain over RNA-alone is modest (+2.8%). This suggests the RNA representation may be the bottleneck. Question: Does replacing the simple PCA encoder (pca_n2000) with a learned variational autoencoder (scvi_n200) improve performance in the multimodal setting? config_007 changes only the RNA encoder relative to config_004, keeping image encoder (resnet50), aggregation (avgpool), fusion (concat), and profile setting (multiprofile) identical. This clean single-variable comparison isolates the effect of RNA representation quality. Why best next experiment: Since RNA drives most of the signal, improving its encoder is the highest-leverage design decision. A positive result would justify further investment in more complex RNA encoders (e.g., scgpt); a null result would indicate PCA is sufficient and redirect attention to fusion or image-encoder choices. Under a limited budget, this experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most impactful design axis.

Evidence: config_007 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat, multiprofile) is the current best at 0.6315 acc, and RNA is the dominant modality (0.5907) while image is weak (0.3275), suggesting asymmetric modality importance. Uncertainty: we have only tested concat fusion; it is unclear whether weighted fusion—letting the model learn per-modality importance—would better exploit this asymmetry or whether the simple concatenation is already sufficient. This experiment (config_005) changes only the fusion strategy from concat to weighted while holding the best-known settings (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, multiprofile) constant, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_007. It is the best use of the next budget slot because fusion is the core mechanism for combining modalities, the result will inform all future multimodal configurations, and a single-variable design avoids confounding with other untested dimensions (image encoder, aggregation, profile setting).

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is the best at 0.6776 acc, and we've established scvi_n200 > pca_n2000 and weighted > concat. However, the image modality alone is very weak (0.3275 with resnet50), so it's unclear whether the image contribution is bottlenecked by encoder capacity. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l improve the multimodal model while holding the best-known RNA encoder (scvi_n200), aggregation (avgpool), and fusion (weighted) fixed? This is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005. Why this is the best next experiment: it directly extends the current best configuration along the highest-uncertainty axis (image representation quality), and the result will tell us whether further investment in image-side design is worthwhile or whether the RNA signal dominates regardless of image encoder strength.

The current best config (config_021: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.7062 acc. We have strong evidence that weighted fusion and ViT-L image encoder are beneficial, but aggregation has only been tested as avgpool. With multiprofile, multiple cell profiles must be combined, and a transformer aggregation could capture inter-profile interactions that simple mean pooling discards. Config_049 changes only aggregation (avgpool→transformer) relative to config_021, cleanly isolating the effect of the aggregation mechanism while holding all other design choices at their empirically validated best values. This is the most informative exploitation step: if transformer aggregation improves performance, it identifies a new productive design axis; if not, it confirms avgpool sufficiency and redirects budget toward other unexplored dimensions (e.g., scgpt encoder or singleprofile).

Evidence: The current best (config_049: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted; acc=0.725) shows consistent gains from each design upgrade (scvi>pca, ViT>ResNet, weighted>concat, transformer>avgpool). However, the fusion effect was only validated with avgpool aggregation (config_005 vs config_007: +0.046). With transformer aggregation, the learned attention mechanism may already capture modality-level weighting, potentially making explicit weighted fusion redundant. Question: Does weighted fusion still provide a meaningful advantage over simple concat when paired with transformer aggregation? config_009 is identical to config_049 except fusion=concat, giving a clean single-variable A/B test. Why best next: It directly clarifies whether one of our key design choices (weighted fusion) is truly necessary or subsumed by the transformer, which affects both final architecture complexity and whether further fusion-level exploration is warranted. Under a limited budget, isolating this interaction at the top-performing configuration is more informative than jumping to an untested RNA encoder (scgpt) that would confound multiple variables.

The current best (config_049: scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) achieves 0.7250, and we have strong evidence that image encoder (ViT-L > ResNet50), aggregation (transformer > avgpool), and weighted fusion all contribute to performance. However, the RNA encoder choice remains underexplored at the top of the performance range: we've only tested pca_n2000 and scvi_n200, with a small gap (~1.3%) between them. config_043 (scgpt, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_049, isolating the effect of the scgpt RNA encoder in the context of the strongest image pipeline. If scgpt outperforms scvi_n200, it identifies a new promising representation axis to exploit; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 as the optimal RNA encoder and redirects budget toward other axes (e.g., profile setting or fusion refinement). This is the most informative next step because the RNA encoder is a fundamental representation choice, the comparison is controlled (only one variable changes), and the outcome directly determines whether further RNA-encoder exploration is warranted under the limited budget.

Evidence: All 9 completed experiments are multiprofile multimodal or single-modality baselines. The best config (config_049, scvi_n200 + vit_l + transformer + weighted) reaches 0.725, but the incremental gain from switching the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 in the multimodal setting was only +0.013 (config_004→config_007), which is small and could be confounded by the image signal. Meanwhile, the rna_only baseline with pca_n2000 (config_029) sits at 0.591. Question: config_015 (rna_only, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_029 (rna_only, pca_n2000, avgpool), isolating the RNA encoder effect without any image or fusion confounds. If scvi_n200 rna_only reaches ~0.68-0.70, the RNA encoder is the primary driver and further gains should target RNA representation; if it stays near 0.59, the image+aggregation pipeline is essential and we should prioritize image-side improvements. This is the highest-information experiment under budget because it decomposes the source of the 0.725 performance, directly guiding whether remaining experiments should focus on the RNA encoder, the image encoder/aggregation, or the profile setting.

With zero completed experiments, the most critical need is to establish a reliable performance reference point for multimodal fusion using well-understood, standard components. config_005 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion) tests the core hypothesis—whether combining RNA and image modalities is viable—while keeping the design simple: pca_n2000 is the most standard and interpretable RNA encoder, imagenet_vit_l is a strong pretrained image encoder, weighted fusion is interpretable (revealing relative modality contribution), and singleprofile with no aggregation eliminates two sources of complexity. If this baseline performs well, it gives a target to beat and confirms the multimodal pipeline; if it underperforms, the failure is likely in the basic fusion or modality contribution rather than in complex aggregation or multiprofile handling. This maximizes the information gained per experiment under a limited budget by reducing confounding variables and establishing a clean anchor for all subsequent comparisons.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_005: multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion → 53.2% acc / 51.6% F1). The most fundamental uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion actually adds value over a single modality, or whether the performance is driven primarily by one modality. Question: config_050 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is a clean ablation that removes the image modality while keeping the same RNA encoder and profile setting as config_005. This isolates the marginal contribution of the image branch. Why this is the best use of the next budget: If RNA-only with PCA performs comparably (~53%), we learn that the image modality is not adding value with this encoder and can redirect effort toward RNA encoder selection (scgpt, scvi) or profile settings. If it performs substantially worse, we confirm multimodal fusion is essential and should prioritize optimizing fusion strategy and image encoder. This single experiment partitions the remaining search space into very different strategic directions, making it the highest-information-gain choice under a limited budget.

Evidence: config_005 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, weighted) achieved 0.532 acc, while config_050 (rna_only, same RNA encoder/profile) achieved 0.485 acc, a ~4.7% gap. However, we cannot yet decompose whether this gain comes from the image modality alone or from the synergy of combining both modalities. Question: config_022 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) provides a clean three-way comparison (RNA-only vs. image-only vs. multimodal) with only the model_setting changed from config_005, isolating the contribution of the RNA branch. Why best next: This is the most fundamental uncertainty—whether multimodal fusion is actually adding value beyond the stronger single modality, or whether one modality dominates. The answer directly determines whether to invest remaining budget in fusion/aggregation design (if synergy exists) or in improving the single dominant modality (if one modality suffices). No other single experiment reduces as much downstream uncertainty under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_005 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, weighted) achieves 0.5318 acc, only modestly above RNA-alone (config_050, 0.4849), while image-alone (config_022) is very weak (0.2266). This indicates RNA is the dominant signal and the image modality contributes little with the current setup. The key uncertainty is whether the RNA representation itself can be improved: we have only tested a linear PCA encoder (pca_n2000) and do not know if a learned deep RNA encoder (scgpt) would capture richer cell-type structure. Question: config_015 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scgpt while keeping everything else identical to config_005 (singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l, no aggregation, weighted fusion), giving a clean single-variable comparison. Why this is the best next experiment: RNA drives most of the predictive signal, so improving its representation has the highest expected leverage on overall accuracy. If scgpt outperforms PCA, it validates learned RNA encoders and directs further exploration (e.g., scgpt + multiprofile); if it does not, we can rule out that axis and redirect budget toward fusion strategy or multiprofile aggregation. This isolates one critical design choice without confounding variables.

Evidence: config_005 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, weighted) is the best result at 0.5318 acc, outperforming RNA-only (0.4849) and image-only (0.2266), confirming that the image modality adds complementary value when fused with pca_n2000. However, the fusion method (weighted) has not been compared against an alternative. Question: config_040 is identical to config_005 except fusion is changed from weighted to concat, providing a clean single-variable A/B test of the fusion strategy. Why this is the best next experiment: understanding whether concat or weighted fusion is superior is a foundational design decision that will inform all subsequent multimodal experiments (multiprofile, different encoders, aggregation). A single-variable comparison isolates the fusion effect without confounding from profile setting, encoder choice, or aggregation changes, making the result maximally interpretable under a limited budget.

Evidence: The current best is config_040 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat) at 0.5353 acc. PCA (pca_n2000) clearly outperforms scgpt (~11 pt gap), and concat marginally beats weighted. The largest untested design axis is profile setting: all completed experiments use singleprofile with no aggregation, so we have no evidence on whether multiprofile + aggregation adds value. Question: config_010 extends config_040 by switching to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation while holding RNA encoder (pca_n2000), image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), and fusion (concat) constant. This isolates the effect of multiprofile + simple aggregation. Why this is the best next experiment: it directly tests the most impactful unexplored dimension (profile/aggregation) on top of our proven best configuration, uses the simplest aggregation (avgpool) to minimize confounding complexity, and avoids simultaneously changing multiple factors. If multiprofile+avgpool helps, it opens a productive exploitation path; if not, we gain confidence that singleprofile is sufficient, saving budget from further multiprofile variants.

The strongest signal so far is that multiprofile with avgpool aggregation (config_010, acc=0.629) dramatically outperforms the best singleprofile multimodal (config_040, acc=0.535), confirming that profile aggregation is a critical design axis. However, we only have one data point for multiprofile aggregation (avgpool). config_039 changes exactly one variable from config_010—replacing avgpool with transformer aggregation while keeping pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, and concat fusion fixed—so it cleanly isolates whether a more expressive aggregation strategy captures inter-profile interactions that simple averaging misses. This is the highest-information next step: if transformer wins, it justifies further investment in complex aggregation; if it ties or loses, it confirms avgpool is sufficient and we should pivot to other axes (e.g., image encoder or fusion) with confidence that aggregation is not the bottleneck. Under a limited budget, this single-variable comparison around the current best configuration maximizes learning per experiment.

Evidence: The current best is config_010 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat; acc 0.6287), which showed a large jump over singleprofile (~0.535) and outperformed transformer aggregation (0.599). However, in the multiprofile setting we have only tested concat fusion. In singleprofile, concat vs weighted was nearly identical (0.535 vs 0.532), but the multiprofile+avgpool pipeline produces richer, higher-dimensional representations where the fusion mechanism may interact differently. Question: config_026 (identical to config_010 but with weighted fusion) isolates the effect of fusion strategy in the multiprofile+avgpool regime. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a clean single-variable comparison against our current best, directly tests whether the fusion choice matters at the new performance level, and the answer will inform whether further multiprofile experiments should use concat or weighted. This is more informative than changing the image encoder (image alone was very weak at 0.23, so its contribution is likely secondary) or the RNA encoder (pca_n2000 already showed clear advantage over scgpt), and it avoids confounding multiple design choices simultaneously.

Evidence: With pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l in multiprofile, we have three of four cells in an aggregation×fusion factorial: avgpool+concat=0.6287 (config_010), transformer+concat=0.5988 (config_039), avgpool+weighted=0.6352 (config_026, current best). The missing cell is transformer+weighted (config_001). Question: Does the avgpool-over-transformer advantage (~3 pts) hold independently of fusion, and does the weighted-over-concat advantage (~0.7 pt) hold independently of aggregation? Completing this 2×2 factorial isolates the main effects and reveals any interaction, which is critical before committing further budget to either aggregation or fusion choices. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a single-variable change from the current best (config_026: avgpool→transformer), it is a single-variable change from config_039 (concat→weighted), and it directly tests whether the current best configuration is truly optimal within this encoder pair or whether transformer+weighted could close or reverse the gap. Under a limited budget, resolving this interaction before exploring new encoders (scvi_n200, resnet50) ensures we build subsequent experiments on a correctly understood baseline.

The current best (config_026: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.635) has been validated across profile setting, aggregation, and fusion choices, but the image encoder dimension remains entirely untested—every completed experiment used imagenet_vit_l. config_007 swaps only the image encoder to resnet50 while holding all other settings identical to config_026, giving a clean single-variable A/B comparison. This is the highest-value next experiment because: (1) image-only performance was very low (0.227), so it's unclear how much the specific image encoder matters in the multimodal context; (2) if resnet50 performs comparably, the image encoder choice is a low-priority design decision and we can focus budget on RNA encoder variants (e.g., scvi_n200); if it degrades significantly, we confirm imagenet_vit_l is essential and should not be swapped. This single experiment resolves a major source of uncertainty across the entire multimodal design space under the limited budget.

With no completed experiments, the most critical uncertainty is establishing a performance floor: how well can we do with the simplest viable model? config_026 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000, no image, no aggregation, no fusion) is the minimal baseline that isolates raw RNA signal quality. It uses PCA (fast, standard) and a single profile to avoid confounding from learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion. This single experiment gives a clean reference against which every subsequent design choice—image modality, learned RNA encoders (scvi/scgpt), multiprofile aggregation, and fusion strategy—can be measured. Starting here respects the principle of not assuming complexity helps, keeps the first experiment fast and interpretable, and maximizes the information gained per experiment by anchoring all future comparisons to a well-defined floor.

We have only one completed experiment (config_026: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), so evidence is extremely sparse. The most critical open question is whether adding image information provides any benefit over RNA alone, since this is the core hypothesis of the multimodal study and the answer determines whether ~60% of the configuration space is worth pursuing. Config_006 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat) is the minimal extension of config_026: it keeps the same RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and profile setting (singleprofile), adding only a pretrained image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) and the simplest fusion (concat). This isolates the effect of the image modality as cleanly as possible. If it substantially outperforms 48.5%, we know image is valuable and can invest further in image-encoder and fusion choices; if it does not, we can focus budget on RNA-side improvements (multiprofile, better RNA encoders) without wasting experiments on multimodal variants.

Evidence: config_006 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, ViT-L, concat) achieved 0.535 acc / 0.519 F1, a clear ~5-point gain over the RNA-only baseline (config_026, 0.485 acc). This confirms the image modality adds value, but all completed experiments used singleprofile. The multiprofile axis is entirely untested and represents a major structural design choice: whether pooling information across multiple profiles (with simple avgpool aggregation) can further improve representation. Question: Does multiprofile + avgpool aggregation, holding RNA encoder (pca_n2000), image encoder (ViT-L), and fusion (concat) constant, outperform the singleprofile baseline? Why this experiment: config_010 is the minimal, single-axis extension of the best-performing config_006, changing only the profile setting (and its necessary companion, a simple aggregation). It isolates the multiprofile effect without confounding with learned encoders, transformer aggregation, or alternative fusion. The answer will determine whether the large multiprofile design space (configs with transformer/avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion, etc.) is worth further budget, making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_010 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.629 acc, a large ~9.3% jump over config_006 (same but singleprofile, no aggregation). This identifies multiprofile + avgpool as the key driver. Uncertainty: we do not know whether the aggregation mechanism itself (avgpool vs. transformer) is a bottleneck or whether simple averaging already captures most of the multiprofile signal. Question tested: config_050 changes only aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding model setting, profile setting, RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion (concat) identical to config_010, isolating the effect of aggregation strategy. Why best next experiment: aggregation is the core mechanism by which multiprofile information is combined, and determining whether a learned (transformer) aggregation meaningfully outperforms simple averaging is a high-impact design decision that will guide whether further complexity (e.g., scgpt/scvi encoders, weighted fusion) is warranted or whether the simpler avgpool route is already near-optimal. This is a clean single-variable comparison, maximizing information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_010 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is our best result at 0.629 acc / 0.599 F1, clearly outperforming singleprofile (0.535) and transformer aggregation (0.599). However, we have only tested concat fusion and have no evidence about whether weighted fusion can better balance the two modalities. Question: config_002 changes exactly one variable—fusion from concat to weighted—while holding model setting, profile setting, RNA encoder, image encoder, and aggregation identical to config_010. This isolates the effect of the fusion strategy. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a clean single-variable comparison to our current best, directly tests an important and unexplored design axis (how modalities are combined), and the result will inform whether further fusion complexity is warranted or whether budget should shift to exploring alternative encoders (e.g., scvi_n200, scgpt) or image backbones.

Evidence: Our best configuration (config_002, acc=0.635) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, and all five completed experiments use PCA. We have no data on whether a learned RNA representation (scvi_n200) could improve performance, which is a major unexplored design axis. Question: config_036 is identical to config_002 in every parameter except RNA encoder (scvi_n200 vs pca_n2000), with all other settings held at their empirically best values (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted). This isolates the effect of the RNA representation. Why best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison against our current best, directly testing whether nonlinear learned embeddings capture biological signal that PCA misses. If scvi_n200 improves accuracy, it opens a promising exploitation direction; if not, we confirm PCA sufficiency and can redirect budget toward the image encoder or other axes with higher expected information gain.

Evidence: The largest single improvement in this search came from switching the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 (config_002→config_036: 0.635→0.706 acc), confirming that RNA representation is the most impactful design choice. However, scgpt has never been tested, leaving open the question of whether a generative pretrained encoder could outperform the variational scvi encoder. Question: config_042 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) is a clean single-variable comparison to our current best (config_036), isolating the RNA encoder effect while holding image encoder, aggregation, fusion, and profile setting constant. Why this is the best next experiment: The RNA encoder dimension showed the largest effect size in our history, so resolving whether scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200 is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact question remaining. If scgpt is competitive, it opens a new promising direction; if scvi_n200 still wins, we confirm the best encoder and can confidently pivot to exploring image encoder or aggregation choices in subsequent experiments.

Evidence: config_036 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) is the current best at 0.706 acc, and scvi_n200 is clearly the dominant RNA encoder (0.706 vs 0.635 for pca_n2000 vs 0.542 for scgpt). However, every experiment to date has used imagenet_vit_l as the image encoder, leaving the image-encoder dimension completely unexplored. Question: config_023 changes only the image encoder (imagenet_vit_l → resnet50) while holding all other settings at their known-best values (scvi_n200, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile), cleanly isolating whether the choice of image encoder matters when paired with the best RNA encoder. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) it addresses a major source of uncertainty—zero data on resnet50 in any multimodal setting; (2) it is a single-variable change from the current best, making the result directly interpretable; (3) if resnet50 is competitive, it broadens the design space and may reveal that the image encoder is less critical than the RNA encoder; if it is substantially worse, it confirms imagenet_vit_l as the right choice and lets us focus remaining budget on aggregation/fusion refinements around config_036.

The current best (config_036: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.706. From the pca_n2000 experiments, aggregation choice showed a larger effect (~3 pts: avgpool 0.629 vs transformer 0.599) than fusion choice (~0.6 pts: weighted 0.635 vs concat 0.629). However, we have only tested transformer aggregation with pca_n2000, not with the superior scvi_n200 encoder. Config_035 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_036, isolating the aggregation effect under the best RNA encoder and image encoder. If transformer aggregation helps with scvi_n200's richer latent representations, it opens a new optimization direction; if not, it confirms avgpool as the correct aggregation and lets us focus remaining budget on other axes (e.g., image encoder or profile settings). This is the highest-information experiment because it tests the most impactful untested design choice at the current performance frontier.

Evidence: scvi_n200 + ViT-L is the strongest encoder combination so far (0.706 avgpool+weighted, 0.725 transformer+weighted). For PCA, weighted fusion marginally outperformed concat (0.635 vs 0.629), but this has not been confirmed for scvi. Uncertainty: we cannot yet decompose whether config_035's 0.725 advantage over config_036's 0.706 is driven by transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, or both. This experiment (config_051: scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) is a clean single-variable change from config_036 (only fusion changes from weighted to concat), directly isolating the fusion effect for the best-performing encoder. If concat is close to weighted, fusion is a minor design choice and the transformer gain is the key lever; if concat is substantially worse, weighted fusion is confirmed as a critical component of the top configuration. This is the most informative single experiment under budget because it resolves a fundamental design question (fusion type) that applies across all aggregation strategies and encoders, rather than testing a narrow interaction.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is no performance baseline at all. The most critical unknown is whether any multimodal or complex configuration actually outperforms a simple unimodal model. Without a floor, we cannot judge whether added complexity (second modality, transformer aggregation, learned encoders) is justified. 2) What this tests: config_006 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is a minimal, standard RNA-only baseline using the simplest encoder (PCA), simplest aggregation (avgpool), and the more informative multiprofile setting. It establishes the performance floor for the primary modality in cellular profiling. 3) Why it is the best first use of budget: Starting with the simplest viable model minimizes training failure risk, gives a clean reference signal, and immediately frames every subsequent multimodal experiment as a test of 'does adding the image modality / a learned encoder / a different fusion strategy improve over this baseline?' This single number will inform whether to invest remaining budget in multimodal exploration or in refining unimodal representations, making it the highest-information-density first experiment.

With only one completed experiment (config_006: rna_only, pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool → 59.1% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether adding the image modality provides any benefit over RNA alone. Config_004 (multimodal, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is the minimal, direct extension of config_006: it keeps the RNA encoder (pca_n2000), profile setting (multiprofile), and aggregation (avgpool) identical, and only adds an image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) with a standard weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of the image modality. If config_004 substantially outperforms config_006, it confirms image adds signal and justifies further investment in multimodal designs; if it performs similarly or worse, it redirects the search toward RNA-encoder or aggregation improvements. Under a limited budget, resolving this foundational question before exploring encoder variants, fusion strategies, or profile settings is the highest-information next step.

Evidence: config_004 (multimodal, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted fusion) achieved acc=0.6352, a clear +4.5pp improvement over the rna-only baseline config_006 (acc=0.5907) with all other settings identical, confirming that image modality contributes. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the 'weighted' fusion strategy is optimal or whether a simpler 'concat' fusion would perform comparably or better. Question: config_011 changes only the fusion from 'weighted' to 'concat' while holding model_setting, profile_setting, RNA encoder, image encoder, and aggregation constant relative to config_004. This isolates the effect of fusion strategy. Why best next: it is a clean single-variable A/B comparison against the current best result, directly informs a fundamental design decision (how to combine modal representations), and the outcome—whether fusion strategy matters or is relatively insensitive—will guide whether subsequent budget is better spent on aggregation, encoder choice, or profile setting.

Evidence: Our best config (config_004, acc=0.635) uses pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted fusion, and we've confirmed multimodal > rna_only (~4.5% gain) and weighted > concat (~0.65% acc, ~1.9% F1 gain).
