However, we have only tested one image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) and one RNA encoder (pca_n2000), leaving major uncertainty about whether the specific image backbone is a critical design choice. Question: config_036 is a clean single-variable swap of the image encoder (imagenet_vit_l → resnet50) while holding all other settings identical to config_004 (pca_n2000, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile). This isolates the effect of image encoder architecture. Why best next: Under a tight budget, establishing whether the image encoder is a bottleneck (or not) is foundational—if resnet50 performs comparably, we know the image side is not the limiting factor and should pivot to RNA encoder or aggregation; if imagenet_vit_l is clearly superior, we confirm our choice and can confidently explore other dimensions. This is more informative than jumping to a multi-variable change (e.g., new RNA encoder + new aggregation) and directly extends our strongest evidence.

Evidence: All four completed experiments use avgpool aggregation, so the effect of aggregation is entirely unexplored. The current best (config_036: pca_n2000 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.639) gives a strong baseline. config_013 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding the best-performing RNA encoder (pca_n2000), image encoder (resnet50), fusion (weighted), and profile setting (multiprofile) constant. This isolates the aggregation effect cleanly. Question tested: Does transformer-based aggregation of multiprofile representations improve over simple average pooling? Why this is the best next experiment: Aggregation is a fundamental architectural choice that has zero coverage in the experiment history, and it is a high-leverage design decision—if transformer aggregation helps, it opens a new optimization axis; if it does not, we confirm avgpool sufficiency and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder or profile-setting variations. It is a single-variable change from the current best, maximizing information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best config (config_036: pca_n2000 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.639) shows that adding image modality to RNA helps (~5 pts over RNA-only), weighted fusion beats concat, avgpool beats transformer aggregation, and resnet50 marginally edges ViT-L. However, all experiments so far use pca_n2000 for RNA—a simple linear projection. The RNA encoder is the largest untested design axis. Question: Does a learned nonlinear RNA representation (scvi_n200) improve upon PCA when all other components are held at their empirically best settings? config_038 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 relative to config_036, cleanly isolating the representation effect. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a single-variable comparison against our strongest baseline, directly tests whether the RNA bottleneck is representation quality (linear vs. learned), and the answer will determine whether to invest remaining budget in more complex RNA encoders (scgpt) or instead explore the profile-setting axis. If scvi_n200 matches or beats PCA, it validates learned representations and motivates testing scgpt; if it underperforms, PCA suffices and we should pivot to profile setting or image-encoder refinements.

Evidence: The largest performance jump so far came from switching the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 (config_036: 0.6390 → config_038: 0.6776, with resnet50/avgpool/weighted). Meanwhile, pca_n2000 shows near-parity between imagenet_vit_l (0.6352) and resnet50 (0.6390). Question: Does the scvi_n200 improvement generalize to imagenet_vit_l, or is it specific to the resnet50 pairing? Testing config_001 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) completes a clean 2×2 factorial over {pca_n2000, scvi_n200} × {resnet50, imagenet_vit_l} with all other factors held constant, isolating the RNA-encoder and image-encoder main effects and their interaction. Why best next: It is a single-variable change from the current best (config_038), directly extends the strongest evidence, and the resulting 2×2 will clarify whether to invest further in scvi_n200 broadly or only in specific pairings—critical information before spending budget on aggregation/fusion variants.

Evidence: config_001 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is the clear best at 0.7062 acc. The only design choice with weak/ambiguous evidence is fusion: with pca_n2000, weighted (0.6352) beat concat (0.6287) by a narrow 0.65% margin (config_004 vs config_011). This small gap suggests the optimal fusion strategy may depend on the quality of the underlying representations. Question: Does concat fusion outperform or match weighted fusion when paired with the stronger scvi_n200 RNA encoder? config_042 changes only fusion (weighted→concat) from the best config, isolating this single variable. Why this is the best next experiment: It is the lowest-risk, highest-information exploitation step—either it improves on the current best (giving a new top config) or it confirms weighted fusion is robustly superior across encoder choices, closing out the fusion design question so future experiments can focus on other axes (e.g., scgpt, singleprofile, or image-only baselines).

Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (0.7062–0.7150 in multimodal vs. 0.6352–0.6390 for pca_n2000), and the current best config (042) pairs scvi_n200 with imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, and concat. However, we have no data on how well scvi_n200 performs as a standalone RNA-only model. config_006 shows pca_n2000 rna_only at 0.5907, but the jump from pca to scvi in the multimodal setting was ~4–7%, so the RNA-only ceiling with scvi is unknown. Question: config_048 (scvi_n200, rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable ablation against config_001 (same RNA encoder, aggregation, profile; only the image modality is removed). It directly quantifies the marginal contribution of the image modality when the RNA representation is strong. Why best next experiment: If scvi_n200 rna_only approaches ~0.68–0.70, the image adds little and further multimodal tuning has diminishing returns, redirecting budget toward RNA encoder improvements (e.g., scgpt) or profile settings. If it drops to ~0.60–0.63, the image modality is essential and we should continue exploiting the multimodal direction. Either way, this single experiment resolves a major architectural uncertainty that would otherwise cloud every subsequent comparison, making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: scvi_n200 consistently outperforms pca_n2000 across all tested settings (+0.04 to +0.07 acc), and the best configuration so far is config_042 (scvi_n200 + vit_l + avgpool + concat, 0.715 acc). However, scgpt has never been tested, leaving a major uncertainty about the RNA encoder landscape. Question: config_040 (scgpt + vit_l + avgpool + concat) is a clean A/B comparison against config_042, isolating the RNA encoder effect while holding image encoder, aggregation, and fusion at their best-known values. Why best next experiment: it tests the single most important unexplored design dimension (RNA encoder type) under the strongest known configuration. If scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, it opens a new promising direction; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 as the optimal RNA representation and redirects budget toward other axes (e.g., singleprofile, transformer aggregation). This is more informative than re-testing transformer aggregation (already shown to hurt in config_013 vs config_036) or image_only baselines (multimodal advantage is already well-established at +0.056 to +0.065 over rna_only).

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero evidence about which modality, encoder, or fusion strategy is effective. The most fundamental uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion adds value over a single-modality baseline at all. 2) What this tests: config_012 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest meaningful RNA-only baseline—PCA introduces no learned parameters, single-profile avoids aggregation confounds, and omitting the image modality isolates RNA signal. It establishes a clean performance floor. 3) Why best under limited budget: A fast, well-understood baseline with minimal training confounds is the highest-information first experiment. It calibrates expected accuracy/F1, tells us whether RNA alone is competitive, and provides the reference against which all subsequent multimodal experiments must be judged. Without this anchor, any multimodal result would be uninterpretable. It is also computationally cheap, preserving budget for later, more complex experiments.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_012: RNA-only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), so uncertainty is high across all design axes. The most fundamental question for a multimodal profiling study is whether adding the image modality provides any signal beyond RNA alone. Question: config_002 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat fusion, no aggregation) is the minimal-change extension of config_012—it keeps the same RNA encoder, same profile setting, and adds only a standard image encoder (ResNet50) with the simplest fusion (concat). This directly isolates the contribution of image information. Why this is the best next experiment: If multimodal outperforms the RNA-only baseline, it justifies further investment in image encoder choice, aggregation, and fusion. If it does not, it redirects the search toward RNA-side improvements (encoder, multiprofile). No other single experiment reduces uncertainty about this core design decision as cleanly, and it avoids changing multiple axes simultaneously.

Evidence: config_002 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc vs config_012 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) at 0.485 acc, suggesting ~4% gain from adding image. However, with only two data points we cannot tell whether the image modality is genuinely contributing or whether the multimodal architecture's added capacity is the source of improvement. Question: config_051 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50, no aggregation/fusion) is the clean image-only baseline that matches config_002 on image encoder and profile setting while removing RNA entirely. If image-only approaches 0.52, RNA adds little and we should focus on image representation; if it drops substantially below 0.48, multimodal fusion is genuinely synergistic and we should invest in better fusion/aggregation. Why this is best: it isolates the single most important design question—relative modality contribution—with a one-variable change from config_002, and the answer will redirect the entire remaining search toward the modality or fusion strategy that actually matters, making every subsequent experiment more targeted under the tight budget.

Evidence: config_002 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc, beating RNA-only (0.485) and image-only (0.208), confirming RNA is the dominant signal and that adding image via concat provides a modest but real boost. However, we have only tested one fusion method (concat) in the multimodal setting. Question: config_006 is identical to config_002 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, making this a clean single-variable A/B comparison that isolates the effect of the fusion mechanism. Why best next: Under a limited budget, the most informative experiment is one that changes exactly one design axis from the current best result. The fusion method is a fundamental architectural choice that will determine how we combine the (dominant) RNA and (weak) image streams; knowing whether weighted fusion helps or hurts relative to concat directly guides all subsequent multimodal experiments and prevents us from carrying a suboptimal fusion forward into more complex multiprofile/aggregation settings.

Evidence: All four completed experiments use pca_n2000 for RNA and singleprofile. RNA is clearly the dominant modality (0.485 vs 0.208 image-only), and multimodal concat adds ~4 pts over RNA-only. However, PCA is a purely linear, untrained dimensionality reduction, and we have zero evidence about whether a learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200, scgpt) could substantially improve the RNA representation. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether the RNA encoder choice is a high-leverage design decision or whether PCA already captures most of the useful signal. This experiment (config_032: multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_002 (same fusion, same image encoder, same profile setting; only RNA encoder changes from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200). If scvi_n200 substantially outperforms PCA, it tells us to invest in learned RNA representations going forward; if it performs similarly, PCA is sufficient and we should prioritize other axes (multiprofile, image encoder). Under a limited budget, isolating the RNA encoder effect on the dominant modality is the highest-information next step before committing to more complex multiprofile or fusion architectures.

Evidence: All five completed experiments use singleprofile; the multiprofile dimension is entirely unexplored. The best configuration so far is config_032 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat) at 0.536 acc, showing that scvi_n200 slightly outperforms pca_n2000 and concat slightly outperforms weighted fusion. Question: Does extending the best-known single-profile setup to multiprofile with transformer aggregation yield a meaningful gain, or does the added complexity fail to help? This directly tests whether multiple profiles carry complementary information that a transformer can exploit. Why best next experiment: The profile setting is the largest unexplored design axis and could have a larger impact than swapping the image encoder (which contributes only ~4% over RNA alone). Config_023 extends config_032 minimally—keeping the proven scvi_n200 encoder, resnet50 image encoder, and concat fusion—while introducing multiprofile with the most expressive aggregation (transformer). If it succeeds, it opens a productive direction; if it fails, we learn that multiprofile does not help under current settings and can redirect budget toward image-encoder or RNA-encoder variants. This is the highest-information experiment available under the constraint that multiprofile necessarily requires an aggregation choice.

The largest performance jump in the study is config_023 (multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat → 0.688) vs config_032 (singleprofile, same encoders, no aggregation, concat → 0.536), a ~15-point gain. However, two variables changed simultaneously: profile setting (single→multi) and aggregation (None→transformer). Since transformer aggregation is only applicable to multiprofile, the key uncertainty is whether the gain comes from having multiple profiles per se or from the transformer's ability to model inter-profile interactions. config_041 (multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is a clean single-variable ablation: it keeps multiprofile and concat fusion identical to config_023 but replaces transformer with a simpler avgpool aggregation. If avgpool performs comparably, the multiprofile signal itself is sufficient and we can avoid transformer cost; if it drops substantially, transformer aggregation is specifically critical for combining profiles. This directly informs whether to invest further in transformer-based architectures or simpler aggregation schemes, making it the highest-information-use experiment under the limited budget.

The current best result is config_023 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) at 0.688 acc, showing that multiprofile + transformer aggregation is the dominant performance driver. In singleprofile, concat and weighted fusion were nearly identical (0.527 vs 0.523), but that comparison was made without multiprofile + transformer aggregation, where the interaction dynamics between modalities may differ. Config_015 is a single-variable change (concat → weighted) from the current best, making it a clean A/B test of the fusion mechanism in the strongest known setup. If weighted fusion helps, it provides a free improvement to the best configuration; if not, it confirms concat is sufficient and redirects the next experiment toward RNA encoder (scgpt) or image encoder (ViT) as the next lever. Under a limited budget, this is the lowest-risk, highest-clarity experiment to either exploit the current best or rule out a design choice before moving to larger architectural changes.

The current best configuration (config_015: scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, transformer, weighted; acc=0.713) establishes that multiprofile + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion is the dominant architecture. However, the RNA encoder has only been tested as scvi_n200 in this best setting. Since RNA is the dominant signal (RNA-only 0.485 vs image-only 0.208), the choice of RNA representation is the most consequential remaining design decision. Config_024 swaps only the RNA encoder to scgpt while holding all other factors at their best-known values (multiprofile, resnet50, transformer, weighted), giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_015. This directly tests whether a pretrained generative RNA model (scgpt) provides a richer representation than the variational autoencoder (scvi_n200) in the multiprofile regime. If scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, it opens a new direction; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 as the preferred encoder and can redirect exploration toward the image encoder or other factors. Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information, most actionable next step.

Evidence: The best-performing configuration is config_015 (multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) at 0.7131 acc. All high-performing runs use resnet50 as the image encoder, yet image-only performance is very low (0.2079), suggesting the image modality's contribution may be underutilized. The image encoder is the one major design axis not yet varied in the multiprofile multimodal regime. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (a stronger, larger pretrained backbone) improve the best-known configuration? Why this is the best next experiment: config_001 changes exactly one variable (image_encoder) from the current best (config_015), keeping scvi_n200, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, and multiprofile fixed. This cleanly isolates the image encoder effect. If it improves performance, it identifies the image modality as a bottleneck worth further investment; if it does not, it confirms the current image encoder is sufficient and redirects attention to other axes (e.g., RNA encoder or aggregation). This is a high-value exploitation step that tests a logically motivated extension of the strongest evidence without conflating multiple changes.

With no completed experiments, the primary uncertainty is whether a standard multimodal pipeline yields reasonable performance and establishes a useful reference point. config_001 tests a well-motivated multimodal baseline: PCA (n=2000) for RNA, ResNet50 for image, avgpool aggregation, and weighted fusion across multiprofiles. All components are standard and well-established, so the result will be interpretable: if performance is strong, it validates the multimodal hypothesis and gives a ceiling for ablation studies; if weak, it flags which component (encoder, fusion, or profile strategy) is underperforming. Choosing a mid-complexity standard configuration (rather than the simplest unimodal baseline or the most complex transformer/scgpt variant) maximizes information per experiment: it simultaneously provides a multimodal reference, a multiprofile reference, and a weighted-fusion reference, enabling efficient follow-up ablations along any single axis.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted → 63.9% acc), evidence is extremely sparse and the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality and fusion mechanism are actually contributing beyond the RNA signal. Config_003 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is a clean ablation of config_001 that changes only the model setting (removing the image branch and fusion) while keeping the same RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation. If config_003 performs comparably to config_001, the image modality adds little value under these encoders and we should focus budget on RNA representation choices; if it performs substantially worse, the image is contributing meaningfully and we should explore image encoder and fusion variations. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the core multimodal design decision before committing further budget to more complex multimodal variants.

Evidence: config_001 (multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.639 acc, while config_003 (rna_only, same RNA settings) achieves only 0.591 acc, confirming that the image modality contributes ~4.8% accuracy. However, we have only tested one image encoder (resnet50) and do not know whether a stronger image representation (imagenet_vit_l) would further improve performance. Question: config_006 changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l while holding all other settings (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted, multimodal) identical to config_001, cleanly isolating the effect of image representation quality. Why best next: With only two experiments done, the most critical uncertainty is whether the image branch is underutilized. Resolving whether a larger, transformer-based image encoder helps (or hurts) directly informs whether to invest further in image-side complexity (aggregation, fusion) in subsequent experiments, making this the highest-information single-variable test under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_001 (pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) achieved 0.639 acc, and config_003 (same but rna_only) achieved 0.591 acc, confirming that adding image modality helps (~+5%). config_006 shows resnet50 and imagenet_vit_l are roughly equivalent with pca_n2000. The largest remaining uncertainty is the RNA encoder: we have only tested pca_n2000 (linear, 2000-dim), while scvi_n200 (learned nonlinear, 200-dim) and scgpt (pre-trained generative) are untested. Question: config_025 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) changes ONLY the RNA encoder relative to config_001, cleanly isolating the effect of a learned nonlinear representation vs. PCA while holding image encoder, aggregation, fusion, and profile setting constant. Why this is the best next experiment: the RNA encoder is the most fundamental representation choice and appears across the majority of remaining configurations; knowing whether scvi_n200 outperforms or underperforms pca_n2000 will guide many subsequent decisions about which encoder family to pursue, and the single-variable design maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

All four completed experiments use avgpool aggregation, leaving the aggregation strategy entirely unexplored. The current best (config_025: scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.6776) establishes a strong baseline, and config_014 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding every other setting identical. This isolates whether a learned, attention-based aggregation of multiple profiles captures interactions that simple averaging misses. Given that the RNA encoder choice (scvi vs pca) produced the largest single gain (~4%), the aggregation mechanism is the next most impactful untested dimension in the multiprofile pipeline. The result is informative either way: improvement confirms transformer aggregation is worth pursuing, while a null or negative result confirms avgpool sufficiency and redirects the budget toward fusion strategy or image encoder choice.

The current best (config_014: scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted; acc=0.713) shows that both the RNA encoder (scvi_n200 over pca_n2000, +3.9%) and aggregation (transformer over avgpool, +3.5%) are critical. However, the image encoder effect has only been tested with pca_n2000, where resnet50 and imagenet_vit_l were nearly identical (0.639 vs 0.635). With scvi_n200's richer learned representations, the image encoder may interact differently. Config_024 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is a clean single-variable change from config_014, isolating the image encoder effect in the context of the best RNA encoder and aggregation. This is the highest-information next step: if imagenet_vit_l improves performance, it identifies a new promising axis; if it is neutral or worse, it confirms resnet50 is sufficient and redirects effort toward fusion or profile settings.

Evidence: Our current best (config_024: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted; acc=0.725) was reached by sequentially improving RNA encoder (pca→scvi), aggregation (avgpool→transformer), and image encoder (resnet50→vit_l), all with 'weighted' fusion. We have zero data on whether 'concat' fusion could outperform 'weighted' in this strong-backbone regime. Question: config_002 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) differs from config_024 in exactly one variable—fusion method—making it a clean A/B test that isolates the fusion contribution. Why this is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information single-variable change available. If concat matches or beats weighted, we immediately identify a new best or confirm equivalence; if it underperforms, we lock in 'weighted' as the correct choice and can confidently move to exploring scgpt or other dimensions. It exploits our strongest evidence (the proven backbone) while resolving the one untested design axis within that regime, avoiding the risk of confounding multiple changes.

Evidence: The current best configuration (config_024: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1. We have strong evidence that scvi_n200 outperforms pca_n2000 (~4% gain) and that transformer aggregation outperforms avgpool (~3.5% gain), but we have zero evidence about scgpt as an RNA encoder. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 when paired with the best-known image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), aggregation (transformer), and fusion (weighted)? This is a clean single-variable swap (RNA encoder only) against config_024, isolating the representation choice. Why best next experiment: RNA encoder is the most impactful design axis identified so far, and scgpt is a fundamentally different learned representation (generative vs. variational) that could capture complementary biological structure. Testing it at the current best settings tells us whether to invest further in the scgpt family or commit to scvi_n200, reducing uncertainty on a high-leverage decision with one experiment.

Evidence: Our best results (config_014: 0.713, config_024: 0.725) all use scvi_n200 + transformer aggregation in a multimodal setting. The earlier pca-based comparison (config_001 vs config_003) suggested multimodal helps by ~5pp, but we have no direct test of whether the image modality contributes when using the much stronger scvi_n200 encoder with transformer aggregation. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether the image branch adds meaningful signal beyond what scvi_n200 + transformer already captures from the RNA profiles, or whether the apparent multimodal gain was an artifact of the weaker pca encoder. This experiment (config_019: rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) directly compares to config_014 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) by removing only the image modality and fusion, keeping RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation identical. If rna_only performs within ~1pp of the multimodal configs, the image branch is not worth its complexity and future effort should focus on RNA-side improvements; if it drops substantially, the image modality is confirmed as a key contributor and we should prioritize optimizing the image encoder and fusion. This is the highest-information experiment under budget because the answer fundamentally redirects the remaining search.

Evidence: The strongest results (0.713–0.725) all use scvi_n200 + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion, and the gap between avgpool and transformer is clear for resnet50 (0.678 vs 0.713). However, we lack the imagenet_vit_l + avgpool data point, leaving the 2×2 grid of {image encoder} × {aggregation} incomplete. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether the large aggregation benefit (≈0.035) is specific to resnet50 or generalizes to imagenet_vit_l, and whether the modest image-encoder advantage (0.725 vs 0.713) persists under avgpool. This experiment (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) changes only aggregation from the current best (config_024), isolating the aggregation effect for the stronger image encoder. If config_018 lands near 0.72, aggregation matters less than currently assumed and the image encoder is the dominant factor; if it drops near 0.67, aggregation is confirmed as the critical design choice across encoders. This single-variable comparison is the most information-efficient next step under a tight budget, as it completes a key factorial and directly informs whether further effort should target aggregation or image-encoder selection.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about how well any modality or configuration performs. The most critical unknown is the performance floor: how well does the simplest single-modality model (RNA alone, single profile) do? Without this baseline, we cannot determine whether adding image data, multiple profiles, or more complex fusion strategies actually improves performance. 2) What this tests: config_002 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) establishes the simplest reasonable RNA-only baseline using the most common RNA encoder in the search space. It isolates the contribution of the RNA modality with minimal confounding complexity (no image, no aggregation, no fusion). 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the single most informative measurement is the reference point against which all other design choices (adding image, switching to multiprofile, changing encoder, adding fusion) will be judged. A simple, interpretable baseline also guards against the assumption that multimodal or multiprofile models are inherently better. Every subsequent multimodal or multiprofile result can be directly compared to this number to quantify the marginal value of each added complexity dimension.

With only one completed experiment (config_002: rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200 → 52.0% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether image information carries useful signal at all. Without an image-only baseline, any future multimodal result cannot be attributed to fusion benefit vs. mere addition of a second modality. config_041 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) directly complements the existing rna_only baseline by matching the profile setting (singleprofile) and using the strongest available image encoder, cleanly isolating the modality effect. This is the highest-information experiment under the current sparse evidence: if image accuracy is low, multimodal gains will likely be modest and RNA-centric; if it is competitive, fusion strategy and encoder choice become the key levers to explore next.

Evidence: We have only two completed experiments. config_002 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) achieved 52.0% accuracy, while config_041 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) achieved only 22.7%, indicating RNA is the dominant modality and image is very weak in this setup. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether the scvi_n200 learned latent representation is actually superior to a simpler linear projection (PCA) for this task. Question tested: config_010 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) differs from config_002 in exactly one variable—the RNA encoder—so it cleanly isolates the effect of learned vs. linear representation while holding model setting, profile setting, and all other hyperparameters constant. Why this is the best next experiment: With a limited budget and only two data points, establishing whether the more complex scvi encoder provides a real advantage over PCA is a foundational question. If PCA matches or exceeds scvi, it simplifies the design space and suggests the bottleneck is elsewhere (e.g., profile setting or fusion). If scvi is clearly better, it validates investing in learned representations for subsequent multimodal experiments. Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty before committing experiments to multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 (config_002) achieves 0.520 acc, while image-only with ViT-L (config_041) is very weak at 0.227 acc. We have no multimodal results yet, so the central uncertainty is whether adding the image modality to the strong RNA signal provides complementary information or merely adds noise. Question: config_005 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, concat fusion, no aggregation) is the simplest possible multimodal combination using the best-performing RNA encoder. It isolates the core question—does any fusion of image into RNA help—without confounding from multiprofile, aggregation, or more complex fusion. Why this is the best next experiment: if concat fusion fails to beat 0.520, we gain strong evidence that the image modality (as currently encoded) is not informative and can deprioritize the large multimodal configuration space, saving budget. If it does beat 0.520, we confirm a promising direction and can then systematically explore fusion type, aggregation, and multiprofile. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the highest-level design decision (multimodal vs. unimodal) before committing to more complex variants.

Evidence: config_005 (multimodal, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat) is the best result so far at 0.532 acc, only marginally above RNA-only scvi (0.520). The image modality contributes a small but consistent boost, and we have only tested one fusion strategy (concat). Uncertainty: it is unknown whether a learned weighted fusion would better balance the dominant RNA signal against the weak image signal (image-only is only 0.227), or whether simple concatenation is already near-optimal. This experiment (config_046) changes only the fusion from concat to weighted while holding RNA encoder (scvi_n200), image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), and profile setting (singleprofile) fixed, giving a clean A/B comparison against config_005. It is the best next step because the fusion strategy is a foundational architectural choice that will condition all subsequent multimodal experiments; resolving it early prevents wasting budget on multiprofile/aggregation variants built on a suboptimal fusion, and the single-variable design maximizes interpretability under the limited budget.

Evidence: All five completed experiments use singleprofile; the best result (config_046, acc=0.537, F1=0.518) uses multimodal with scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l and weighted fusion. RNA dominates (0.520 vs 0.227 for image-only), scvi_n200 beats pca_n2000 by ~3.5 pp, and weighted fusion slightly edges concat. Uncertainty: The profile setting (single vs. multiprofile) and aggregation strategy are completely unexplored—no experiment has tested whether multiple profiles plus an aggregation step can improve on the best single-profile result. Question: Does adding multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool) to our best encoder/fusion combination yield a meaningful gain over config_046? Why this is the best next experiment: config_033 changes exactly one design axis (singleprofile→multiprofile + avgpool) while holding the proven best encoders (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l) and fusion (weighted) constant, giving a clean, interpretable comparison against config_046. If it helps, we can then explore transformer aggregation; if it does not, we efficiently rule out a large sub-space of multiprofile configurations and focus remaining budget on other axes (e.g., scgpt encoder, resnet50 image encoder).

Evidence: config_033 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) achieved 0.706 acc / 0.667 F1, a dramatic ~17-point jump over the best singleprofile multimodal result (config_046, 0.537). This identifies multiprofile as the dominant design lever. The aggregation method (avgpool) is the one untested variable within this otherwise proven recipe. Question: config_001 is identical to config_033 except aggregation changes from avgpool to transformer, isolating the effect of a more expressive cross-profile aggregation. Why best next experiment: it is a clean single-variable exploitation of the strongest evidence in the search. If transformer outperforms avgpool, we immediately gain a better configuration; if not, we confirm avgpool is sufficient and can redirect budget to other axes (e.g., RNA encoder or image encoder) without ambiguity. No other available config isolates this question as cleanly.

The largest performance jump in the history is from singleprofile to multiprofile (0.537 → 0.725 with scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted). The critical uncertainty is whether this multiprofile gain is driven primarily by the RNA modality, the image modality, or their interaction. config_019 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) is a clean single-variable ablation of config_001: it removes only the image modality while keeping the RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation identical. If config_019 approaches ~0.70, the image contributes little and future effort should focus on RNA encoder/aggregation; if it drops substantially (e.g., to ~0.55–0.60), the image modality is a meaningful contributor in the multiprofile setting and image encoder selection becomes a priority. This is the highest-information experiment under the limited budget because it directly partitions the multiprofile gain between the two modalities and will determine where to invest remaining experiments.

The best configuration so far is config_001 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted; acc=0.725). The dominant signal is clearly RNA (rna_only multiprofile=0.653 vs image_only≈0.227), yet we have only tested scvi_n200 and pca_n2000 as RNA encoders; scgpt remains untested. Config_034 changes exactly one variable from the best config (RNA encoder: scvi_n200→scgpt) while holding the multiprofile + transformer + weighted + imagenet_vit_l regime fixed. This isolates the effect of RNA representation quality in the highest-performing setting. If scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, it broadens our design space; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 is the right encoder and redirects budget toward image-encoder or fusion variations. Under a limited budget, testing the most impactful untested component (RNA encoder) in the proven best regime is the highest-information single experiment.

The current best (config_001: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.725 acc. In single-profile, weighted vs concat fusion made almost no difference (0.537 vs 0.532), but that regime is far from the multiprofile performance ceiling. Config_032 is identical to config_001 except fusion=concat, giving a clean single-variable test of whether fusion strategy matters in the high-performing multiprofile+transformer regime. If concat matches weighted, fusion can be treated as a non-critical design dimension, freeing budget to explore image encoder (resnet50) or RNA encoder (pca_n2000) variations. If concat is notably worse, it confirms weighted fusion is a meaningful lever worth preserving. This is the most informative next step because it directly extends the strongest evidence with the minimal possible change, reducing uncertainty about a core design axis before committing further experiments to other dimensions.

With no completed experiments, there is no evidence to exploit, so the priority is establishing a clean reference point that maximizes the information value of subsequent ablations. config_003 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, no aggregation, concat) is the simplest multimodal configuration using the most common encoders (scgpt for RNA, ViT-L for image) and the simplest fusion (concat). It directly tests the study's primary hypothesis—whether combining RNA and image modalities improves validation accuracy—while keeping the design space minimal (single profile, no aggregation) so that any performance can be cleanly attributed. The natural follow-up experiment (config_004, rna_only singleprofile scgpt) would then isolate the image contribution with a single-variable comparison. Starting here gives the highest-leverage baseline from which to build a structured ablation ladder across profile setting, encoder choice, aggregation, and fusion strategy under the limited budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_003: multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, concat → acc 0.435), the single most important uncertainty is whether the image modality actually contributes meaningful signal or whether a simpler RNA-only model is competitive. config_004 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt, no aggregation, no fusion) is a clean single-variable ablation of config_003: the only difference is the removal of the image encoder and concat fusion, while keeping the same RNA encoder (scgpt), profile setting (singleprofile), and no aggregation. If config_004 matches or exceeds config_003, the image modality is not adding value and the search should pivot toward RNA-encoder and profile-setting choices. If config_003 is clearly better, multimodal fusion is justified and we can invest subsequent experiments in optimizing encoder choices, aggregation, and fusion strategy. This is the highest-information experiment under a tight budget because the answer reshapes the entire remaining search direction, and it changes exactly one design axis relative to the only data point we have.

Evidence: config_003 (multimodal, scgpt+imagenet_vit_l, singleprofile, concat) achieved 0.4348 acc / 0.4234 F1, while config_004 (rna_only, scgpt, singleprofile) achieved 0.4106 acc / 0.3785 F1 — a ~2.4% accuracy and ~4.5% F1 gap. This is suggestive but based on a single pair, so it is unclear whether the image modality is a strong independent signal or whether the small gain is noise/complementarity. Question: config_025 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is the clean ablation that isolates the image modality's standalone contribution while holding the image encoder and profile setting identical to config_003. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It directly tests whether the 2.4% multimodal lift is driven by a genuinely informative image channel or by a weak/noisy addition. (2) The result will sharply guide all subsequent experiments — if image_only is weak, the multimodal benefit is complementary and we should prioritize fusion/aggregation design; if image_only is competitive, we should invest in stronger image encoders or multiprofile image aggregation. (3) It changes only the model setting (multimodal→image_only) relative to config_003, satisfying the principle of isolating one design variable. (4) Under a tight budget, resolving this fundamental question about modality value is more informative than, e.g., swapping fusion to weighted (config_031) or changing the image backbone (config_015), which are secondary refinements that depend on knowing whether the image signal is worth optimizing.

Evidence: config_003 (multimodal, scgpt+imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieves 0.4348 acc, only marginally above RNA-only config_004 (0.4106), while image-only config_025 is very weak (0.2266). This small multimodal gain raises the question of whether the image signal is genuinely useful but poorly integrated, or simply uninformative. Question: config_031 changes only the fusion strategy (concat → weighted) while holding all other settings identical to config_003 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, no aggregation). This isolates the effect of fusion on multimodal performance. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a single-variable comparison that directly tests whether a learned weighting can extract more value from the image modality. If weighted fusion improves over concat, it confirms the image carries useful signal and justifies further investment in multimodal configurations (aggregation, multiprofile, alternative encoders). If it does not, it strongly suggests the image modality with imagenet_vit_l is not contributing meaningfully, redirecting the remaining budget toward RNA encoder or profile-setting improvements. Under a limited budget, resolving this uncertainty about whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing is the highest-value information gain.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_003 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, concat) at 0.4348 acc, with RNA clearly dominant (rna_only 0.4106 vs image_only 0.2266) and concat slightly beating weighted fusion. The profile/aggregation axis is completely untested. Question: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation improve performance while keeping the same encoders (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l) and the same fusion (concat)? Why this is the best next step: config_009 is the most direct, minimal extension of the current best config—only profile_setting and aggregation change, isolating the effect of multiprofile + aggregation. Using avgpool (rather than transformer) is a conservative first probe of this axis; if it helps, a follow-up with transformer aggregation becomes a clean comparison. This is more informative than jumping to a new encoder or a more complex aggregation, as it reduces uncertainty about whether the profile dimension matters at all before investing in more complex variants.

The strongest evidence so far is that multiprofile + avgpool aggregation (config_009, acc=0.5176) substantially outperforms the singleprofile baseline (config_003, acc=0.4348), an ~8-point gain attributable to profile aggregation. The key open question is whether the aggregation method itself matters: does a learned transformer aggregation capture inter-profile interactions that a simple average pool misses, or is avgpool already near-optimal? config_001 changes only the aggregation (avgpool→transformer) relative to config_009, keeping scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, and concat fusion fixed, making it a clean single-variable test. This is preferred over testing fusion method (e.g., config_016) because aggregation is the more fundamental design axis in the multiprofile setting, and the expected performance delta is larger. A positive result would justify further investment in learned aggregation; a null or negative result would confirm that simple pooling suffices and redirect effort toward other axes (e.g., RNA encoder choice or image encoder). Under a tight budget, resolving this uncertainty about the most impactful multiprofile design choice is the highest-value next experiment.

Evidence: Multiprofile with avgpool+concat (config_009, acc=0.5176) substantially outperforms singleprofile multimodal (config_003, acc=0.4348), and in singleprofile the image-only model is very weak (0.2266) while RNA-only is moderate (0.4106). This suggests RNA is the dominant modality, but we have no multiprofile RNA-only baseline. Question: config_018 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is the direct ablation of config_009 with the image modality removed, isolating how much of the multiprofile gain is driven by RNA profile aggregation versus the image contribution. Why best next: If RNA multiprofile alone approaches ~0.50, the image modality adds little and we should focus budget on RNA encoder/aggregation variants; if it drops substantially (e.g., <0.45), the image is essential in the multiprofile regime and we should prioritize image encoder and fusion choices. This single-variable ablation maximally reduces uncertainty about the most important architectural question before committing further experiments.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_018 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) at 0.5305 acc / 0.5152 F1, which surprisingly outperforms the best multimodal setup (config_009, 0.5176). This suggests the RNA representation is the dominant signal, yet we have only tested one RNA encoder (scgpt). Uncertainty: We have zero evidence on whether scvi_n200 or pca_n2000 would improve upon scgpt in the multiprofile setting. This experiment tests the RNA encoder choice in isolation (only rna_encoder changes from config_018), keeping the best-known profile setting (multiprofile) and aggregation (avgpool) fixed. If scvi_n200 exceeds scgpt, it reveals a better representation and opens a new search direction; if it underperforms, it confirms scgpt as the preferred encoder and lets us redirect budget toward fusion or image-encoder questions. Under a limited budget, resolving the RNA encoder question is more informative than re-testing aggregation (which already has moderate evidence favoring avgpool) because the RNA encoder is the primary signal in the top-performing model and remains completely unexplored.

The strongest evidence so far is that scvi_n200 dramatically outperforms scgpt as an RNA encoder (config_006: 0.650 acc vs config_018: 0.530 acc, both rna_only/multiprofile/avgpool). The critical open question is whether adding the image modality provides any benefit on top of this already-dominant RNA representation. For scgpt, multimodal did not help in the multiprofile setting (config_009: 0.518 < config_018: 0.530), but scvi_n200 is a fundamentally different learned latent and the interaction is unknown. config_029 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is the minimal-change extension of config_006: it keeps the same RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation, and only adds the image branch with concat fusion (necessary for two modalities). This directly isolates the marginal contribution of image information given the best RNA encoder. If it matches or exceeds 0.650, image is additive; if it falls below, the scvi_n200 latent already captures what image would contribute, and future budget should focus on RNA-side improvements rather than multimodal fusion.

The current best is config_029 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat; acc 0.7150). The only untested dimension within this otherwise-optimal setting is aggregation method. With scgpt, avgpool (0.5176) narrowly beat transformer (0.5070), but scvi_n200 produces learned variational representations that may interact differently with attention-based aggregation. Config_014 changes only aggregation (avgpool→transformer) while holding encoder, image model, profile setting, and fusion constant, cleanly isolating this variable. If transformer helps, it opens a new optimization axis; if not, it confirms avgpool and redirects budget toward the image-encoder or fusion question. This is the highest-information single-variable test available for the current best configuration.

With no prior experiments, the most critical initial question is whether the basic multimodal pipeline (combining RNA and image features) is viable and what performance floor it establishes. config_001 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the simplest multimodal configuration: it uses standard, well-understood encoders (PCA for RNA, ResNet50 for image) and the most straightforward fusion (concatenation) with a single profile. This isolates the fundamental question of whether combining two modalities is informative at all, without confounding from learned encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or weighted fusion. Its result will serve as a reference point for every subsequent comparison: if it performs well, we can test whether better encoders (scgpt, scvi), multiprofile aggregation, or weighted fusion add value; if it underperforms, we can diagnose whether the bottleneck is the encoder choice, the fusion strategy, or the modality combination itself. As the first experiment, establishing this simple multimodal baseline maximizes the interpretability of all future comparisons and reduces the largest source of uncertainty—whether the multimodal design space is worth exploring in depth.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat → acc 0.527). The most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality actually contributes value over an RNA-only model. config_045 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000, no image, no fusion) is the cleanest possible ablation: it matches config_001 on RNA encoder (pca_n2000), profile setting (singleprofile), and removes only the image modality. This isolates the effect of multimodality with a single design change. If config_045 performs comparably to config_001, the image modality is not adding signal and we should redirect budget toward RNA encoder/aggregation choices. If config_045 is substantially worse, the image is valuable and we can confidently invest in multimodal fusion and encoder variations. Establishing this baseline before exploring fusion strategies, multiprofile aggregation, or alternative encoders is the highest-information-use experiment under a limited budget.

We have two data points: RNA-only (pca_n2000, singleprofile) at 0.4849 acc and multimodal (pca_n2000 + resnet50, concat, singleprofile) at 0.5266 acc. The ~4.2% gap suggests image information helps, but we cannot yet decompose whether the gain comes from the image signal itself, the fusion mechanism, or architectural complexity. config_026 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the exact image-only counterpart to config_045, completing the RNA-only / image-only / multimodal decomposition with all other settings held constant. If image-only is near 0.48, the multimodal gain is primarily from RNA; if near 0.53, image dominates; if in between, both modalities contribute additively. This decomposition is the single most important piece of missing evidence: it determines whether future budget should target better image encoders, better RNA encoders, better fusion strategies, or multiprofile aggregation. No other available configuration isolates this question as cleanly with a single variable change from an already-tested setting.

Evidence: config_001 (multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieves 0.5266 acc, while RNA-only with the same encoder (config_045) achieves 0.4849, and image-only (config_026) is very weak at 0.2079. This shows RNA is the dominant signal and the image adds a modest ~4% boost. The RNA encoder (pca_n2000) is a linear, unsupervised projection and may be a bottleneck. Question: Does replacing PCA with a learned encoder (scgpt) improve multimodal performance while holding all other factors (singleprofile, resnet50, concat fusion) constant? config_043 is a clean single-variable comparison against config_001, isolating the RNA representation effect. Rationale: Since RNA drives most of the predictive signal, improving its representation is the highest-leverage design choice to test next. A positive result would justify further exploration of learned encoders and multiprofile aggregation; a null result would indicate PCA is already near-optimal and redirect effort toward image encoder or fusion strategy. This is the most informative use of the next budget slot.

Evidence: RNA encoder choice showed the largest effect so far — pca_n2000 (config_001, acc=0.527) substantially outperformed scgpt (config_043, acc=0.427) in an otherwise identical multimodal/resnet50/concat/singleprofile setup. Image alone is weak (0.208), confirming RNA dominates. Uncertainty: we have not yet tested scvi_n200, the third available RNA encoder, so we cannot yet rank all encoder options or determine whether the pca_n2000 advantage is general or specific. This experiment (config_028: multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat) is a clean single-variable swap against config_001, isolating the RNA encoder effect. It is the best use of the next budget slot because resolving the RNA encoder question (pca vs scgpt vs scvi) is the highest-leverage design decision identified so far; the result will constrain or open up many downstream experiments involving multiprofile, alternative image encoders, and fusion strategies.

Evidence: Our best result so far is config_028 (scvi_n200, resnet50, concat, singleprofile) at 0.5362 acc. We know RNA dominates (0.4849 rna_only vs 0.2079 image_only), and the multimodal gain over RNA-only is modest (~4 pts for pca_n2000). We have only tested concat fusion across all multimodal runs, so the effect of fusion strategy is completely uncharacterized. Question: config_027 (scvi_n200, resnet50, weighted, singleprofile) changes only the fusion from concat to weighted relative to config_028, cleanly isolating the fusion effect. Why this is the best next experiment: Fusion is a fundamental design axis that will influence every future multimodal configuration. If weighted fusion outperforms concat, it suggests the weak image signal (0.2079 alone) benefits from learned down-weighting, and we should adopt weighted fusion going forward. If concat matches or exceeds weighted, we confirm simple concatenation is sufficient and can redirect budget toward testing the image encoder (ViT-L) or multiprofile aggregation. This single-variable comparison maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The best multimodal configs (scvi_n200 + resnet50) achieve ~0.54 accuracy, while rna_only with pca_n2000 is 0.485 and image_only is only 0.208. However, we lack a direct rna_only baseline using scvi_n200, the best-performing RNA encoder. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether the image modality is genuinely contributing to the multimodal performance or whether the gains come entirely from the scvi_n200 encoder. Question tested: config_011 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) provides a clean single-variable comparison against config_028 (multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat = 0.5362), isolating the marginal contribution of the image branch. Why best use of budget: This is a foundational question — if rna_only with scvi_n200 approaches 0.54, the image adds little and future effort should focus on RNA improvements (multiprofile, aggregation); if it lags significantly, the image is genuinely informative and we should invest in better image encoders (e.g., imagenet_vit_l). No other single experiment resolves this uncertainty as directly, and the answer will efficiently guide all subsequent experiments.

All seven completed experiments use singleprofile; the profile-setting dimension (single vs. multi) is entirely unexplored and is a major design axis. The best RNA encoder identified is scvi_n200 (rna_only singleprofile: 0.5203; multimodal singleprofile: 0.5362–0.5399). By testing config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool), I directly compare against config_011 (same encoder, singleprofile, 0.5203) while changing only the profile setting and adding the simplest aggregation (average pooling). This isolates whether multiple profiles with simple averaging add signal over a single profile, without confounding from image modality or fusion. If multiprofile+avgpool improves over 0.5203, it justifies further investment in transformer aggregation and multimodal multiprofile variants; if not, it saves budget by ruling out the profile dimension early. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice given that the profile axis is the largest source of remaining uncertainty.

The strongest result so far is config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) at 0.6501 acc, a massive jump over its singleprofile counterpart config_011 (0.5203). This establishes multiprofile + avgpool as the dominant design axis. The critical open question is whether avgpool is the optimal aggregation or whether a transformer-based aggregation can further improve multiprofile performance. config_013 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_002, isolating the aggregation mechanism while holding model setting, profile setting, and RNA encoder constant. The answer directly determines which aggregation to pair with any future multimodal multiprofile experiments, making it the highest-information experiment under the limited budget. If transformer outperforms avgpool, it signals a richer profile-level interaction model; if avgpool holds or wins, it confirms the simpler strategy and redirects exploration toward other variables (e.g., adding image, changing encoder).

The strongest finding so far is that multiprofile dramatically improves RNA-only performance (scvi_n200: 0.52 single-profile → 0.65 multiprofile, a +0.13 gain), while aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) and fusion choice (weighted vs concat) show only marginal differences. No multimodal multiprofile configuration has been tested yet, leaving a critical uncertainty: does the multiprofile benefit transfer when an image modality is also present? config_044 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) directly tests this by combining the best-known RNA encoder (scvi_n200), image encoder (resnet50), aggregation (transformer, marginally better than avgpool), and fusion (weighted, marginally better than concat) in the multiprofile multimodal setting. It can be cleanly compared against config_027 (same encoders and fusion, single-profile) to isolate the multiprofile effect in the multimodal context. This is the highest-value next experiment because the multiprofile gain is the largest effect observed, and confirming or refuting its transfer to multimodal will determine the dominant design direction for all subsequent experiments.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so we have no baseline for either modality. The central question in a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether combining modalities improves over the best single modality, but this cannot be assessed without knowing how well each modality performs alone. 2) What this tests: config_028 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the simplest possible image-only model—no aggregation, no fusion, a well-understood pretrained encoder. It establishes the performance floor for the image modality and confirms that the pipeline works end-to-end with minimal confounds. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, a clean unimodal baseline is the highest-information first step because (a) it is fast and has few failure modes, (b) it provides the reference needed to interpret every subsequent multimodal result (e.g., config_001, 009, 019), (c) it isolates the image encoder and single-profile setting so that later experiments can cleanly attribute gains to added modalities, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion strategy, and (d) if it already performs strongly, it immediately reshapes the search toward understanding whether RNA adds value rather than wasting budget on multimodal variants that may not help.

1) Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_028: image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) yielding ~20.8% accuracy. This establishes a baseline but tells us nothing about whether the RNA modality contributes any signal. 2) Question: config_009 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, resnet50, weighted) directly tests whether adding an RNA representation (scGPT) to the same image backbone (ResNet50) and same profile setting improves over the image-only baseline. It isolates the multimodal contribution while holding image encoder and profile setting constant. 3) Why best: With only one data point, the highest-uncertainty decision is whether RNA adds value at all. scGPT is a learned biological representation giving RNA its best chance to contribute; weighted fusion is the simplest combination strategy, so a positive result is informative and a negative result is strong. This single experiment tells us whether to invest remaining budget in multimodal exploration or refocus on image-only improvements (encoder choice, multiprofile aggregation).

The two completed experiments show image-only (resnet50, singleprofile) is very weak (acc 0.208) while multimodal with scgpt+resnet50 and weighted fusion jumps to 0.421. This large gap tells us RNA information is critical, but it does not decompose how much of the 0.421 comes from the RNA modality alone versus the image modality or their interaction. Config_038 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) is the cleanest next experiment: it removes the image branch from config_009 while keeping the same RNA encoder and profile setting, isolating the marginal contribution of the image modality. If RNA alone approaches ~0.40, the image adds little and future budget should target RNA encoder or profile improvements; if RNA alone is substantially lower (e.g., ~0.25–0.30), the multimodal fusion is genuinely valuable and we should next optimize fusion strategy and image encoder. Resolving this uncertainty before testing fusion variants (config_012) or image encoder upgrades (config_002) ensures we invest the remaining budget on the modality that actually drives performance, making this the highest-information experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA (scgpt, singleprofile) is the dominant signal (acc 0.411, F1 0.378), image alone is weak (0.208), and multimodal weighted fusion gives only a marginal gain over RNA alone (0.421 vs 0.411 acc; 0.412 vs 0.378 F1). The profile setting (single vs multi) is a completely unexplored dimension that could substantially shift the performance landscape. Question: Does switching from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation improve the RNA representation? This experiment (config_011: rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is a clean, single-variable comparison against config_038 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt, no aggregation), isolating the multiprofile+aggregation effect on the dominant modality. Why this is best under budget: If multiprofile helps RNA, it justifies investing further experiments in multiprofile multimodal configurations; if it does not, we can confidently restrict the search to singleprofile and focus remaining budget on RNA encoder choice or image encoder quality. Testing this in the RNA-only setting (rather than multimodal) avoids confounding the profile effect with fusion/aggregation interactions, giving the clearest signal about one of the largest unexplored design axes.

The strongest evidence so far is that multiprofile aggregation (avgpool) with scgpt boosts RNA-only accuracy from 0.411 (config_038) to 0.530 (config_011), a +0.119 gain. Meanwhile, multimodal singleprofile (config_009, 0.421) barely exceeds RNA singleprofile (0.411), suggesting resnet50 image adds little in the singleprofile regime. The critical open question is whether the multiprofile benefit transfers to the multimodal setting and whether image becomes more useful when RNA is better aggregated. config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is the minimal, single-variable extension: it adds multiprofile+avgpool to config_009 and adds resnet50+weighted to config_011, keeping all other choices (scgpt, resnet50, weighted) identical to prior runs. This cleanly isolates the interaction between multiprofile aggregation and image fusion, telling us whether to invest further in multimodal multiprofile or focus on RNA-side improvements. Under a tight budget, this one experiment resolves the most important design uncertainty.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_011 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) at 0.530 acc, and the multimodal multiprofile config_019 (same but +resnet50, weighted fusion) only reaches 0.525, suggesting the image adds little with avgpool aggregation. The dominant design question now is whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer vs. avgpool) can improve the multiprofile representation that drives most of the performance gain. Question: config_032 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, transformer) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_011, isolating the aggregation strategy. Why this is best: If transformer aggregation helps, it identifies a concrete lever to push past 0.530 and informs whether to pair it with multimodal fusion in later experiments. If it does not, we can rule out that direction and focus budget on image encoder quality or fusion strategy. Either outcome reduces uncertainty about an important design axis with one experiment, making it the highest-information next step under the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA is the dominant signal (rna_only 0.411 vs image_only 0.208), multiprofile with avgpool is the best setting so far (config_011, scgpt: 0.530), and multimodal with resnet50+weighted does not clearly beat rna_only (config_019: 0.525 ≈ config_011: 0.530). Uncertainty: We have only tested one RNA encoder (scgpt) across all experiments. It is unknown whether the learned scgpt representation is essential or whether a simpler linear projection (pca_n2000) captures the same discriminative signal. Question: config_007 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) differs from our best result config_011 only in the RNA encoder, giving a clean single-variable comparison. Why best next experiment: RNA is clearly the primary information source, so understanding whether the encoder choice matters is more fundamental than tuning image-side or fusion details. If pca_n2000 matches scgpt, it simplifies the search space and suggests the bottleneck is elsewhere (aggregation, fusion, or image contribution). If scgpt is clearly superior, it confirms we should keep scgpt and focus remaining budget on image encoder or fusion strategy. This is the highest-information single change given current evidence.

The strongest evidence so far is config_007 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) at 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1, which substantially outperforms scgpt-based multiprofile models (0.514–0.530). The key remaining uncertainty is whether adding the image modality can further improve on this strong RNA signal, or whether it dilutes performance (as seen with scgpt, where multimodal 0.525 ≈ rna_only 0.530). Config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is the minimal single-variable extension of config_007: it keeps the same RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation, and only adds the image branch with weighted fusion. This cleanly isolates the contribution of the image modality under the best-performing RNA representation. Under a limited budget, resolving whether multimodal fusion is worthwhile with pca_n2000 is the highest-value question, as it determines whether subsequent experiments should invest in image-encoder upgrades or focus on RNA-side refinements.

Evidence: config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is the best result so far at 0.639 acc / 0.620 F1, clearly outperforming the RNA-only baseline (config_007, 0.591) and all scgpt-based configs. The fusion method (weighted vs concat) is the one design axis not yet varied around this best configuration. Question: config_040 changes only the fusion from weighted to concat while holding model_setting, profile_setting, both encoders, and aggregation identical to config_020, giving a clean single-variable test of whether a concatenation-based fusion (letting the classifier learn cross-modal interactions) outperforms a learned weighted sum. Why this is the best next step: under a tight budget, isolating one variable against the current best is the most information-efficient choice. If concat improves on weighted, it identifies a concrete lever to push performance higher; if it does not, we can rule out fusion as a productive direction and redirect budget toward image-encoder or aggregation choices with confidence, rather than spending experiments on a less-informative multi-variable change.

Evidence: The current best is config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.639). We know pca_n2000 >> scgpt for RNA encoding, multiprofile > singleprofile, and weighted > concat fusion. However, the image encoder (resnet50) is the one major design axis not yet explored at the top-performing level—image alone scored only 0.208 with resnet50, suggesting the image branch may be underperforming. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l (config_047) improve over resnet50 while holding all other settings identical to config_020? This is a clean single-variable comparison that isolates the image-encoder effect. Why best next: It directly extends the strongest known configuration along the most impactful untested dimension. If ViT-L helps, we gain a new best and confirm image quality matters; if not, we confirm resnet50 is sufficient and can redirect budget to aggregation or other axes. This is more informative than testing transformer aggregation (where prior scgpt evidence suggests only a ~1.5% gap) or introducing an entirely new RNA encoder (scvi_n200) which would confound multiple variables.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so we have zero information about which design choices (modality, profile setting, encoder, aggregation, fusion) actually matter or whether added complexity over a simple baseline provides any benefit. The most critical unknown is the performance floor of the simplest viable model. 2) What this tests: config_009 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the cleanest, most interpretable baseline—standard PCA on RNA with a single profile and no image modality, aggregation, or fusion. It establishes a reference performance level against which every more complex configuration (multimodal, multiprofile, learned encoders) must be compared to justify its added cost. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the single most informative first step is to anchor the search with a simple, fast, well-understood baseline. If config_009 performs well, all subsequent multimodal/multiprofile experiments must clearly beat it to be justified, sharply reducing the effective search space. If it performs poorly, we immediately know we must explore image or learned-encoder paths. Either outcome dramatically reduces uncertainty about the most important design axis (does RNA alone suffice?) and guides every subsequent experiment more efficiently than jumping into a complex multimodal configuration whose failure would be hard to attribute.

With only one completed experiment (config_009: RNA-only, PCA-2000, single profile, ~48.5% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether adding image data provides any signal at all in this multimodal cellular profiling task. config_008 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, no aggregation, concat fusion) directly tests this by keeping the RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and profile setting (singleprofile) identical to the baseline, while introducing the minimal set of new variables required to add an image modality (ResNet50 + simple concat). This isolates the effect of modality/fusion as much as possible without confounding with encoder choice or profile complexity. If it substantially outperforms 48.5%, we know images carry complementary signal and can then explore better encoders/fusion. If it does not, we can redirect budget toward RNA encoder improvements or multiprofile settings. Testing an image-only baseline first would be informative but delays the practically central question of whether the multimodal combination works, and testing a more complex multimodal config (e.g., multiprofile + transformer aggregation) would confound too many variables with only one reference point.

Evidence: config_008 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc / 0.510 F1, a clear +4.2% improvement over the RNA-only baseline (config_009, 0.485 acc). This confirms that the pca_n2000 + resnet50 + concat combination is a strong foundation. Uncertainty: We have no evidence yet on whether multiprofile aggregation adds value beyond the single-profile setting. This experiment (config_003) tests exactly that question by switching from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation while holding the RNA encoder (pca_n2000), image encoder (resnet50), and fusion (concat) identical to config_008. This is the cleanest possible comparison to isolate the effect of multiprofile + avgpool, changing only the profile/aggregation axis. Under a limited budget, confirming or ruling out the multiprofile benefit on top of the already-validated multimodal pipeline is the highest-information next step before investing in more complex variations (different encoders, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion).

Evidence: config_003 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.619 acc, a large +9.2% jump over config_008 (same but singleprofile, no aggregation at 0.527). This shows multiprofile + avgpool is the dominant driver so far. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether avgpool is the optimal aggregation or whether a transformer aggregation would further improve multiprofile integration. Question tested: config_014 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other settings identical to config_003 (pca_n2000, resnet50, concat, multiprofile), cleanly isolating the aggregation effect. Why this is the best next experiment: aggregation is the most recently introduced and highest-impact design axis; resolving whether a more expressive aggregator (transformer) helps or whether simple averaging already captures the multiprofile benefit will either open a new high-performing direction or confirm we should focus remaining budget on image encoder or fusion method. A single-variable comparison with the current best is the most information-efficient use of the next slot.

The current best (config_003: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat; acc 0.619) uses PCA—a linear, untrained dimensionality reduction—as the RNA encoder. The only other dimension we've tested is aggregation (avgpool > transformer), while the RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion strategy remain unexplored. Config_011 changes exactly one variable (RNA encoder: pca_n2000 → scvi_n200) while holding everything else fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat), giving a clean single-factor comparison. This tests whether a nonlinear, learned RNA representation (scVI) captures structure that PCA misses, which is a fundamental design decision for cellular profiling. If scvi_n200 significantly outperforms PCA, it signals that representation quality on the RNA side is a major lever and justifies further exploration (e.g., scgpt). If it does not, PCA is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward image-encoder or fusion questions. Under a limited budget, isolating the RNA-encoder effect is the highest-information next step because it addresses the most basic representational assumption in the current best model.

Evidence: The current best (config_011, acc 0.632) uses scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + concat in a multimodal multiprofile setup.
