We know multimodal helps (+4% over rna_only) and multiprofile helps substantially (+9% over singleprofile), but all experiments so far have used resnet50 as the image encoder. Uncertainty: We have zero evidence on whether a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) would further improve performance, which is a representation-level question with potentially large impact. This experiment (config_020: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is a clean single-variable change from config_011, isolating the image encoder effect. It is the best next experiment because the image representation quality is a more fundamental and potentially higher-impact design axis than fusion mechanism (concat vs weighted), and resolving whether the image modality can contribute more signal directly informs whether to invest further in image-side design choices.

The current best configuration (config_020: scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) achieves 0.715 accuracy, and the largest single gain came from upgrading the image encoder to ViT-L. However, all multiprofile experiments so far have used concat fusion exclusively, leaving the fusion strategy as an untested design lever in the best-performing regime. Config_027 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted relative to config_020, providing a clean single-variable comparison. This is the most informative next step because: (1) it directly tests whether learned modality weighting can further improve on the current best, (2) it isolates the fusion effect without confounding changes to encoder, aggregation, or profile setting, and (3) the result will clarify whether further gains should be sought in fusion, RNA encoder (e.g., scgpt), or aggregation (e.g., transformer) under the ViT-L setting, guiding subsequent experiments efficiently under the limited budget.

The current best (config_020: scvi_n200, vit_l, avgpool, concat, acc 0.715) establishes a strong baseline. The largest remaining uncertainty is the RNA encoder choice: we have only tested pca_n2000 and scvi_n200, while scgpt is completely unexplored. config_021 changes exactly one variable from config_020 (RNA encoder scvi_n200 → scgpt) while holding the known-best image encoder (vit_l), aggregation (avgpool), fusion (concat), and profile setting (multiprofile) fixed. This isolates the effect of the RNA representation. Because scgpt is a generative single-cell model with a fundamentally different inductive bias than scvi, the prior uncertainty is high—it could substantially outperform or underperform scvi_n200. By contrast, the aggregation question (avgpool vs transformer) already has evidence favoring avgpool (config_003 vs config_014, ~4-pt gap), making a transformer test with vit_l lower expected information gain. Testing scgpt is therefore the highest-value single-variable experiment: it either confirms scvi_n200 as the preferred RNA encoder or reveals a new promising direction, directly reducing uncertainty about a core design axis under the limited budget.

The current best configuration (config_020: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieves 0.715 accuracy. The only untested single-variable modification in this neighborhood is aggregation: switching from avgpool to transformer (config_050 keeps all other settings identical). We have one prior data point suggesting avgpool > transformer (config_003 vs config_014 with pca+resnet50: 0.619 vs 0.579), but that was with weaker encoders. With the richer, higher-dimensional representations from ViT-L, transformer aggregation may better capture inter-profile interactions that simple averaging discards. This experiment directly tests whether the aggregation preference shifts with stronger image representations, isolates a single design decision, and either yields an improved configuration or confirms avgpool as optimal—making it the highest-value next step for exploiting the most promising region under a limited budget.

Evidence: The best-performing config is config_050 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, concat; 0.7207 acc), closely followed by config_020 (same but avgpool; 0.7150). We have two data points on fusion type with avgpool (concat 0.7150 vs weighted 0.7062), but no data on how fusion interacts with transformer aggregation. Question: Does weighted fusion complement or conflict with transformer aggregation in the scvi_n200 + ViT-L setting? This is a clean single-variable test (concat → weighted) holding all other factors at their best-known values. Why best next experiment: It directly extends the top-performing configuration to either find a new best or confirm concat is optimal, resolving the fusion question in the transformer regime with minimal confounding. Under a tight budget, isolating this one interaction is more informative than a broader exploration when the current best direction is already well-supported.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so we have zero knowledge of the performance floor for either modality. The most fundamental uncertainty is whether the image modality alone provides useful signal for this task, and at what level. Without a baseline, any multimodal result would be uninterpretable—we could not attribute performance to image, RNA, or fusion. 2) What this tests: config_019 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50, no aggregation, no fusion) is the simplest possible image-only model. It isolates the image modality with a well-understood encoder (ResNet50), a single profile (no aggregation complexity), and no fusion step. This gives a clean reference performance for the image branch. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the highest-value first experiment is one that establishes a performance anchor with minimal confounding variables. This single run lets every subsequent experiment be interpreted as a delta: does adding RNA help (compare to rna_only), does multiprofile help (compare to multiprofile image_only), does a stronger image encoder help (compare to ViT-L), does fusion strategy matter (compare concat vs. weighted multimodal). Starting with the simplest, most interpretable baseline maximizes the information gained per experiment and avoids the risk of over- or under-attributing performance to a complex multimodal configuration before we know what each component contributes.

Evidence: Only one experiment (config_019: image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) has been completed, yielding ~21% accuracy, which is very low and provides minimal signal about which design axes matter. The biggest uncertainty is whether RNA information adds any predictive value over image alone, which is the central question of a multimodal cellular profiling study. This experiment (config_038: multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat) is the cleanest possible extension of config_019: it holds the image encoder (resnet50) and profile setting (singleprofile) constant and adds only a standard RNA encoder (scvi_n200) with simple concat fusion. This isolates the effect of adding the RNA modality. If accuracy improves substantially, RNA is informative and we can then explore encoder/aggregation/fusion choices. If it does not improve, we know the bottleneck lies elsewhere (e.g., image encoder quality, profile complexity) and should pivot. Under a tight budget, this single-variable comparison to the existing baseline is the highest-information next step.

The two completed experiments show that image-only (config_019, acc=0.208) performs very poorly, while multimodal with scvi_n200 + resnet50 (config_038, acc=0.536) performs much better. The critical uncertainty is whether the image modality is genuinely contributing to the 0.536 result or whether the performance is driven almost entirely by the RNA encoder. Config_022 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_038—the only difference is the removal of the image branch. If RNA alone approaches 0.536, the image is not adding value and the search should focus on RNA encoder choice and multiprofile aggregation. If RNA alone is substantially lower, the image is a meaningful contributor and subsequent experiments should explore image encoders and fusion strategies. This is the highest-information experiment under the limited budget because it resolves the fundamental question of whether multimodality is warranted before investing further experiments in image-side or fusion-side design choices.

Evidence: The three completed experiments show that image-only with resnet50 performs near chance (acc 0.208), RNA-only with scvi_n200 is strong (acc 0.520), and multimodal with scvi_n200+resnet50 (concat) gives only a marginal gain over RNA alone (0.536 vs 0.520). This small multimodal lift raises the question of whether the image modality simply lacks discriminative signal for this task, or whether resnet50 is too weak to extract it. Question: config_017 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat) changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to a much stronger ViT-L while holding RNA encoder, profile setting, and fusion method identical to config_038. This cleanly isolates the image-encoder effect. Why this is the best next experiment: If ViT-L substantially improves the multimodal score, it reveals that the image modality contains more usable signal than resnet50 could capture, justifying further investment in image-side design (aggregation, fusion). If it does not, it strongly suggests the image modality contributes little regardless of encoder, redirecting the remaining budget toward RNA-side or profile-setting decisions. Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design axis under a tight budget, and the single-variable change keeps the comparison interpretable.

Evidence: Our four completed experiments establish that (a) image-only resnet50 is very weak (0.208), (b) RNA-only scvi_n200 is moderate (0.520), and (c) multimodal scvi_n200+resnet50 with concat fusion is the best so far (0.536), with imagenet_vit_l offering negligible improvement (0.532). All tested configurations use singleprofile; the multiprofile dimension is completely unexplored. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles (via avgpool) improve or degrade performance relative to the singleprofile baseline? config_002 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the minimal-change extension of our best result config_038—only the profile setting changes from single to multi, with avgpool as a simple, interpretable aggregation. This cleanly isolates the profile-setting effect. Why this is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, resolving whether multiprofile is beneficial or harmful is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact design question remaining. If multiprofile helps, it opens a rich sub-space (aggregation type, encoder choice) to exploit; if it hurts, we can prune many configurations and focus on singleprofile refinements. A singleprofile fusion-method test (e.g., weighted vs concat) would be a smaller, lower-uncertainty question by comparison.

The largest performance jump in the history is from singleprofile to multiprofile (config_038: 0.536 → config_002: 0.632, ~10% gain). However, it is unclear whether this gain is driven primarily by the multiprofile RNA representation or by the interaction between multiprofile RNA and the image modality. config_050 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) isolates this by testing multiprofile RNA without any image input, using the same encoder and aggregation as the current best (config_002). If config_050 approaches ~0.60, the multiprofile gain is largely an RNA-representation effect and the image contributes modestly; if it stays near the singleprofile RNA baseline (~0.52), the multiprofile gain requires the image interaction. This single-variable change from config_022 (only profile_setting and the necessary aggregation change) cleanly answers a foundational question that will determine whether future effort should focus on improving RNA encoders, image encoders, or fusion/aggregation strategies—making it the highest-information experiment under a limited budget.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with scvi_n200 and avgpool (config_050, acc=0.650) is our best result and notably outperforms the multimodal counterpart (config_002, acc=0.632), indicating RNA is the dominant signal and the current avgpool aggregation may not be fully exploiting multiprofile information. Only avgpool has been tested as an aggregation strategy. Question: Does transformer-based aggregation capture richer cross-profile interactions than simple averaging, potentially closing or exceeding the current best? Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable extension of our top-performing config (only aggregation changes from avgpool→transformer), directly testing whether a more expressive aggregation mechanism can improve the dominant RNA signal. The result will inform whether to invest in transformer aggregation across all modalities and whether the small RNA-only vs. multimodal gap is an aggregation artifact or a fundamental modality limitation.

Key evidence: multimodal multiprofile with avgpool+concat (config_002, acc=0.632) underperforms RNA-only multiprofile (config_050 avgpool=0.650, config_044 transformer=0.653), which is counterintuitive. In the RNA-only setting, transformer aggregation gave a small but consistent edge over avgpool (0.653 vs 0.650). Config_018 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other settings identical to config_002 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat). This clean single-variable comparison directly tests whether the aggregation mechanism—which we know matters for RNA profiles—also rescues the multimodal model's underperformance relative to RNA-only. If transformer aggregation closes or narrows the gap, it implicates profile aggregation as the bottleneck; if not, the issue lies in fusion or image-feature quality, guiding subsequent experiments toward weighted fusion or alternative image encoders. Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information next step because it isolates one design axis with existing supporting evidence rather than introducing multiple simultaneous changes.

The current best is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, transformer, concat; acc=0.688), which shows that transformer aggregation with multimodal fusion substantially outperforms avgpool (0.632) and RNA-only transformer (0.653). In the singleprofile setting, resnet50 and imagenet_vit_l performed nearly identically (0.536 vs 0.532), but that context lacked multiprofile aggregation. With transformer aggregation, the image features interact with multiple RNA profiles, so a more expressive image encoder (ViT-L) could capture richer spatial features that complement the RNA representations. config_028 is a clean single-variable change from config_018 (only image encoder: resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l), isolating the effect of image representation quality in the best-performing configuration. If it improves, it signals that image encoder capacity is a key lever; if not, it confirms resnet50 suffices and redirects attention to RNA encoder or fusion choices. This is the highest-information next step under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_028 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + ViT_L, transformer, concat) is the current best at 0.721 acc / 0.681 F1. All high-performing experiments to date use concat fusion; weighted fusion has never been tested in the multiprofile + transformer regime. Question: Does changing fusion from concat to weighted (while holding every other variable identical to config_028) improve performance, or is concat already sufficient? This isolates the fusion axis cleanly. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a single-variable change from the current best, directly testing a design axis (fusion) that is completely unexplored in the high-performing regime. If weighted fusion helps, we gain a clear improvement; if not, we eliminate fusion as a lever and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder alternatives (scgpt, pca_n2000). Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information, lowest-risk next step.

No experiments have been completed, so the primary uncertainty is the performance floor: what can a simple single-modality model achieve? config_014 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most interpretable RNA baseline available. It establishes a clean reference point with minimal confounding (no image modality, no learned encoder, no aggregation/fusion), so any future improvement can be attributed to specific design choices (better RNA encoder, adding image modality, multiprofile, aggregation, fusion). Starting from this floor is the most information-efficient first step: it calibrates expectations, confirms the pipeline works, and provides the anchor against which all subsequent multimodal and multiprofile experiments will be judged. Under a limited budget, a clean baseline is more valuable than an early gamble on a complex configuration whose gains cannot yet be decomposed.

Evidence: The only completed experiment (config_014: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) yields ~48.5% validation accuracy, giving a single baseline but leaving the central question of the study unanswered—does adding image information improve multimodal cellular profiling? Uncertainty: We have no data on whether image features contribute any signal, making it impossible to prioritize among the many multimodal configurations. Question tested: config_006 keeps the RNA encoder (pca_n2000), profile setting (singleprofile), and aggregation (none) identical to config_014, adding only an imagenet_vit_l image encoder and a simple concat fusion. This isolates the effect of the image modality with minimal confounds. Why this is the best next experiment: With a limited budget and only one data point, the highest-value question is whether the second modality is worth pursuing at all. A positive result justifies investing further in image encoder choice, aggregation, and fusion; a null or negative result redirects effort toward RNA encoder variants and profile settings. Choosing the strongest available image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) maximizes the chance of detecting a true benefit, and concat is the simplest fusion, avoiding confounding from learned weighting.

Evidence: config_006 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieves 0.535 acc, outperforming config_014 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) at 0.485 acc, confirming that adding the image modality with concat fusion provides a meaningful ~5% boost. Uncertainty: We have no evidence yet on whether multiprofile with aggregation improves over singleprofile. Question tested: config_024 is the minimal extension of config_006—same model setting, same RNA encoder (pca_n2000), same image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), same fusion (concat)—but switches to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. This isolates the effect of multiprofile + simple averaging without confounding changes to encoders or fusion. Why best: It directly extends the current best configuration with the smallest possible change, making the result easy to attribute to the profile/aggregation decision. If it improves, we gain confidence that multiprofile is worth pursuing and can then test transformer aggregation or other encoders; if it does not, we avoid wasting budget on more complex multiprofile variants.

The current best (config_024: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat; acc 0.629) shows that multiprofile + avgpool aggregation provides a large gain over singleprofile (config_006, acc 0.535). The most natural and informative next step is to test whether a more expressive aggregation mechanism (transformer) can further improve over avgpool while holding all other design choices constant. config_013 differs from config_024 in exactly one variable (aggregation: avgpool → transformer), making it a clean single-factor comparison. If transformer outperforms avgpool, it signals that the aggregation architecture is a key lever and justifies further exploration of transformer-based designs; if it performs similarly or worse, it confirms that simple pooling is sufficient and redirects budget toward other dimensions (e.g., RNA encoder or fusion strategy). This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best (config_024, acc=0.629) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, and all four completed experiments share this encoder. We have strong evidence that multimodal + multiprofile + avgpool + concat + imagenet_vit_l is a promising backbone, but the RNA representation has been held constant. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether a learned, non-linear RNA encoder (scvi_n200) captures complementary or superior transcriptomic structure compared to PCA-2000, which is a linear dimensionality reduction. Question: config_049 changes exactly one variable relative to config_024 (rna_encoder: pca_n2000 → scvi_n200), isolating the effect of the RNA encoder while holding model setting, profile setting, image encoder, aggregation, and fusion fixed. Why best next: The RNA encoder is the most fundamental unexplored design axis; a clean single-variable test against the current best maximizes information per experiment. If scvi_n200 improves performance, it opens a productive direction (learned encoders); if it does not, it confirms PCA sufficiency and redirects budget toward other dimensions (e.g., fusion strategy or image encoder). This is more informative than testing a secondary knob like weighted fusion (config_001) because the representation choice is likely to have a larger and more structurally important effect.

Evidence: config_049 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) is the best at 0.715 acc, and with pca_n2000 we saw avgpool (0.629) outperform transformer (0.599) by ~3%. However, this aggregation comparison was only made with the weaker pca_n2000 encoder. Question: Does the aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) still matter when using the superior scvi_n200 representation, or does the richer latent space make the two strategies equivalent? This experiment (config_007) is a clean single-variable change from the best config—only swapping avgpool for transformer—so it isolates the aggregation effect under the current best RNA encoder. Why this is the best next experiment: it either confirms avgpool as the robust choice (letting us lock in aggregation and spend remaining budget on other dimensions like fusion or image encoder) or reveals that transformer aggregation interacts favorably with scvi_n200's richer representation, which would open a new optimization direction. Either outcome reduces uncertainty about a core design axis before we commit further experiments.

Evidence: The strongest signal is that scvi_n200 dramatically outperforms pca_n2000 (config_049: 0.715 vs config_024: 0.629), and the current best is config_007 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat, multiprofile) at 0.721 acc. All six completed experiments use concat fusion; the effect of fusion strategy in the high-performing scvi_n200 regime is completely untested. Question: config_017 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted while holding all other settings at their best-known values (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, multiprofile). This isolates the fusion effect as a single-variable comparison against config_007. Why this is the best next experiment: It is the cleanest exploitation of the current best direction—testing whether a learned fusion weighting can improve on simple concatenation without confounding the result with changes to encoder, aggregation, or profile setting. A positive result would yield an immediate performance gain; a null result would confirm concat sufficiency and redirect budget toward other unexplored axes (e.g., image encoder or scgpt).

Evidence: All completed experiments used imagenet_vit_l as the image encoder, so the image representation choice is completely unexplored. The RNA encoder (scvi_n200 vs pca_n2000) and profile setting (multi vs single) have been shown to matter substantially, but we have no information on whether a lighter image encoder (resnet50) is competitive or a bottleneck. Question: config_015 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) differs from config_049 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat, acc=0.715) in exactly one variable—the image encoder—making it a clean single-factor comparison. Why best next experiment: Under a limited budget, isolating the image encoder effect is critical because it determines whether we should continue investing in the larger ViT-L backbone or whether a simpler encoder suffices. If resnet50 is competitive, it tells us the image representation is not the current bottleneck and we should focus on RNA encoder (e.g., scgpt) or fusion details; if it degrades significantly, it confirms imagenet_vit_l is essential and justifies keeping it in all future configurations. This single experiment reduces uncertainty about a major untested design axis without confounding multiple changes.

The strongest evidence so far is that the RNA encoder choice is the dominant design variable: switching from PCA_n2000 to scvi_n200 (config_024→config_049) yielded a large ~8-point accuracy gain with all other settings held constant. The current best configuration (config_017: scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted → 0.725 acc) has been reached, but scgpt has not been tested in any experiment. config_012 (scgpt, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) is a clean, single-variable swap against config_017, isolating the effect of the RNA encoder while keeping the image encoder, aggregation, and fusion at their best-performing values. This is the highest-information experiment available: if scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, it opens a new promising direction; if it falls short, it confirms scvi_n200 as the preferred encoder and redirects budget toward refining aggregation/fusion or image-encoder choices. No other untested configuration addresses this critical, unexplored variable as directly.

The strongest evidence so far points to scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile as the best direction (0.715–0.725), but we lack a critical single-modality baseline: what does the image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) achieve on its own with multiprofile and avgpool? Config_034 (image_only, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool) directly isolates the image contribution using the same image encoder and aggregation as our best multimodal configs (e.g., config_049). If image-only approaches ~0.70, the RNA modality adds little and further multimodal tuning has limited upside; if it is substantially lower (e.g., ~0.55–0.60), RNA provides meaningful complementary signal and justifies continued multimodal exploration. This single experiment resolves the most important open design question—whether the multimodal fusion is genuinely additive or the image alone is near the ceiling—making it the highest-information-gain choice under a limited budget.

With zero completed experiments, the most critical uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion provides any benefit over a unimodal baseline. Without a reference floor, no multimodal result can be interpreted. config_004 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) establishes a clean, standard RNA-only baseline: it uses a well-understood linear encoder (pca_n2000), the multiprofile setting that matches the majority of multimodal candidates, and simple avgpool aggregation. This makes it directly comparable to multimodal extensions such as config_015 or config_033 (which add resnet50 + a fusion mechanism), isolating the effect of adding the image modality. Choosing RNA-only over image-only is preferred because the RNA encoder dimension (pca vs scgpt vs scvi) is the more variable and less certain axis in this design space, and RNA is the primary biological signal in cellular profiling. This single experiment reduces the largest source of uncertainty—whether the multimodal premise is even supported—before spending budget exploring the multimodal configuration space.

Evidence: Only one experiment is complete (config_004: RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool → acc 0.591, F1 0.573). The single most important unresolved question is whether the image modality carries useful signal for this task at all, since this determines whether any of the ~35 multimodal configurations are worth pursuing. Question tested: config_012 (image-only, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool) holds profile setting and aggregation identical to config_004, so the only change is modality (RNA → Image). This gives a clean unimodal image baseline to compare against the RNA-only result. Why this is the best next step: With only one data point, the highest-uncertainty design decision is modality value. Establishing the image-only baseline before investing in multimodal fusion experiments avoids wasting budget on complex fusion/aggregation configurations if image information is uninformative. It also isolates the modality effect without confounding with encoder, fusion, or aggregation choices.

Evidence: config_004 (rna_only, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieves 0.59 acc, while config_012 (image_only, resnet50, avgpool) achieves only 0.33 acc, suggesting the image modality with ResNet50 is very weak. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether the poor image performance is due to the encoder choice (ResNet50) or whether the image modality simply lacks signal for this task. This experiment (image_only, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool) isolates the image encoder as the single variable changed from config_012, directly testing whether a stronger pretrained ViT-L encoder can make the image modality competitive. This is the best use of the next budget slot because it is a clean single-variable comparison that will decisively inform whether multimodal fusion experiments are worth pursuing or whether the search should focus on improving the RNA modality (e.g., better encoders or aggregation). Without knowing if image carries any useful signal, investing in multimodal configurations risks wasting limited budget on a fundamentally uninformative modality.

Evidence: config_004 (RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool) achieves 0.591 accuracy, while both image-only models (resnet50: 0.328, ViT-L: 0.332) are far weaker, indicating RNA dominates the signal. The central question for this multimodal profiling study is whether fusing the weak image signal with the strong RNA signal improves or degrades performance. config_033 keeps the RNA side identical to config_004 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only resnet50 with simple concat fusion, isolating the effect of adding the image modality. This is the most informative next step because it directly answers whether multimodal fusion is worthwhile before investing experiments in more complex fusion (weighted, transformer) or alternative encoders. If it helps, we exploit by trying better fusion; if it hurts, we redirect budget toward RNA-side improvements (aggregation, encoder choice).

Evidence: config_033 (multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.6186 acc / 0.6103 F1, beating RNA-only (0.5907) and showing that even weak image features add value via concat fusion. All four completed experiments use avgpool aggregation, so the effect of transformer aggregation on multiprofile data is completely untested. Question: Does replacing avgpool with transformer aggregation improve performance by better modeling inter-profile dependencies, holding all other design choices (pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) constant? Why this is the best next step: It is a clean single-variable comparison against the current best configuration, isolating the aggregation design choice. Aggregation is a fundamental architectural decision that affects how multiprofile information is combined and could yield a larger gain than swapping the already-weak image encoder (resnet50 vs ViT-L showed only ~0.4% difference in image-only runs). Under a limited budget, resolving whether transformer aggregation matters before investing in more complex RNA encoders or fusion strategies is the highest-information next experiment.

Evidence: RNA is the dominant signal (rna_only pca_n2000: 0.5907 vs image_only: ~0.33), and the best config so far (config_033: multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat = 0.6186) uses a simple PCA encoder for RNA. We have zero evidence on whether a learned RNA encoder (scgpt or scvi_n200) can improve on PCA. Question: config_005 (scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is a clean single-variable swap of only the RNA encoder relative to config_033, isolating the effect of representation learning vs. linear dimensionality reduction on the dominant modality. Why this is best: Since RNA accounts for most of the predictive signal, the RNA encoder choice is the highest-leverage unexplored axis. A single-variable comparison against our current best (config_033) maximizes information per experiment and directly informs whether investment in learned encoders is warranted before exploring fusion or image-encoder variations.

Evidence: config_033 (pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the best result at 0.6186 acc, showing that multimodal fusion over RNA-only (0.5907) provides a modest gain, and that avgpool aggregation outperforms transformer (config_014, 0.5793). However, all multimodal results so far use concat fusion; we have no data on whether weighted fusion could further improve performance. Question: config_015 changes only the fusion method (concat → weighted) while holding every other variable at its best-known value (pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, multiprofile). This isolates the effect of the fusion mechanism. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a clean single-variable comparison to config_033, directly testing an important and currently unexplored design axis (fusion strategy). If weighted fusion helps, it identifies a clear improvement path; if not, it confirms concat is sufficient and redirects budget toward other axes (e.g., image encoder or RNA encoder). This is more informative than testing imagenet_vit_l (image-only results show resnet50 and vit_l are nearly identical at ~0.33, suggesting low expected information gain in the multimodal context) or scvi_n200 (pca_n2000 already strongly outperforms scgpt, making scvi_n200 less likely to change the picture).

Evidence: The current best config (config_015: pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.6390 acc, and we know weighted fusion > concat (0.639 vs 0.629) and avgpool > transformer (0.619 vs 0.579) with the same encoders. However, we have NOT tested whether a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) improves the multimodal model when all other settings are held at their best-known values. Image-only results (resnet50: 0.328, ViT-L: 0.332) are too close to draw conclusions in isolation. Question: config_030 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is a clean single-variable swap of the image encoder (resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l) against the current best config_015. This directly isolates the effect of image encoder quality. Why best next: It tests the most important unexplored axis (image encoder strength) with minimal confounds, and the answer determines whether further investment in image representation is worthwhile or whether the modality's contribution is inherently limited. A single-variable comparison against the current champion is the most information-efficient use of the next budget slot.

All 8 completed experiments use multiprofile, leaving the singleprofile dimension completely unexplored. The best configuration so far (config_015: pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.639 acc, and we have strong evidence that pca_n2000 is the best RNA encoder, resnet50 is at least as good as vit_l, and weighted fusion outperforms concat. config_022 holds all of these best-known settings fixed and changes only the profile setting to singleprofile (with aggregation=None, as required by that setting). This directly tests whether the multiprofile + aggregation pipeline adds meaningful value over a simpler single-profile architecture. If singleprofile performs comparably, it identifies a simpler, more efficient model; if it performs substantially worse, it confirms that the multiprofile aggregation step is a critical design component. Given zero prior data on singleprofile and the limited budget, resolving this major architectural uncertainty is more informative than fine-tuning within the already well-characterized multiprofile space (e.g., testing transformer+weighted or a new RNA encoder), where expected gains are likely small.

Evidence: The current best is config_015 (pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.639 acc. We know transformer aggregation hurt performance with concat fusion (config_014: 0.579 vs config_033: 0.619), but that comparison confounds aggregation and fusion simultaneously. We have not tested transformer aggregation paired with weighted fusion. Question: config_048 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all else at the current best (pca_n2000, resnet50, weighted), cleanly isolating whether the aggregation–fusion interaction matters. Why best next: It is a single-variable extension of the top configuration (exploitation), directly answers whether avgpool is truly superior to transformer under weighted fusion, and the result will either confirm avgpool as the correct aggregation (guiding all future multimodal experiments) or reveal a hidden interaction that could unlock further gains. Under a tight budget, this clean A/B comparison against the current best is more informative than exploring an untested RNA encoder (scvi_n200) or a second image encoder, where the expected signal is smaller given the large gap already seen between pca_n2000 and scgpt.

With no prior experiments, the most important uncertainty is whether a basic multimodal setup provides a viable performance baseline for this task. config_002 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat) is the simplest, most standard multimodal configuration: it uses well-established pretrained encoders (ImageNet ViT-L for images, scVI for RNA), the simplest profile setting (singleprofile), and the simplest fusion (concat), avoiding confounding from aggregation or weighted fusion. This establishes a reference performance against which all more complex multimodal variants (multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and unimodal baselines (image-only, RNA-only) can later be compared. Testing the simplest multimodal setup first is the highest-information use of the first experiment: if it performs well, we validate the multimodal hypothesis and can exploit by exploring which added complexity helps; if it underperforms, we learn that the basic fusion or encoder choice is the bottleneck before investing in more complex configurations.

With only one completed experiment (config_002: multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, concat fusion, acc≈0.532), the most fundamental uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion actually adds value over a unimodal baseline. config_005 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l, no aggregation) is the cleanest single-variable comparison to config_002—it removes only the RNA modality while keeping the same image encoder and profile setting. If image-only performs comparably (~0.53), it suggests the RNA signal contributes little and future effort should focus on image representation and aggregation; if it performs substantially worse, it confirms multimodal fusion is worthwhile and justifies further exploration of RNA encoders and fusion strategies. Establishing this unimodal baseline is more informative than testing a second fusion strategy or a different RNA encoder, because it resolves the highest-level design question (is multimodal necessary?) before committing budget to finer-grained comparisons within the multimodal space.

Evidence: config_002 (multimodal, scvi_n200, ViT-L, singleprofile, concat) achieved 0.532 acc, while config_005 (image_only, ViT-L, singleprofile) achieved only 0.227 acc. This large gap suggests RNA carries most of the signal, but we cannot yet quantify how much of the multimodal performance comes from RNA alone versus the image modality. Question: config_008 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) isolates the RNA contribution by removing the image modality while keeping the same RNA encoder and profile setting as config_002. If RNA-only ≈ 0.53, the image adds little and future effort should focus on RNA encoder/aggregation choices; if RNA-only is substantially lower, the image modality is genuinely complementary and fusion strategy becomes a high-value design axis. Why this is the best next experiment: it is the single most informative ablation given only two completed runs—it resolves the fundamental uncertainty about modality contribution with a minimal, controlled change (only model_setting differs from config_002), and its result will most efficiently direct all subsequent experiments under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_002 (multimodal, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieved 0.532 acc, only marginally above RNA-alone scvi_n200 (0.520), while image-alone was very weak (0.227). This suggests the RNA encoder is the dominant signal source and the image contributes little. Uncertainty: we have only tested one RNA encoder (scvi_n200); it is unknown whether scgpt produces a more informative representation that could raise the ceiling. Question: config_023 changes exactly one variable relative to config_002 (RNA encoder scvi_n200 → scgpt) while holding model_setting, profile_setting, image_encoder, aggregation, and fusion constant. This cleanly isolates the effect of the RNA representation. Why best next: the RNA encoder is the highest-leverage design choice given that RNA drives most of the signal; a single-variable comparison against our current best (config_002) maximizes information per experiment and avoids confounding with fusion or image-encoder changes. If scgpt substantially outperforms scvi_n200, it redirects the search toward scgpt-based configurations; if not, it confirms scvi_n200 is adequate and we can pivot to fusion or profile-setting questions.

Evidence: config_002 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, concat, singleprofile) achieves 0.532 acc, barely above rna_only (0.520), indicating the image modality contributes very little under concat fusion. scvi_n200 clearly outperforms scgpt (~10 pt gap). The key uncertainty is whether the near-zero image contribution is due to the fusion mechanism (concat vs. weighted) or to the image representation itself. Question tested: config_051 is identical to config_002 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, isolating the effect of fusion strategy on how much the image modality can contribute. Why best next experiment: it is a clean single-variable comparison from the current best configuration, directly tests whether a better fusion mechanism can unlock image value, and the answer (weighted helps or not) will determine whether subsequent budget should go toward multiprofile/aggregation (if fusion was the bottleneck) or toward a different image encoder (if the image features are inherently weak). This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the superior RNA encoder (0.520 rna_only vs 0.435 multimodal with scgpt), weighted fusion slightly edges out concat (0.537 vs 0.532), and the image modality adds a small but real benefit over RNA-only (~1.2%). However, we have only tested imagenet_vit_l as the image encoder. Uncertainty: it is unknown whether resnet50 would match, exceed, or underperform imagenet_vit_l in the multimodal setting, and this choice will affect the final configuration. Question: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, weighted fusion) is a clean single-variable swap of the image encoder relative to our best result (config_051, same but imagenet_vit_l). This isolates the image-encoder effect while holding the RNA encoder, profile setting, and fusion strategy at their best-supported values. Rationale: Under a tight budget, this is the highest-information next step because it (a) builds on our strongest evidence, (b) changes only one variable to cleanly attribute any performance shift to the image encoder, and (c) directly informs whether we should invest remaining budget in resnet50-based or ViT-based multimodal pipelines for subsequent multiprofile/aggregation experiments.

All six completed experiments use singleprofile with no aggregation, leaving the multiprofile+aggregation dimension completely untested. The best result so far is config_016 (scvi_n200, resnet50, weighted, singleprofile; acc=0.540). The small multimodal gain over RNA-only (~1-2%) suggests the current single-profile setup may be underutilizing available information. config_028 directly extends the best configuration by switching to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation while keeping the same encoders (scvi_n200, resnet50) and fusion (weighted). This isolates the effect of multiprofile+aggregation with the simplest, most robust aggregation method, avoiding the confound of simultaneously introducing a more complex transformer aggregator. If it improves on 0.540, we gain evidence that multi-profile information is valuable and can then explore transformer aggregation; if not, we learn that added complexity is not warranted, saving budget from pursuing that direction.

Evidence: config_028 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieved the best performance (acc=0.678, F1=0.646), showing that multiprofile with avgpool aggregation provides a ~14-point boost over singleprofile. However, we have only tested avgpool aggregation in the multiprofile setting; the effect of transformer aggregation remains untested. Question: config_045 is identical to config_028 except aggregation changes from avgpool to transformer (all other settings: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, weighted). This isolates the effect of aggregation strategy in the most promising configuration family. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison against our current best, directly testing whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) can further improve over simple avgpool. Given the limited budget, confirming or ruling out transformer aggregation in the top-performing setup is the highest-information experiment before exploring other dimensions (image encoder, fusion, RNA encoder variants).

The current best (config_045: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted; acc=0.713) shows that multiprofile + transformer aggregation is the dominant driver of performance. However, in singleprofile, RNA alone (0.520) was nearly as strong as multimodal (0.532–0.540), while image-only was very weak (0.227), suggesting the image modality contributes little. The critical open question is whether this pattern holds in the multiprofile+transformer regime, where cross-modal interaction dynamics may differ. config_024 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) is a clean one-variable ablation of the image modality from the current best. If it approaches ~0.70, the image modality is redundant and future effort should focus on RNA encoder and aggregation refinements; if it drops substantially, the image modality becomes essential in multiprofile and we should optimize the image encoder. This single experiment resolves a fundamental design decision (is multimodality needed?) that will shape all remaining budget allocation, making it the highest-information experiment available.

The current best (config_045: 0.713 acc) uses resnet50 as the image encoder in a multiprofile + transformer + weighted fusion setting. The only prior evidence on image encoder choice comes from singleprofile experiments (config_016 resnet50: 0.540 vs config_051 imagenet_vit_l: 0.537), where the difference was small and the regime was fundamentally different (no multiprofile aggregation). config_038 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_045, isolating the effect of image encoder in the high-performing multiprofile + transformer regime. This is critical because the image encoder determines the quality of the visual representation being fused, and confirming whether resnet50's advantage persists (or reverses) when paired with transformer aggregation will guide all subsequent multimodal experiments. Under the limited budget, this is the highest-information exploitation step: it either validates the current best's encoder choice (allowing us to fix that variable) or reveals a better encoder that could push performance further.

With no prior evidence, the most important uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion provides meaningful value over unimodal approaches, and what a strong 'standard' multimodal configuration achieves. config_004 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion) is the most informative first experiment because: (1) it directly tests the core hypothesis of the study—whether combining RNA and image modalities helps—using strong, well-motivated defaults for each component (learned scVI embedding for RNA, pre-trained ViT-L for images); (2) by choosing singleprofile and weighted fusion, it keeps the design simple and interpretable, so any future degradation can be attributed to specific design choices rather than compounding complexity; (3) it establishes a performance reference point that will anchor all subsequent comparisons (multiprofile, alternative encoders, transformer aggregation, concat fusion, unimodal baselines). Starting here avoids the risk of a complex configuration failing for ambiguous reasons, and the result will efficiently guide whether to explore multiprofile/aggregation next or to test unimodal baselines to quantify the multimodal gain.

With only one completed experiment (config_004: multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion → acc 0.537), the most critical uncertainty is whether the multimodal fusion is actually adding value over a strong unimodal baseline. Config_011 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is a clean ablation of config_004 that removes only the RNA modality while keeping the same image encoder and profile setting. If image-only ViT-L achieves comparable accuracy (~0.53-0.54), it reveals that the RNA modality is not contributing meaningfully and we should redirect budget toward image-model optimization or simpler architectures. If it is substantially lower, it confirms that multimodal fusion is genuinely beneficial and justifies further investment in multimodal configurations. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the fundamental design choice (multimodal vs. unimodal) before spending further budget on fine-tuning fusion methods, aggregation, or profile settings that may be irrelevant if one modality dominates.

We have an image-only baseline (config_011: 22.7% acc) and a multimodal result (config_004: 53.7% acc), but no RNA-only baseline. This large gap tells us RNA contributes substantially, but we cannot yet determine whether the multimodal fusion is genuinely additive or whether RNA alone would already achieve ~50%+. Config_023 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is a clean single-modality experiment using the same RNA encoder and profile setting as our best multimodal result, making it a controlled complement to config_011. Together, these two single-modality baselines bracket the multimodal result and reveal whether the 53.7% reflects true cross-modal synergy or is dominated by RNA. This is the most decision-relevant uncertainty to resolve next: if RNA alone is already ~50%, we should focus budget on RNA representation improvements rather than multimodal fusion complexity; if RNA alone is much lower, the multimodal combination is genuinely valuable and we should invest in optimizing fusion and image encoders. No other single experiment would reduce this foundational uncertainty as efficiently.

Evidence: The current best (config_004, multimodal/singleprofile/scvi_n200/imagenet_vit_l/weighted) achieves 0.5375 acc, only ~1.7% above RNA-only (config_023, 0.5203), while image-only is far weaker (0.2266). This suggests the image modality contributes modestly and the fusion mechanism may be a critical determinant of whether that contribution is realized. Question: config_002 is identical to config_004 except fusion changes from 'weighted' to 'concat', making it a clean single-variable A/B test that isolates the effect of fusion strategy. Why this is the best next experiment: Fusion is the most fundamental design decision in any multimodal model—it governs how the two modalities interact. Understanding whether weighted vs. concat matters will inform every subsequent multimodal experiment (profile setting, encoder choice, aggregation). Because the multimodal gain over RNA-only is small, knowing whether a different fusion could widen or eliminate that gap is essential before investing in more complex configurations (multiprofile, transformer aggregation, etc.). This minimal-change comparison maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: All four completed experiments are singleprofile with no aggregation. RNA is the dominant signal (rna_only 0.5203 vs image_only 0.2266), and the multimodal gain over RNA alone is modest (~1.7%). Weighted fusion slightly outperforms concat (0.5375 vs 0.5321). The multiprofile + aggregation dimension is completely untested and represents the largest source of remaining uncertainty. Question: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation improve performance when keeping the same encoders (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l) and fusion (weighted) as our best result (config_004)? Why this is the best next experiment: config_009 is a minimal, clean extension of config_004—only the profile setting and (necessarily coupled) aggregation change. It directly tests whether temporal/multi-profile information adds value on top of the already-strong RNA signal, without confounding the result with a new encoder or fusion strategy. If it improves, multiprofile+aggregation becomes a promising direction to exploit; if it does not, we can rule out that dimension and focus budget on encoder choice or other factors.

The dominant finding so far is the massive jump from singleprofile (~0.537) to multiprofile (0.706) in config_009, but it is unclear whether this gain comes from having multiple profiles per cell or from the synergistic multimodal combination. config_035 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is the cleanest single-variable comparison to config_009: it removes only the image modality while keeping the same RNA encoder and aggregation. If RNA-only multiprofile also approaches ~0.70, the gain is profile-driven and image encoders become low priority; if it drops substantially, the multimodal fusion is essential and we should focus on image encoder and fusion choices. This experiment also directly contrasts with config_023 (RNA singleprofile, 0.520) to isolate the multiprofile effect without any image confound. Under a limited budget, resolving whether the multiprofile gain is modality-independent or fusion-dependent is the highest-value uncertainty to reduce before committing further experiments to encoder or fusion variants.

Evidence: The multiprofile setting produced the largest performance jump (config_009: 0.706 vs config_004: 0.537), making aggregation strategy a critical design choice. However, all multiprofile experiments so far (config_009, config_035) have used avgpool; we have zero data on whether transformer aggregation could further improve multiprofile performance. Question: config_041 is identical to config_009 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted) except aggregation changes from avgpool to transformer, cleanly isolating the effect of aggregation method. Why this is the best next experiment: Aggregation is a fundamental architectural decision that, if transformer helps, would benefit all multiprofile configurations and could yield a meaningful accuracy gain. Testing it as a single-variable change from our current best (config_009) gives the highest information-per-experiment ratio under a limited budget, while avoiding the confound of simultaneously altering encoder or fusion.

Evidence: The current best configuration (config_041: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted; acc=0.725) has only been tested with one RNA encoder (scvi_n200). The RNA encoder is a major unexplored design axis, and RNA is the dominant modality (RNA-only multi-profile already reaches 0.650 vs image-only at ~0.23). Question: config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is a clean single-variable swap of RNA encoder (scvi_n200 → scgpt) within the best-performing regime, directly isolating the effect of RNA representation quality. Why best next experiment: Under a limited budget, resolving whether a different RNA foundation model (scgpt) meaningfully shifts performance in the top-performing configuration is the highest-information experiment. If scgpt improves, it opens a new optimization axis; if it matches or underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 is sufficient and redirects effort to other variables (e.g., image encoder or fusion). This avoids changing multiple factors simultaneously and builds directly on the strongest evidence we have.

Evidence: config_041 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is the current best at 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1, and we know multi-profile + transformer aggregation + scvi_n200 is the dominant combination. However, we have no direct comparison of fusion method (weighted vs. concat) under the transformer aggregation setting. Question: Does concat fusion match or exceed weighted fusion when paired with transformer aggregation and the best encoders? This isolates a single variable (fusion) from the current best configuration. Why this is the best next experiment: It is the cleanest single-factor extension of our top result, directly testing whether the 0.725 ceiling can be pushed higher on the fusion axis. If concat performs comparably, it confirms weighted is not a binding constraint; if it underperforms, we confirm the current best is near-optimal on that axis and can redirect budget toward the image-encoder question (resnet50 vs. ViT-L).

Evidence: The current best (config_041, 0.725 acc) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + transformer + weighted. All high-performing experiments have used imagenet_vit_l; the image encoder axis is completely unexplored in the promising regime. The RNA encoder (scvi_n200 >> scgpt), profile setting (multi >> single), and aggregation (transformer >= avgpool) effects are already well-characterized. Question: Does swapping imagenet_vit_l for resnet50 (config_015) meaningfully change performance while holding scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, and weighted fusion constant? This isolates the image encoder effect in the high-performing region. Why this is the best next experiment: It is the single largest untested design axis in the regime where performance is already strong (~0.72). If resnet50 performs comparably, it informs cost/efficiency trade-offs; if it degrades significantly, it confirms imagenet_vit_l is a critical component and narrows future search. No other single-variable experiment in the available set would reduce as much uncertainty about a major design choice.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is no performance reference and no information about which design axes (modality, profile setting, encoder choice, aggregation, fusion) actually matter. The highest-priority uncertainty is establishing a baseline performance level for a multimodal model using standard, well-motivated components. 2) What this tests: config_051 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, resnet50, concat) is a clean multimodal baseline that uses a learned single-cell RNA encoder (scgpt), a standard image backbone (resnet50), a single profile (eliminating the aggregation variable entirely), and the simplest fusion (concat). It establishes the reference performance for the study's core question—whether combining RNA and image modalities is informative—while keeping every other design choice at its most standard value. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Starting with the simplest reasonable multimodal configuration on the study's main path (rather than a fully complex multiprofile/transformer/weighted setup) means that in subsequent experiments we can add one axis of complexity at a time (e.g., multiprofile + aggregation, a different RNA encoder, a stronger image backbone, weighted fusion) and attribute performance changes to that single change. It also avoids the risk that a poor result is confounded by multiple simultaneously exotic choices. This maximizes the information gained per experiment under the limited budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_051: multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, resnet50, concat → acc 0.427), the most critical uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion actually provides a meaningful advantage over a unimodal baseline. config_018 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) is the cleanest single-factor comparison: it is identical to config_051 except the image modality is removed. If RNA-only performs comparably (~0.42–0.44), the image contributes little and we should focus budget on RNA representation and profile/aggregation choices. If RNA-only is substantially lower, the image is a key signal and we should next explore image encoder variants (e.g., imagenet_vit_l). This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most fundamental design decision (multimodal vs. unimodal) before committing further experiments to more complex multimodal configurations.

Evidence: config_051 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt+resnet50, concat) achieved 0.4275 acc vs config_018 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) at 0.4106, suggesting a modest multimodal benefit. However, with only two data points, we have no information on whether multiprofile adds value over singleprofile—a decision that affects roughly half the search space. Question: Does multiprofile (with the simplest aggregation, avgpool) improve over singleprofile when all other factors (scgpt RNA encoder, resnet50 image encoder, concat fusion) are held constant? Why this is the best next experiment: config_002 is the most controlled comparison to config_051, changing only profile_setting (single→multi) and adding the minimally necessary aggregation (avgpool). If multiprofile+avgpool does not clearly beat 0.4275, it strongly suggests multiprofile is not the key lever and we can focus budget on singleprofile variants (fusion, encoders). If it does improve, it validates the multiprofile direction and motivates testing transformer aggregation next. This single experiment reduces the largest remaining architectural uncertainty with minimal confounding variables.

The strongest evidence so far is that multiprofile with avgpool aggregation (config_002, acc=0.512) substantially outperforms singleprofile with no aggregation (config_051, acc=0.427), an ~8.5-point gap. This tells us that combining multiple profiles helps, but it does not tell us whether the aggregation *mechanism* matters or whether the gain is simply from having more data to average. Config_001 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, transformer, concat) is a single-variable change from config_002, swapping only avgpool for transformer aggregation. If transformer significantly improves over avgpool, it indicates profiles carry heterogeneous information requiring structured combination, justifying further investment in aggregation design. If the gain is marginal, it confirms simple averaging is sufficient and we should redirect budget toward other axes (e.g., image encoder or fusion method). This is the most informative next step because it isolates the aggregation decision while holding all other design choices at their currently best-known values.

Evidence: config_002 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the best at 0.5121, far exceeding config_051 (multimodal, singleprofile) at 0.4275, confirming multiprofile is a major driver. However, the multimodal-vs-rna_only gap at singleprofile is only ~1.7% (config_051 vs config_018), which is weak and possibly noise. We have no multiprofile rna_only baseline to determine whether the image modality is actually contributing at the multiprofile level. Question: config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is a clean single-variable ablation of config_002—removing only the image modality. If it performs near 0.51, the image adds little and we can simplify; if it drops substantially, the image is essential and we should invest in image-encoder choices (e.g., ViT-L). Why this is best: under a limited budget, resolving whether the image modality is a meaningful contributor is the highest-value uncertainty to reduce before committing further experiments to image-encoder or fusion variations. It also guards against over-investing in a more complex multimodal pipeline if a simpler rna_only multiprofile model is competitive.

Evidence: Multi-profile with avgpool aggregation is clearly the strongest setting (config_008 rna_only=0.5305, config_002 multimodal=0.5121), and avgpool outperforms transformer aggregation (0.5121 vs 0.4710). Notably, the RNA-only model (config_008) slightly outperforms the multimodal counterpart (config_002) by ~1.8%, suggesting the image modality with concat fusion may not be contributing effectively. Question: Is the suboptimal fusion strategy (concat) the reason the image modality underperforms? Config_048 isolates a single variable—changing fusion from concat to weighted—while holding model_setting, profile_setting, rna_encoder, image_encoder, and aggregation identical to config_002. This gives a clean A/B comparison on fusion and a three-way benchmark against config_008 (RNA-only). Why best next step: It is the most targeted experiment to determine whether the image channel can be made useful with scgpt+resnet50, which directly informs whether to invest remaining budget in image-encoder or fusion variations versus committing to RNA-only or alternative RNA encoders. A single-variable change maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The best multimodal config (config_048: multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.525, while the best rna_only config (config_008: multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) achieves 0.530. This suggests the image modality with ResNet50 has not yet provided a clear advantage over RNA alone. The most important open question is whether a stronger image encoder (ImageNet ViT-L) can make the multimodal model outperform the RNA-only baseline. config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) differs from config_048 only in the image encoder, making it a clean single-variable comparison. If it outperforms both config_048 and config_008, it confirms that image information is valuable but was underexploited by ResNet50; if it does not, it strongly supports that the image modality is not contributing meaningfully in this task, redirecting effort toward RNA encoder or aggregation choices. This is the highest-information experiment under the limited budget because it resolves the central question of whether multimodality is worth pursuing.

All seven completed experiments use scgpt as the RNA encoder, leaving the RNA representation choice as the largest unexplored design dimension. The current best config (config_019: scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile, acc=0.542) establishes a strong baseline. config_007 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) is an exact A/B comparison that changes only the RNA encoder from scgpt to pca_n2000, isolating the effect of learned vs. linear RNA representations. If PCA performs comparably, it indicates the task does not require a complex RNA encoder and simplifies the design space; if it underperforms significantly, it confirms that a learned representation is essential and motivates further comparison with scvi_n200. This single-variable experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about one of the most impactful design choices while keeping all other settings at their empirically best values (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted, imagenet_vit_l), making it the highest-information next step under a limited budget.

1) Evidence: config_007 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted + multiprofile) achieved 0.635 acc, a dramatic ~9-point jump over config_019 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, same other settings) at 0.542. This strongly implicates the RNA encoder as the dominant factor. However, we also know imagenet_vit_l modestly outperforms resnet50 with scgpt (config_019: 0.542 vs config_048: 0.525). 2) Question: config_006 (pca_n2000 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted + multiprofile) is a single-variable swap of the image encoder from imagenet_vit_l to resnet50, directly comparing against config_007. This isolates whether the 0.635 result is driven primarily by the RNA representation (pca_n2000) or requires the specific combination with imagenet_vit_l. 3) Why best next experiment: This is the cleanest, most informative single-variable test from the current best configuration. If pca_n2000 + resnet50 performs comparably, it confirms the RNA encoder is the key lever and the image encoder is secondary—guiding all future experiments toward RNA representation choices. If it drops substantially, it reveals a critical interaction effect. Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty about which design axis to prioritize under a limited budget, making this the highest-information-value experiment available.

The strongest evidence so far is that pca_n2000 as RNA encoder dramatically outperforms scgpt (~0.64 vs ~0.51-0.54 accuracy). However, with scgpt, rna_only multiprofile avgpool (config_008: 0.530) actually outperformed the corresponding multimodal setup (config_002: 0.512), suggesting the image modality may not be adding value with that encoder. The critical open question is whether this pattern holds for pca_n2000: does the image encoder contribute meaningfully on top of an already strong RNA representation? config_022 (rna_only, pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-factor comparison against config_006 (multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted: 0.639), isolating the effect of the image modality. If rna_only pca_n2000 approaches or exceeds 0.639, it reveals the image is redundant and redirects the search toward simpler RNA-only pipelines; if it falls well below, it confirms the multimodal benefit and justifies further multimodal exploration. Under a limited budget, resolving this fundamental design question is more informative than fine-tuning aggregation or fusion within the already-promising multimodal pca_n2000 space.

With no completed experiments, the primary uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion provides a meaningful advantage over single-modality baselines, and what a reasonable reference performance looks like. Config_007 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, no aggregation, concat) is a clean, standard multimodal setup: it uses a well-established learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200), a standard image backbone (ResNet-50), the simplest profile setting, and the simplest fusion (concat) without additional aggregation. This isolates the core multimodal-fusion question while keeping other design dimensions at their simplest defaults, so any future performance change can be attributed to a specific modification. It establishes a reference point against which we can later compare single-modality baselines (to quantify the fusion gain) and more complex variants (multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, ViT-L image encoder) to determine which design axes actually matter under a limited budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_007: multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, None, concat → 53.6% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether the multimodal fusion is actually contributing value or whether a single modality performs comparably. config_033 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200, None, None) is the cleanest single-variable ablation of config_007: it keeps the same RNA encoder (scvi_n200), same profile setting (singleprofile), and removes only the image modality. If RNA-only achieves similar accuracy, the image modality and fusion machinery are not adding value, and budget should shift toward single-modality or different encoder choices. If RNA-only is substantially worse, it confirms the image modality contributes and justifies continued investment in multimodal configurations. This baseline is essential before spending further experiments on more complex multimodal variants, making it the highest-information-use next step under a limited budget.

Evidence: config_007 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200+resnet50, concat) achieved 0.5362 acc / 0.5158 F1, modestly outperforming config_033 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) at 0.5203 acc / 0.4982 F1. This suggests a small but consistent benefit from the image modality, but we have no evidence yet about whether multiprofile aggregation helps. Uncertainty: The profile setting (single vs. multi) is a fundamental design axis we have not explored; all completed experiments used singleprofile. Question: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation improve validation accuracy/F1 while keeping the same encoders (scvi_n200, resnet50) and fusion (concat) as our best config? Why this is the best next step: config_011 is the minimal, single-axis extension of config_007 (only profile_setting changes, with the necessary addition of avgpool aggregation that multiprofile requires). It isolates the effect of profile diversity and aggregation without simultaneously changing encoders or fusion, making the result interpretable. If it improves, it validates multiprofile as a productive direction; if not, it confirms singleprofile sufficiency and redirects budget toward encoder or fusion variations.

The largest performance jump so far is config_011 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat: 0.632) vs config_007 (same but singleprofile, no aggregation: 0.536), a ~10-point gain. The critical uncertainty is whether this gain comes from the multiprofile+avgpool design or from the multimodal (image) component. config_041 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a clean ablation that removes only the image modality while keeping the multiprofile and avgpool settings identical to config_011. If it performs near 0.63, the profile/aggregation design is the primary driver and we should focus future budget on RNA encoder and aggregation choices. If it drops substantially toward config_033's 0.52, then the image modality is essential for the multiprofile+avgpool benefit, and we should prioritize image encoder and fusion choices. This single experiment resolves a major fork in the search strategy and is the highest-information use of the next slot.

The key finding from completed experiments is that RNA-only multiprofile (config_041, acc=0.650) surprisingly outperforms multimodal multiprofile with the same RNA encoder, image encoder, and aggregation (config_011, acc=0.632). This suggests the image modality is not contributing positively under concat fusion. Config_043 is identical to config_011 except it replaces concat with weighted fusion, making it a clean single-variable test of whether the fusion strategy is the bottleneck. If weighted fusion closes or reverses the gap, it tells us the image modality has signal that concat fails to leverage; if it does not, it strengthens the case that resnet50 image features are not informative for this task. This is the highest-information next step because it directly isolates the fusion mechanism—the one untested design axis in the best-performing multimodal setup—without confounding changes to encoder, profile, or aggregation.

Evidence: The current best is config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.678 acc. We've established that multiprofile >> singleprofile (+0.10-0.14) and weighted > concat fusion (+0.046), but we have only tested avgpool as the aggregation mechanism. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether the simple average pooling adequately captures inter-profile interactions, or whether a transformer-based aggregation could yield further gains by learning which profiles are most informative per cell. Question tested: config_023 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other settings identical to config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, weighted), giving a clean single-variable comparison. Why this is the best next experiment: Aggregation is a fundamental architectural choice that determines how multiprofile information is combined—a dimension we have not yet explored. A positive result would open a new improvement axis; a null result would confirm avgpool sufficiency and redirect budget toward encoder choices (scgpt, ViT). This is more informative than, e.g., swapping the RNA encoder, because if aggregation is already suboptimal, encoder improvements may be confounded by the aggregation bottleneck.

Evidence: The current best (config_023, multimodal/multiprofile/transformer/weighted, acc=0.713) outperforms rna_only/multiprofile/avgpool (config_041, acc=0.650), but this gap conflates two changes: adding the image modality AND switching from avgpool to transformer aggregation. We know weighted fusion > concat at the avgpool level (0.678 vs 0.632), and transformer > avgpool at the weighted level (0.713 vs 0.678), but we have no data on whether transformer aggregation alone (without image) can close most of that gap. Question: config_001 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) is a clean single-variable ablation of config_023—removing only the image modality while keeping the best aggregation and profile settings. This directly isolates the marginal contribution of the image modality at the transformer aggregation level. Why best use of budget: If rna_only+transformer approaches 0.713, the image modality is not adding meaningful value and further multimodal experiments are low-value; if it stays near 0.65–0.67, the image modality is genuinely contributing and we should exploit multimodal directions (e.g., better image encoders or fusion). This single experiment resolves a fundamental design uncertainty that will determine the entire remaining search strategy, making it the highest-information next step.

The current best (config_023: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted, acc=0.713) shows a clear ~0.06 advantage over the matching rna_only transformer setup (config_001, acc=0.653), indicating the image modality is contributing meaningfully.
