However, all experiments so far have used ResNet50 as the image encoder. config_029 swaps only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l while keeping the proven multiprofile + transformer + weighted pipeline intact. This single-variable change directly tests whether a stronger, more expressive image representation can amplify the multimodal gain, which is the largest unexplored design axis with high potential impact. It is more informative than testing fusion (weighted vs concat) because the image encoder is a fundamental representation bottleneck, and a positive result would justify further investment in image-side improvements, while a null result would confirm ResNet50 is sufficient and redirect effort to RNA encoder or fusion choices.

Evidence: The current best config (029: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, acc=0.725) has only been tested with scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder. All 8 completed experiments use scvi_n200, leaving the RNA encoder dimension entirely unexplored. Question: config_010 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is a single-variable swap of the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt at the current best configuration, directly isolating whether a generative-pretrained RNA encoder (scgpt) can match or exceed the VAE-based scvi_n200 in the multimodal pipeline. Why best next experiment: RNA encoder is the largest remaining untested design axis, and testing it at the top-performing configuration level (exploitation) while probing a fundamentally different encoder family (exploration) gives the highest information-per-experiment ratio. A positive result opens a new optimization direction; a negative result confirms scvi_n200 and lets us focus remaining budget on other dimensions (e.g., fusion, image-only baselines) with reduced uncertainty.

The current best configuration is config_029 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted; acc=0.725). We have strong evidence that weighted fusion outperforms concat under avgpool aggregation (config_043: 0.678 vs config_011: 0.632), but we have not tested this comparison under transformer aggregation. config_008 is a single-variable change from config_029 (fusion: weighted→concat), isolating the interaction between aggregation type and fusion strategy. If concat performs comparably with transformer, it simplifies the design space and suggests the transformer already handles cross-modal weighting; if it is notably worse, it confirms weighted fusion is essential regardless of aggregation. This is the cleanest exploitation step from the current best while resolving an important design uncertainty, making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

With no completed experiments, there is zero evidence about any design choice, so the priority is establishing a strong, interpretable reference point. config_001 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, concat) uses the most established and standard components across every dimension: scgpt is the most widely validated RNA encoder, resnet50 is the canonical image backbone, avgpool is the simplest aggregation, and concat is the simplest fusion. This 'canonical' multimodal multiprofile configuration serves as the natural anchor for the study. From this single data point, subsequent experiments can isolate one variable at a time (e.g., swap scgpt→pca_n2000 to test RNA encoder impact, swap resnet50→imagenet_vit_l to test image encoder impact, swap concat→weighted to test fusion, or drop to rna_only/image_only to test whether multimodality adds value over single-modality baselines). Choosing a more complex or non-standard configuration first would conflate multiple untested choices and make it harder to attribute performance to specific design decisions under a limited budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, concat → acc 0.512), the most critical uncertainty is whether the multimodal fusion is actually contributing value or whether the low accuracy reflects a fundamental limitation of the setup. config_018 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is the cleanest single-factor comparison to config_001: it removes only the image modality and fusion while holding the RNA encoder (scgpt), profile setting (multiprofile), and aggregation (avgpool) constant. If RNA-only performs comparably to 0.512, it suggests the image modality or fusion strategy is not adding signal, redirecting effort toward better unimodal representations or fusion design. If RNA-only is substantially worse, it confirms the image contributes meaningful information and justifies further multimodal exploration. Under a tight budget, establishing whether the core multimodal premise is valid before investing in more complex multimodal variants (transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, ViT encoders) is the highest-information-value next step.

Evidence: config_018 (RNA-only, scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) achieves 0.530 acc / 0.515 F1, outperforming config_001 (multimodal, scgpt+resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.512 acc / 0.477 F1. This suggests that adding the image branch with concat fusion is actively harmful. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether the underperformance stems from the fusion strategy (concat may dilute informative RNA features with noisy image features) or from the image encoder/modality itself. Question tested: config_004 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted (keeping scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, multiprofile identical to config_001), isolating the effect of fusion. Why best next experiment: it is a clean single-variable comparison against config_001, so the result directly tells us whether the fusion mechanism is the bottleneck. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds the RNA-only baseline, it justifies further investment in multimodal configurations with better fusion; if it does not, it shifts focus toward the image encoder or confirms RNA-only as the stronger direction—either outcome efficiently narrows the search space under limited budget.

Evidence: The RNA-only baseline (config_018, scgpt, avgpool) achieves 0.530 accuracy, outperforming both multimodal configs with resnet50 (config_001: 0.512 concat, config_004: 0.525 weighted). This suggests resnet50 image features are not adding value, but we have not yet tested whether a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) changes this picture. Question: Does replacing resnet50 with imagenet_vit_l (while holding all other settings constant: scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) make the image modality informative enough to close or reverse the gap to the RNA-only baseline? Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison against config_004 (only image encoder changes), directly isolating the effect of image representation quality. The result will clarify whether the image modality has any utility at all, which is the most consequential architectural decision remaining. If config_031 still underperforms config_018, it strongly suggests image features are not contributing and we should focus on RNA encoder/aggregation choices. If it matches or exceeds config_018, it validates the multimodal direction and motivates further fusion/aggregation exploration.

Evidence: The best-performing config so far is config_031 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.542), but it has a notably lower F1 (0.483) than the RNA-only baseline config_018 (acc=0.530, F1=0.515), raising the question of whether the RNA representation (scgpt) is the bottleneck. We have only tested one RNA encoder (scgpt) across all four experiments, leaving the RNA encoder dimension entirely unexplored. Question: config_007 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, multiprofile) is a clean single-variable swap of the RNA encoder from scgpt to scvi_n200 while holding the image encoder, aggregation, fusion, and profile setting identical to config_031. This isolates the effect of the RNA representation. Why this is the best next experiment: The RNA encoder is a fundamental design axis with zero prior evidence; if scvi_n200 substantially outperforms scgpt, it reshapes the entire search space, and if it underperforms, it confirms scgpt as the preferred encoder and lets us focus remaining budget on aggregation/fusion. This is more informative than testing transformer aggregation (config_048) because the representation quality is a prerequisite for any downstream aggregation to be effective, and the small accuracy gap between multimodal and RNA-only suggests the current RNA representation may be limiting the multimodal benefit.

The dominant finding is config_007 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, multimodal) achieving 0.706 accuracy, a massive jump over all other experiments (~0.51–0.54). The critical uncertainty is whether this gain is driven by the scvi_n200 RNA encoder itself or by its specific interaction with the image modality in fusion. Config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_018 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool, 0.530). If config_005 also shows a large accuracy gain, the RNA encoder is the primary driver and subsequent experiments should exploit scvi_n200 across fusion/aggregation settings. If it remains near 0.53, the multimodal interaction is the key, redirecting effort toward fusion and image-encoder choices. Resolving this distinction is the highest-value information gain for the remaining budget, as it determines the entire direction of future experiments.

Evidence: config_007 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is the strongest configuration at 0.706 acc / 0.667 F1, clearly outperforming both the scgpt-based multimodal models (~0.51-0.54) and the scvi_n200 RNA-only baseline (0.650). All completed experiments use avgpool aggregation; transformer aggregation has not been tested on any configuration. Question: Does replacing avgpool with transformer aggregation improve performance on the best-performing setup, or is simple averaging sufficient? This is a single-variable change (avgpool → transformer) from config_007, cleanly isolating the aggregation mechanism while holding RNA encoder, image encoder, profile setting, and fusion constant. Rationale: Aggregation determines how multiprofile information is combined, a foundational design choice. If transformer aggregation helps, it generalizes to other encoder combinations; if it does not, we can rule out that axis for the scvi_n200 family and focus remaining budget on fusion or image-encoder comparisons. This is the highest-information single step to exploit the strong scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l signal.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_003 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, acc=0.725). We have strong evidence that scvi_n200 is a far superior RNA encoder to scgpt, and that multimodal fusion with transformer aggregation and weighted fusion is beneficial. However, we have zero data on how resnet50 performs as the image encoder when paired with scvi_n200 — all scvi_n200 multimodal experiments used imagenet_vit_l. Question: config_012 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + transformer + weighted) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_003, isolating the image encoder choice in the highest-performing regime. Why this is the best use of the next budget: (1) It tests a fundamental architectural decision — whether the more expensive imagenet_vit_l is truly necessary or whether resnet50 suffices — which has major practical implications. (2) It is a controlled one-variable comparison, making the result interpretable. (3) If resnet50 performs comparably, it simplifies the design space and redirects future experiments toward other levers (e.g., profile setting, aggregation variants). If imagenet_vit_l is clearly superior, it confirms the importance of a strong image backbone and justifies further investment in that direction. This reduces uncertainty about a key design axis with no prior data in the scvi_n200 regime.

Evidence: The current best configuration is config_003 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1. All scvi_n200 multimodal models substantially outperform scgpt-based ones, and within scvi_n200, transformer aggregation + weighted fusion + imagenet_vit_l is the top combination. However, we have only tested weighted fusion with scvi_n200; the scgpt experiments (config_001 vs config_004) showed only a marginal weighted-over-concat advantage (~1.3% acc). Question: config_046 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) isolates the fusion method as the sole variable relative to the current best, testing whether weighted fusion provides a genuine contribution in the high-performing scvi_n200 regime or whether concat is sufficient. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable A/B comparison against the incumbent best, directly reducing uncertainty about a core design choice (fusion) without introducing confounds. If concat matches weighted, the design space simplifies; if weighted is clearly superior, we confirm the current best is well-chosen. Under a limited budget, exploiting the strongest evidence while isolating one remaining uncertainty is more efficient than jumping to a less-explored axis (e.g., singleprofile) that would change multiple variables simultaneously.

The RNA encoder axis has only been tested with scgpt (~0.51-0.54) and scvi_n200 (~0.65-0.72); pca_n2000 remains completely untested, leaving a large uncertainty about whether a simple linear dimensionality reduction can approach the performance of a learned generative representation. Config_019 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is a controlled comparison that holds model setting, profile setting, and aggregation constant while varying only the RNA encoder, enabling a direct three-way contrast with config_018 (scgpt, 0.530) and config_005 (scvi_n200, 0.650). This isolates the representation effect cleanly. If pca_n2000 approaches scvi_n200, it suggests the learned representation is not the critical factor and a cheaper encoder suffices; if it falls near scgpt, it confirms that a learned generative model is essential. Under a limited budget, resolving this fundamental question about representation quality is more informative than marginal tweaks to fusion or aggregation in an already well-characterized scvi_n200 regime.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero evidence about whether multimodal fusion adds value over a single modality, which encoder is strongest, or which design choices matter. The most fundamental uncertainty is the performance ceiling of each individual modality. 2) What this tests: config_004 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) establishes a strong single-modality baseline using the most powerful and well-validated image encoder in the available set (ViT-L pretrained on ImageNet). It is simple—no aggregation or fusion—so any performance is attributable purely to the image representation. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, a clean, strong baseline is the most informative anchor. Every subsequent multimodal experiment can be interpreted relative to this number: if multimodal configurations fail to exceed it, the added complexity is not justified; if they do, the gain is quantified. Starting with the strongest available single-modality model also avoids the risk of underestimating the baseline (which would make multimodal gains look artificially large). This single experiment reduces the largest source of uncertainty before any fusion, aggregation, or profile-setting decisions are made.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_004: image_only, singleprofile, ViT-L → 22.7% acc), leaving almost no information about whether the RNA modality contributes any signal for this task. Uncertainty: The most fundamental open question is whether RNA expression provides useful classification signal at all, independent of image. Question tested: config_009 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200, no aggregation/fusion) establishes a clean RNA-only baseline using a well-validated single-cell embedding (scVI), with the same singleprofile setting as the image baseline to keep the comparison fair. Why best next step: With only one data point, the highest-value experiment is one that isolates a single modality's contribution. If RNA-only performs comparably to image-only, both modalities carry signal and multimodal fusion is worth pursuing; if it is much worse, image dominates and we should focus budget on image-side improvements. This simple, low-confound experiment reduces the largest source of uncertainty before committing budget to more complex multimodal configurations where multiple variables (RNA encoder, aggregation, fusion) would be entangled.

Evidence: RNA (scvi_n200, singleprofile) achieves 52% accuracy vs. image (ViT-L) at only 22.7%, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. However, we have only one RNA data point, so we cannot yet judge whether 52% reflects the ceiling of RNA-based models or is specific to the scvi_n200 encoder. Uncertainty: Whether the RNA encoder choice (learned scvi vs. linear PCA) materially affects performance. This experiment (config_012: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_009, isolating the RNA encoder effect while holding profile setting and modality constant. It is the best use of the next budget slot because: (1) it reduces uncertainty about the RNA baseline before investing in more complex multimodal experiments, (2) if PCA matches or beats scvi_n200, it signals that the signal is linearly accessible and multimodal fusion may be more feasible; if PCA is much worse, it confirms the value of learned RNA representations and guides which encoder to pair with image in multimodal settings, (3) it changes only one variable, making the result interpretable.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 (config_009, acc=0.520) is our strongest baseline, while image-only with imagenet_vit_l (config_004, acc=0.227) is weak. We have zero multimodal results, so the central open question is whether fusing image features with the best RNA encoder actually improves over RNA alone. Question tested: config_039 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion, no aggregation) is the simplest possible multimodal extension of our best RNA baseline. It isolates the fusion benefit by (a) using the already-validated best RNA encoder, (b) using the image encoder whose standalone performance we already know, (c) keeping singleprofile to match the RNA baseline, and (d) using weighted fusion rather than concat, which can learn to downweight a weak image modality if it does not contribute. Why best next experiment: Under a tight budget, the highest-value question is whether multimodality helps at all before investing in multiprofile, transformer aggregation, or alternative encoders. This experiment gives a clean, interpretable signal: if it beats 0.520, multimodal fusion is worth further exploration; if it does not, we can redirect budget toward RNA encoder or profile-setting improvements. It changes only one design axis (adding image + fusion) relative to config_009, making the result easy to attribute.

Evidence: RNA encoder choice has shown a meaningful effect (scvi_n200: 0.520 vs pca_n2000: 0.485 in rna_only, a ~3.5% gap), and the current best multimodal result (config_039, 0.537) only marginally beats rna_only scvi_n200 (0.520), suggesting the RNA representation is the dominant signal source. Uncertainty: scgpt, a fundamentally different RNA encoder (masked-language-model based), has not been tested in any setting. Question: config_042 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) provides a clean one-variable comparison against config_009 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200), isolating the RNA encoder effect without confounding from image, fusion, or profile settings. Why best next: Completing the RNA-encoder ranking (scvi_n200 vs pca_n2000 vs scgpt) is the highest-information experiment because it determines which encoder to pair with image in subsequent multimodal tests. If scgpt substantially outperforms scvi_n200, the search direction shifts; if not, we can confidently exploit scvi_n200 in multimodal settings. This avoids changing multiple variables at once and directly reduces uncertainty about the most impactful design axis.

All five completed experiments use singleprofile, leaving the profile-setting dimension entirely unexplored. The best singleprofile result is config_009 (rna_only, scvi_n200, acc=0.520), and the best overall is config_039 (multimodal, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted, acc=0.537). Before investing budget in complex multimodal-multiprofile configurations, I need to know whether multiprofile actually adds signal. config_028 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is the cleanest possible test: it matches config_009 in modality and RNA encoder, changing only the profile setting (and the necessary aggregation). If multiprofile with a simple avgpool aggregation improves on 0.520, it justifies exploring multiprofile multimodal configs (e.g., config_045). If it does not, we learn that profile multiplicity is not a useful axis and can redirect budget toward fusion-type or image-encoder comparisons. This single experiment reduces the largest remaining uncertainty with minimal confounding variables.

Evidence: The largest single gain observed is from multiprofile+avgpool aggregation in the RNA-only setting (config_028: 0.650 vs config_009 singleprofile: 0.520, a +0.13 jump). Separately, adding image to singleprofile RNA gave a modest boost (config_039: 0.537 vs config_009: 0.520). Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the multiprofile+avgpool gain transfers to the multimodal setting or whether the two effects are additive/synergistic. This experiment (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) directly tests that combination while keeping all other choices at their best-evidenced values (scvi_n200 as top RNA encoder, imagenet_vit_l as the image encoder used in the only other multimodal result, avgpool as the aggregation that drove the largest gain, weighted fusion as in config_039). It is a clean one-variable extension of config_028 (adding image+fusion) and of config_039 (adding multiprofile+avgpool), making it the most informative next step under budget constraints.

The strongest evidence so far is that multiprofile with avgpool aggregation (config_028, RNA-only: 0.650) and multimodal multiprofile with avgpool + weighted fusion (config_045: 0.706) are the top performers, with scvi_n200 and imagenet_vit_l as the best encoders. The single biggest remaining uncertainty about the best configuration is whether the simple avgpool aggregation over multiple profiles is optimal, or whether a learned transformer aggregation could capture inter-profile interactions and push performance further. config_021 changes exactly one variable (aggregation: avgpool → transformer) relative to the current best config_045, keeping scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, and weighted fusion fixed. This isolates the aggregation effect cleanly. Under a limited budget, resolving whether the aggregation mechanism is a bottleneck is more informative than, e.g., swapping the image encoder or fusion type, because if transformer aggregation does not help, we can confidently commit to avgpool and focus remaining experiments on other axes; if it does help, it opens a high-value direction.

The current best configuration (config_021: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted; acc=0.725) has only been tested with 'weighted' fusion. The fusion strategy is a critical design decision that determines how RNA and image representations are combined, yet no high-performing configuration has used 'concat' fusion. Config_031 is an exact single-variable comparison to config_021, changing only fusion from weighted to concat while holding all other settings (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, multiprofile) constant. This cleanly isolates the effect of fusion strategy. If concat outperforms weighted, it reveals that a learned combination is superior and opens a new optimization direction; if it underperforms, it confirms weighted fusion is the right choice and redirects budget toward other untested dimensions (e.g., image encoder or RNA encoder). Under a limited budget, resolving this fundamental architectural question with a controlled A/B comparison is more informative than exploring a second variable simultaneously.

Evidence: The strongest gains so far come from (a) multi-profile aggregation (+0.13 over single-profile for RNA-only scvi_n200) and (b) transformer aggregation over avgpool in the multimodal multi-profile setting (0.7250 vs 0.7062, config_021 vs config_045). However, we have no RNA-only multi-profile result with transformer aggregation—only avgpool (config_028, 0.6501). Uncertainty: It is unclear whether the transformer's ~0.02 advantage in the multimodal setting stems from better cross-modal interaction or from generally superior multi-profile aggregation. Question tested: config_005 (RNA-only, multi-profile, scvi_n200, transformer) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_028, isolating the aggregation mechanism without confounding from the image modality. If it matches or exceeds 0.6501, the transformer benefit is a general multi-profile aggregation gain; if it plateaus, the transformer's value is specific to cross-modal fusion. Why this is the best next experiment: It reduces uncertainty about a core architectural choice (aggregation) in a well-characterized regime with a clear baseline, directly informs whether future effort should prioritize cross-modal fusion design or profile-aggregation design, and costs only one experiment in a setting where all other variables are already well understood.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about which design choices (modality, profile, encoder, aggregation, fusion) matter. The single most important unknown is the performance floor of the simplest reasonable model. 2) What this tests: config_002 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000, no aggregation, no fusion) is the most standard and minimal RNA baseline in cellular profiling. It isolates the core task (classification from bulk/PCA-reduced RNA) without any learned encoders, multiprofile complexity, or fusion. 3) Why it is the best use of the first budget slot: Establishing this clean baseline is a prerequisite for interpreting every subsequent experiment—without it, we cannot determine whether multimodality, multiprofile aggregation, or learned encoders (scGPT, scVI) actually add value over a simple PCA projection. It is also fast to train (no heavy encoder), making it an efficient first data point. All future multimodal or multiprofile configurations can be directly compared against this floor to quantify the marginal contribution of each added design dimension.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_002: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) at ~48.5% accuracy, giving us a weak baseline with no information about whether multiprofile representations add signal. Question: Does moving from single to multiple profiles (with the simplest aggregation, avgpool) improve performance while keeping the same PCA encoder? This isolates the profile/aggregation structural decision without confounding it with encoder or modality changes. Why this is the best next experiment: Multiprofile is a fundamental design axis that governs a large fraction of the remaining search space. Testing it with the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and the already-established PCA encoder gives a clean, low-risk comparison to the baseline. If multiprofile+avgpool substantially improves accuracy, it validates the multiprofile direction and justifies investing further in aggregation and fusion choices; if it does not, we can deprioritize many multiprofile configurations and focus budget on encoder or modality questions instead.

Evidence: config_002 (singleprofile, pca_n2000, no aggregation) scored 0.485 acc, while config_021 (multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) scored 0.591 acc—a +0.106 jump showing that multi-profile aggregation is highly beneficial. However, we only know avgpool works; we don't know whether a learned transformer aggregation captures inter-profile interactions that simple averaging misses. Question: config_006 is a clean single-variable change from config_021 (only aggregation: avgpool → transformer), isolating the effect of aggregation sophistication while holding encoder (pca_n2000), profile setting (multiprofile), and modality (rna_only) constant. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It directly extends our strongest result with the minimal change, giving the clearest signal. (2) The aggregation choice is a foundational architectural decision that will inform every subsequent multimodal experiment—knowing whether transformer or avgpool is superior before adding image modality prevents confounding. (3) It is computationally cheaper than testing a new learned encoder. (4) With only 2 completed experiments, reducing uncertainty on this core design axis is more valuable than jumping to a multimodal configuration where multiple new variables (image encoder, fusion, cross-modal interaction) would be introduced simultaneously.

Evidence: Multiprofile + avgpool (config_021, acc=0.591) is the clear best so far, outperforming singleprofile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). All three completed experiments use pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, so we have no information about whether a learned encoder (e.g., scgpt) could further improve performance. Question: Does replacing the linear PCA representation with the pre-trained scgpt encoder improve validation accuracy when holding profile (multiprofile) and aggregation (avgpool) fixed at their best-known settings? Why this is the best next step: It is a single-variable change from our strongest result, cleanly isolating the effect of the RNA encoder. If scgpt helps, it justifies further investment in learned representations and multimodal fusion; if it does not, it tells us PCA is sufficient and we should pivot budget toward testing image contributions or fusion strategies. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The best RNA-only configuration (config_021: multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieves 0.591 accuracy, and we've established that multiprofile >> singleprofile and avgpool >> transformer. The largest unexplored design dimension is whether adding image information improves upon this strong RNA-only baseline. Question: Does adding a standard image encoder (resnet50) with simple concatenation fusion to the best-known RNA pipeline yield a meaningful gain over 0.591? Why this experiment: config_024 keeps the three RNA-side choices (multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) fixed at their empirically best values and introduces only one new factor (image via resnet50 + concat), making it the cleanest single-variable test of the multimodal hypothesis. If it exceeds 0.591, we confirm images add complementary signal and can then explore better image encoders/fusion; if it does not, we learn that at least standard image features don't complement this RNA representation, redirecting budget toward RNA-side refinements. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best (config_024: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat; acc=0.619) shows that adding ResNet50 image features to the strong RNA backbone (pca_n2000 + avgpool) yields a meaningful gain over RNA-only (0.591). We also know avgpool > transformer and multiprofile > singleprofile, so those choices are settled. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether the image encoder quality is a bottleneck—ResNet50 is a relatively modest backbone, and a stronger pretrained encoder (ImageNet ViT-L) could provide richer visual representations that better complement the RNA signal. Question: config_029 changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l while holding all other settings identical to config_024, cleanly isolating the effect of image representation quality. Why this is the best next experiment: The image encoder is a high-impact design axis with no prior evidence in this search; a single-variable comparison against the current best directly tells us whether investing in a more powerful image model is worthwhile, which would guide all subsequent multimodal experiments. This is more informative than testing a minor fusion tweak (concat vs weighted) because the potential performance delta is larger and the design decision is more consequential.

Evidence: The current best configurations are config_029 (ViT-L, avgpool, concat: acc=0.629, F1=0.599) and config_024 (ResNet50, avgpool, concat: acc=0.619, F1=0.610), both using pca_n2000 + multiprofile + avgpool. The fusion strategy has only been tested as 'concat' in multimodal settings; weighted fusion remains unexplored. Question: Does weighted fusion (allowing learned modality weighting) outperform simple concatenation for combining RNA and image features? config_030 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted relative to config_029, isolating this single design decision. Why best next: It is the cleanest single-variable extension of the current best configuration, directly testing an unexplored and architecturally important design axis. A positive result would justify further exploration of weighted fusion across other encoder combinations; a null result would confirm concat as sufficient and redirect effort toward other levers (e.g., RNA encoder or aggregation). Under a limited budget, this maximizes information gain about a high-impact design choice while staying close to the proven high-performing region.

Evidence: The current best (config_030, acc=0.635) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder with imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, and weighted fusion. We have tested pca_n2000 and scgpt for RNA encoding, but scvi_n200 (a learned variational latent representation) remains untested in the multimodal setting. Question: config_019 is identical to config_030 except it swaps pca_n2000 → scvi_n200, cleanly isolating the RNA encoder effect while holding image encoder, aggregation, fusion, and profile setting at their known-best values. Why this is the best next experiment: It tests the single most important unexplored design dimension (RNA representation quality) with a minimal one-variable change from the current best, directly informing whether a nonlinear learned latent space can outperform a linear PCA projection in the multimodal pipeline. The result will either confirm pca_n2000 is sufficient or open a new promising direction, making it highly informative under the limited budget.

The strongest evidence so far is that scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted (config_019, acc 0.706) is the best configuration, with the RNA encoder choice (scvi_n200 vs pca_n2000) providing the largest single gain (+0.071). The one untested design dimension in this top-performing setup is aggregation: in RNA-only experiments avgpool beat transformer (0.591 vs 0.519), but that comparison used the simpler pca_n2000 encoder. With scvi_n200's richer per-profile representations, a transformer aggregator could potentially capture inter-profile interactions that a simple mean discards. config_031 changes only aggregation (avgpool→transformer) relative to config_019, isolating this single factor. If it matches or beats 0.706, it opens a new optimization axis; if it underperforms, it confirms avgpool is robust across encoder quality and redirects effort toward other levers. Under a tight budget, this single-variable test from the current best is the highest-information next step.

Evidence: The largest performance jump in the study came from switching the RNA encoder from PCA to scvi_n200 (0.635→0.706, config_030→config_019), while the image encoder switch from ResNet50 to ViT-L with PCA yielded only a ~1–2% gain (0.619→0.629, config_024→config_029). However, we have not tested whether the image encoder gap widens or narrows when paired with the stronger scvi_n200 encoder. Question: config_051 (scvi_n200 + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_019 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted → 0.706), isolating the image encoder effect under the best RNA encoder. Why this is the best next experiment: If the gap is small, we confirm the RNA encoder dominates and can focus future budget on RNA-side improvements or aggregation; if the gap is large, ViT-L is essential and we should prioritize image-side enhancements. This directly informs where to allocate remaining experiments and avoids conflating the two encoder contributions, making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about whether multimodal fusion, multiprofile aggregation, or learned encoders (scGPT, scVI) provide any benefit over a simple single-modality model. The most critical unknown is the performance ceiling of each individual modality. 2) What this tests: config_015 (image_only, singleprofile, ResNet50, no aggregation, no fusion) is the simplest possible image-based classifier. It establishes a clean performance baseline for the morphology modality alone, free from confounding by RNA fusion, profile aggregation, or encoder complexity. 3) Why it is the best first use of budget: Before investing in complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations, we need a reference point. A simple, well-understood baseline (ResNet50 on single images) is the most interpretable anchor: any future multimodal or multiprofile experiment can be directly compared to it to determine whether added complexity is justified. It also reduces uncertainty about the image modality's standalone contribution, which is essential for interpreting all subsequent fusion and aggregation experiments.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_015: image_only, singleprofile, resnet50 → acc 0.208, F1 0.172), which establishes a weak baseline. The critical uncertainty is whether adding the RNA modality provides any benefit over image-only features at all. Question: config_008 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, no aggregation, concat) keeps the image encoder (resnet50) and profile setting identical to the baseline, adds the simplest RNA representation (PCA, no learned parameters), and uses the simplest fusion (concatenation). This isolates the effect of adding RNA information with minimal confounding. Why this is the best next step: With a budget-limited search and only one data point, the highest-information experiment is to determine whether the multimodal direction is viable at all. If config_008 substantially outperforms config_015, we gain confidence to invest in richer RNA encoders, multiprofile settings, and learned aggregation/fusion. If it does not, we avoid wasting budget on increasingly complex multimodal variants and can redirect toward image-encoder upgrades or RNA-only baselines. Changing only the modality (and using the simplest possible RNA pipeline) makes the comparison clean and interpretable.

Evidence: config_015 (image_only, resnet50) scored 0.208 while config_008 (multimodal, pca_n2000+resnet50, concat) scored 0.527, indicating RNA is the dominant signal. However, we cannot yet decompose how much of the 0.527 comes from RNA alone versus synergistic interaction with image. Question: config_045 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) uses the exact same RNA encoder as our best model, giving a clean single-variable comparison. If RNA-only ≈ 0.527, image adds little and we can simplify; if RNA-only is substantially lower, the multimodal combination is genuinely synergistic and further multimodal optimization is warranted. Why this is the best next experiment: it is the single most informative missing data point for the modality-contribution question, uses the same encoder as the current best to isolate one variable, and directly informs whether to invest remaining budget in multimodal fusion/aggregation refinements or in RNA-encoder improvements.

Evidence: config_008 (multimodal, PCA, ResNet50, concat) achieves 0.527 acc, while image-only ResNet50 (config_015) is very weak at 0.208 and RNA-only PCA (config_045) is 0.485. The modest ~4% multimodal gain over RNA-only suggests the image branch may be underperforming due to a weak encoder. Question: config_016 changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L (keeping PCA, singleprofile, concat identical to config_008), cleanly isolating the effect of image representation quality. Why best next: With only 3 experiments done, the single largest uncertainty is whether the image modality can contribute more if given a stronger backbone. This single-variable comparison directly tells us whether to invest further in the image branch or focus on RNA encoder/fusion improvements, making it the highest-information experiment under budget constraints.

Evidence: Our best result so far is config_016 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + concat, singleprofile) at 0.535 acc / 0.519 F1, with config_008 (same but resnet50) at 0.527. RNA alone (pca_n2000) achieves 0.485, showing RNA is the dominant modality. However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (PCA n2000, a linear method) and one image encoder pair. The most critical untested design axis is the RNA representation: does a learned deep encoder (scgpt) outperform linear PCA? Uncertainty: It is unclear whether the RNA bottleneck is in the encoding method or elsewhere. Question tested: config_031 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + concat, singleprofile) is a clean single-variable swap from config_016, isolating the effect of RNA encoder (pca_n2000 → scgpt) while holding image encoder, fusion, and profile setting constant. Why this is the best next experiment: Under limited budget, resolving whether a learned generative RNA encoder meaningfully improves over PCA is the highest-information single experiment. If scgpt substantially outperforms PCA, it redirects the search toward learned encoders and multiprofile transformer aggregation. If it does not, PCA is near-optimal and we can confidently invest remaining budget in fusion strategy, multiprofile aggregation, or image encoder choices. This avoids confounding multiple variables and directly extends our strongest evidence.

Evidence: Our best result (config_016, acc=0.535) uses pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + concat fusion. We have strong evidence that PCA >> scGPT for the RNA encoder and that multimodal outperforms either unimodal baseline. However, all multimodal experiments so far used concat fusion; weighted fusion is completely untested. Question: config_003 is identical to config_016 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, isolating the fusion strategy as the single variable. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It is a clean one-variable A/B test against our strongest configuration, directly answering whether learned fusion weights improve over simple concatenation. (2) Fusion strategy is a foundational design choice that would affect every future multimodal configuration, so resolving it early has high leverage. (3) It avoids the confound of simultaneously changing profile setting and aggregation (as any multiprofile test would require), keeping the interpretation clean under a tight budget. (4) If weighted fusion helps, it immediately upgrades our best-known recipe; if it does not, we confirm concat is sufficient and can redirect effort toward the unexplored multiprofile axis with confidence.

Evidence: Our best singleprofile result (config_016: pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + concat, acc=0.535) clearly outperforms rna_only (0.485) and image_only (0.208), and fusion method (concat vs weighted) makes negligible difference. However, all six completed experiments are singleprofile; we have zero evidence on whether multiprofile + aggregation can improve performance. Question: config_044 extends our best singleprofile configuration (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat) to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool), directly testing whether additional profiles add signal beyond what a single profile captures. Why this is the best next step: (1) It isolates the multiprofile/aggregation question while holding the proven-best encoders and fusion constant, avoiding confounds from simultaneously changing multiple variables. (2) Starting with avgpool (simpler than transformer) is more informative: if it helps, multiprofile is beneficial without complex aggregation; if it doesn't, we can then test whether transformer aggregation is specifically needed. (3) The potential upside is large—if multiprofile pushes accuracy meaningfully above 0.535, it opens a productive search direction; if it doesn't, we efficiently rule out that axis and refocus on encoder or fusion refinements.

The strongest evidence so far is that multiprofile with avgpool aggregation (config_044, acc 0.629) substantially outperforms the best singleprofile multimodal result (config_016, acc 0.535), indicating that how profiles are aggregated is a critical design axis. However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool) in the multiprofile setting. config_038 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) differs from config_044 only in aggregation (transformer vs avgpool), giving a clean, single-variable comparison. If transformer aggregation improves performance, it reveals that inter-profile relationships are complex enough to benefit from attention-based modeling; if not, avgpool is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward other axes (e.g., fusion or image encoder). This is the highest-information next step because it directly extends the best-performing configuration while isolating the most impactful untested design choice.

Evidence: The strongest performance driver identified so far is the multiprofile + avgpool setting (config_044: 0.629 vs config_016 single-profile: 0.535), with pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + concat as the best-known encoder/fusion combination. RNA encoder choice has shown the largest single-variable effect (pca_n2000 vs scgpt: ~10% gap in single-profile), yet scvi_n200 remains completely untested across all experiments. Question: config_051 isolates the effect of switching the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 while holding all other components at their empirically best settings (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat). This tests whether a learned nonlinear variational representation captures cell-type structure that linear PCA misses, particularly under multiprofile aggregation where richer per-profile embeddings may benefit more from nonlinear compression. Why best next experiment: It changes exactly one variable (RNA encoder) from the current best configuration, directly addresses the largest remaining uncertainty (untested encoder class), and has high potential upside if scvi_n200 outperforms PCA. A negative result would also be informative, confirming PCA's sufficiency and redirecting effort toward other axes.

Evidence: config_051 (scvi_n200, vit_l, avgpool, concat, multiprofile) is the current best at 0.715 acc, and with pca_n2000, avgpool outperformed transformer aggregation by ~3% (0.629 vs 0.599). However, we have no evidence on whether this aggregation preference holds with the substantially stronger scvi_n200 encoder. Question: config_017 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer (keeping scvi_n200, vit_l, concat, multiprofile), cleanly isolating whether a more expressive aggregation mechanism can exploit the richer scvi_n200 representation. Why best next: It is a single-variable comparison directly against the current best, tests an important design axis at the performance frontier, and the outcome (whether transformer helps or hurts) will either open a new exploitation direction or confirm avgpool as the robust choice, reducing uncertainty about aggregation before committing further experiments.

With zero completed experiments, the priority is to establish a multimodal baseline using standard, simple choices across all design dimensions so that subsequent experiments can isolate the effect of changing one variable at a time. config_015 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) uses PCA as the RNA encoder (simple, interpretable baseline), ResNet50 as the image encoder (standard architecture), avgpool for aggregation, and concat for fusion — all minimal-complexity choices. This anchor lets me later test: (a) whether a learned RNA encoder (scvi/scgpt) improves over PCA, (b) whether ViT-L outperforms ResNet50, (c) whether transformer aggregation beats avgpool, (d) whether weighted fusion beats concat, and (e) whether singleprofile suffices vs. multiprofile. Starting here maximizes the number of clean single-variable comparisons available in subsequent experiments under the limited budget.

We have only one completed experiment (config_015: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat → 0.619 acc). The most critical uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion actually adds value over a single-modality baseline. config_023 (image_only, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool) is the cleanest single-variable comparison: it keeps the same image encoder (resnet50), profile setting (multiprofile), and aggregation (avgpool), differing only in the removal of the RNA modality. If image-only performance is close to 0.619, the RNA modality contributes little and we should focus on image encoder quality; if it is substantially lower, RNA is a meaningful contributor and we can exploit multimodal directions. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most fundamental design decision (multimodal vs. unimodal) under a limited budget, and avoids changing multiple variables simultaneously.

We have two completed experiments: config_015 (multimodal, pca_n2000+resnet50, avgpool, concat) at 0.619 acc and config_023 (image_only, resnet50, avgpool) at 0.328 acc. The ~29-point gap shows RNA adds substantial value, but we cannot yet decompose how much signal comes from RNA alone versus a synergistic interaction. config_013 (rna_only, pca_n2000, avgpool, multiprofile) completes the three-way modality decomposition (image_only vs RNA_only vs multimodal) while holding the RNA encoder, aggregation, and profile setting identical to config_015. If RNA-only approaches ~0.50, the image contribution is modest and future effort should target RNA encoder or fusion; if RNA-only is near image-only (~0.33), the gain is strongly synergistic and fusion/aggregation design becomes the priority. This single experiment resolves the largest remaining uncertainty about where to invest limited budget, making it more informative than testing a new encoder or fusion variant before we know which modality is the primary driver.

Evidence: config_015 (multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieves 0.6186 acc, only ~2.8% above RNA-only (config_013, 0.5907), while image-only (config_023) is very weak at 0.3275. This suggests the image modality contributes little, likely because ResNet50 is a relatively weak encoder for cellular images. Question: config_002 changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (keeping pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool, concat identical to config_015), directly testing whether a stronger image representation unlocks more signal for fusion. Why best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison against config_015, isolating the effect of image representation quality. If ViT-L substantially improves the multimodal model, it confirms the image encoder was the bottleneck and justifies further investment in image-side design (aggregation, fusion). If it does not, it indicates the image modality itself is limited regardless of encoder strength, redirecting effort toward RNA encoders or profile settings. Under a tight budget, this single experiment resolves a high-uncertainty question about whether the image branch is worth further optimization.

Evidence: All four completed experiments use avgpool aggregation with multiprofile, and the current best (config_002, acc=0.629) combines pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + concat fusion. We have no data on whether the aggregation method (how multiple profiles are combined) meaningfully affects performance. Question: config_024 is a clean single-variable change from config_002, swapping only avgpool → transformer aggregation while keeping pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, and concat fixed. This isolates whether a learned, attention-based aggregation of profiles can outperform uniform averaging. Why this is the best next experiment: With multiprofile data, the aggregation step is a fundamental architectural choice that directly governs how profile-level information is integrated. Transformer aggregation could capture non-uniform profile importance that avgpool cannot. Testing this on the current best configuration (config_002) gives the highest information value: if it helps, we identify a compounding architectural improvement; if it doesn't, we confirm avgpool is sufficient and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder or profile-setting questions. It avoids changing multiple variables simultaneously and builds directly on the strongest existing evidence.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_002 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat, acc=0.6287). RNA is clearly the dominant signal (RNA-only=0.5907 vs image-only=0.3275), and the multimodal gain over RNA-only is modest (~0.04). We have only tested PCA (a linear encoder) for RNA, leaving open whether a learned encoder (scvi_n200) captures nonlinear structure that PCA misses. Question: config_042 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 while keeping the image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), aggregation (avgpool), and fusion (concat) identical to config_002, giving a clean single-variable test of RNA representation quality. Why this is the best next experiment: Because RNA is the primary driver of performance, improving its representation has the highest expected impact. A positive result would justify further exploration of learned RNA encoders (e.g., scgpt) and potentially larger multimodal gains; a null result would confirm PCA sufficiency and redirect effort toward profile setting or fusion strategy. This is a high-information, low-confound experiment that directly extends the current best configuration.

Evidence: config_042 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.7150 acc, a large jump over config_002 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.6287, showing scvi_n200 is a far stronger RNA representation. However, we have only one scvi_n200 experiment and cannot yet attribute the gain to the RNA encoder alone versus the multimodal combination. With pca_n2000, RNA-only was 0.5907 vs multimodal 0.6287 (image added ~3.8 pp). Question: Does the image modality still contribute meaningful value when paired with the much stronger scvi_n200 encoder? config_010 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) isolates this by removing the image modality while keeping everything else aligned with config_042. Why best next experiment: It is a single-variable ablation of the current best configuration, directly reducing uncertainty about whether multimodal fusion is necessary or whether scvi_n200 alone drives the performance. This determines whether remaining budget should target multimodal refinements (fusion, aggregation) or RNA-encoder variants, making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under a limited budget.

Evidence: config_042 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat, multiprofile) is the clear best at 0.715 acc, and we have strong evidence that scvi_n200 and imagenet_vit_l are the dominant design choices. However, fusion strategy has never been tested—only concat has been used. Question: Does weighted fusion (config_040) improve over concat when all other settings match the best configuration? This is a clean single-variable comparison (fusion: concat→weighted) that isolates the effect of fusion while holding the proven-best encoder, image model, aggregation, and profile setting fixed. Rationale: Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information exploitation step—it directly extends the strongest evidence, tests an unexplored design axis (fusion), and the result will tell us whether further tuning of the best configuration is worthwhile or whether we should pivot to exploring scgpt or singleprofile next.

Evidence: RNA encoder is the most impactful design choice (scvi_n200 yields 0.650 RNA-only vs 0.591 for pca_n2000; multimodal scvi_n200+ViT-L reaches 0.715). However, scgpt has not been tested in any experiment, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of the RNA representation space. Question: config_008 (scgpt, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) is a single-variable change from the current best (config_042: scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, concat), isolating the effect of RNA encoder while holding image encoder, aggregation, and fusion constant. Why best next: The uncertainty around scgpt is the largest remaining unknown among all design dimensions. If scgpt is competitive or superior, it opens a new promising direction; if clearly inferior, we can confidently rule it out and consolidate on scvi_n200. This high-uncertainty, single-variable experiment maximizes information gain per budget unit compared to small refinements around the already-well-characterized scvi_n200+ViT-L configuration.

All 9 completed experiments use multiprofile, so the effect of profile setting (multiprofile vs singleprofile) is completely untested. The current best configuration (config_042: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, concat → 0.7150) strongly suggests that the scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + concat combination is the most promising direction. config_014 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, singleprofile, None, concat) changes only the profile setting relative to config_042, making it a clean isolated comparison of whether multiprofile averaging actually contributes to the ~0.715 accuracy or whether a single profile is sufficient. This is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact design question remaining: if singleprofile matches multiprofile, the pipeline is substantially simpler; if multiprofile is clearly superior, it validates the added complexity and focuses future effort on optimizing within the multiprofile space. Under a limited budget, resolving this fundamental axis before further tuning aggregation or fusion is the most efficient use of the next experiment.

With no prior experiments completed, the highest-priority question is whether basic multimodal fusion provides any signal over single-modality baselines, and what a reasonable 'floor' for multimodal performance looks like. config_011 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, no aggregation, concat) is the simplest multimodal configuration: it uses the most standard RNA encoder (scvi_n200), a lightweight and well-established image encoder (resnet50), no profile aggregation, and the simplest fusion (concat). This isolates the core question—does combining RNA and image representations via basic concatenation help?—without confounding from multiprofile aggregation, transformer pooling, or weighted fusion. Establishing this baseline first lets every subsequent experiment be interpreted as a controlled addition of complexity (e.g., multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, or stronger encoders), making the search trajectory maximally informative under a limited budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_011: multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200+resnet50, concat, acc≈0.536), the most critical uncertainty is whether the multimodal fusion is actually adding value over a unimodal baseline. config_008 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is the cleanest ablation: it keeps the exact same RNA encoder and profile setting as config_011 while removing only the image branch. This isolates the contribution of the image modality and the fusion step. If RNA alone performs comparably (~0.53+), the added complexity of multimodal fusion is questionable and subsequent experiments should focus on improving the RNA representation or trying a different image encoder. If RNA alone is substantially worse, it confirms the image modality is essential and justifies investing further in fusion/aggregation design. This single-variable comparison is the highest-information experiment under a limited budget, as it answers the foundational 'does multimodal help?' question before spending experiments on secondary design choices like fusion type, aggregation, or multiprofile settings.

We have multimodal (config_011: 0.5362) and rna_only (config_008: 0.5203) baselines, but no image_only baseline. This leaves a critical uncertainty: is the ~1.6% multimodal gain due to genuinely complementary information, or simply from added model capacity? config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50, no aggregation, no fusion) is the cleanest single-variable comparison to config_008, matching profile setting, aggregation, and fusion while swapping modality. It uses the same resnet50 encoder as config_011, enabling a direct three-way decomposition (RNA vs image vs both). Under a tight budget, resolving whether the image modality contributes independent signal is the highest-priority question, as it determines whether all downstream fusion, aggregation, and multiprofile experiments are worth pursuing or whether RNA-centric designs should be prioritized.

Evidence: RNA-only (scvi_n200) achieves 0.520 acc, image-only (resnet50) is very weak at 0.208, and the multimodal model (scvi_n200 + resnet50) barely improves over RNA-only (0.536 vs 0.520). This suggests the resnet50 image encoder is not contributing meaningful signal. The key uncertainty is whether a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) can make the image modality actually useful in a multimodal setting. config_002 changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l relative to config_011, keeping all other settings identical (scvi_n200, singleprofile, concat fusion, no aggregation). This isolates the effect of image encoder quality. If config_002 substantially exceeds config_011, the image modality is worth further investment (multiprofile, aggregation, fusion tuning). If it does not, we can confidently deprioritize image-heavy configurations and focus budget on RNA-side improvements (multiprofile, alternative RNA encoders). This single-variable comparison is the highest-information experiment available for resolving the central design question of whether multimodal fusion is worthwhile.

All four completed experiments use singleprofile, so the effect of multiprofile is completely untested—this is the largest source of design uncertainty. The evidence shows RNA (scvi_n200) is the dominant signal (rna_only=0.520 vs image_only=0.208), and multimodal with resnet50+concat (config_011, 0.536) is the best result so far. config_050 keeps the same model setting, encoders (scvi_n200 + resnet50), and fusion (concat) as config_011 but switches to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates the profile-setting effect with minimal confounding: if multiprofile+avgpool substantially improves over 0.536, it justifies investing further in transformer aggregation and other multiprofile variants; if it does not, we can deprioritize the large multiprofile portion of the search space. Under a limited budget, resolving this binary question is more informative than testing a smaller-axis change like weighted vs concat fusion.

Evidence: config_050 (multiprofile, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.632 accuracy—a large jump over all singleprofile results (~0.53), showing that multiprofile aggregation is the dominant design lever. However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool) in the multiprofile setting. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether the profiles interact in ways that a learned transformer aggregation could exploit beyond simple averaging. Config_001 (transformer aggregation, all else identical to config_050) provides a clean single-variable comparison that isolates the effect of aggregation method. If transformer substantially outperforms avgpool, it signals that profile interactions are complex and worth further investment; if it is comparable, avgpool is sufficient and we can redirect budget to other axes (fusion, encoder choice). Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information next step because it directly extends the strongest result found so far while testing a critical, unexplored design choice.

The strongest result (config_001: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat → 0.688) came from multiprofile + transformer aggregation, but we cannot yet attribute the gain to the image modality vs. the RNA multiprofile signal alone. Image-only performance is very weak (0.208), and in singleprofile the image adds only ~1.6% over RNA alone (0.536 vs 0.520). config_049 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) is a clean single-variable ablation of config_001 that isolates whether the image contributes meaningfully in the multiprofile+transformer regime. If rna_only+multiprofile+transformer approaches 0.688, the image is redundant and we should focus budget on RNA encoder variants (scgpt, pca_n2000); if it is substantially lower, the image provides complementary signal and we should explore image encoder and fusion choices. This resolves the single most important uncertainty for directing all subsequent experiments under the limited budget.

The current best is config_001 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat; acc=0.688). The single most informative next step is to isolate the effect of fusion strategy by changing only concat→weighted while holding all other settings identical (config_013). In singleprofile, fusion choice was never directly compared, and in the multiprofile+transformer setting the transformer already performs cross-profile aggregation, so the role of the final cross-modality fusion step (concat vs. learned weighted combination) is an open question. If weighted fusion helps, it is a free improvement on the best config; if not, we confirm concat is sufficient and can redirect budget toward image-encoder or RNA-encoder variations. This single-variable comparison maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

The current best (config_013, acc=0.713) uses scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder in a multiprofile + transformer + weighted-fusion architecture. The only RNA encoder tested in this top architecture is scvi_n200, leaving a critical uncertainty: does the choice of learned RNA representation matter? Since RNA is the dominant signal source (rna_only multiprofile+transformer = 0.653 vs image_only = 0.208), the RNA encoder is likely the highest-leverage design choice remaining. config_042 (scgpt, resnet50, transformer, weighted, multiprofile, multimodal) changes only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt while holding all other settings identical to config_013, giving a clean A/B comparison. If scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, it broadens the viable encoder space; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200's advantage and redirects budget toward image-encoder or other factors. This is the most informative single-variable experiment under the limited budget.

The current best configuration (config_013: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted; acc=0.713) establishes that multiprofile + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion is the dominant design. However, the image encoder choice remains underexplored in this top setting: resnet50 and imagenet_vit_l were only compared in single-profile mode (0.536 vs 0.532, nearly tied), and no multiprofile+transformer+weighted run has used imagenet_vit_l. Config_039 changes exactly one variable from config_013 (image encoder: resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l), making it a clean ablation of the image representation. If ViT-L matches or beats ResNet50 here, it opens a richer image backbone for future tuning; if it underperforms, it confirms ResNet50's adequacy and redirects budget toward other axes (e.g., RNA encoder alternatives). This is the highest-information single experiment available because it resolves a key representation uncertainty in the already-validated best pipeline without confounding multiple changes.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about how well any modality or design choice performs. The most fundamental uncertainty is whether the RNA signal alone is sufficient for the task, which determines how much value (if any) the image modality and multimodal fusion can add. 2) What this tests: config_015 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt, no aggregation, no fusion) is the simplest possible RNA-only model using a strong pretrained foundation-model encoder (scgpt). It establishes the performance floor for the RNA modality in isolation, with no confounding from image features, fusion strategy, or aggregation. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the highest-value first measurement is a clean, interpretable baseline. All subsequent multimodal experiments (configs 002–051) can be directly compared against this number to isolate the marginal contribution of the image modality and the fusion/aggregation choices. Choosing a more complex multimodal config first would conflate many design dimensions and make it impossible to attribute performance to any single choice. Starting with the strongest RNA encoder (scgpt) ensures the baseline is not artificially low, making any future multimodal gain a meaningful signal rather than a trivial one.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: I have a single RNA-only baseline (config_015: singleprofile, scgpt → acc 0.411, F1 0.378). The most critical open question is whether the image modality carries any discriminative signal at all. Without an image-only baseline, any future multimodal result would be uninterpretable—improvement could come from image information, from multiprofile/aggregation machinery, or from both. 2) What this tests: config_041 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l, no aggregation, no fusion) isolates the contribution of the image modality under the same simplicity constraints as the RNA baseline (single profile, no aggregation, no fusion). It directly answers: 'Does image data alone provide comparable or complementary signal to RNA?' 3) Why it is the best use of the next experiment: It is the single most informative experiment to reduce uncertainty about the fundamental design decision (include image or not). It changes only the modality relative to config_015 while holding profile setting, aggregation, and fusion constant, giving a clean unimodal-to-unimodal comparison. This baseline is a prerequisite for interpreting any subsequent multimodal or multiprofile experiment, making it the highest-value next step under a limited budget.

Evidence: RNA (scgpt, singleprofile) achieves 41.1% acc while image (ViT-L, singleprofile) achieves only 22.7% acc, indicating RNA is the dominant modality. The critical uncertainty is whether the weaker image modality provides complementary information that improves upon RNA alone. This experiment (config_049: multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, concat fusion) is the most controlled test of that question—it keeps the same RNA encoder, same image encoder, and same singleprofile setting as both prior experiments, adding only the image stream and a simple concat fusion. If accuracy exceeds ~41%, multimodal fusion is worth further investment; if it does not, we can redirect the remaining budget toward RNA-specific improvements (multiprofile, aggregation, alternative encoders). This is the highest-information next step under a limited budget because it resolves the fundamental architectural question before committing experiments to the much larger multimodal configuration space.

Evidence: All three completed experiments use singleprofile. RNA-only (scgpt) achieves 0.411 acc, image-only (ViT-L) is weak at 0.227, and multimodal concat (scgpt+ViT-L) reaches 0.435 acc / 0.423 F1 — a modest but consistent gain, especially in F1. The largest untested design dimension is the profile setting (single vs. multiprofile), which also introduces the aggregation choice. Question: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile (with the simplest aggregation, avgpool) improve performance while keeping the same encoders (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l) and fusion (concat) as the best result (config_049)? This isolates the profile/aggregation effect with minimal confounding. Why this is the best next experiment: config_006 changes only the profile setting (and adds the simplest aggregation) relative to the current best, making it a clean controlled comparison. If multiprofile+avgpool helps, we gain a new promising axis and can later test transformer aggregation; if it does not, we rule out profile multiplicity as a key lever and redirect budget toward encoder or fusion choices. Under a limited budget, resolving this high-uncertainty, high-impact design question with a single-variable change is more informative than jumping to a more complex configuration (e.g., transformer aggregation or a different encoder) that would confound multiple factors.

The strongest result so far is config_006 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.5176 acc, a large jump over config_049 (same encoders, singleprofile, no aggregation, concat) at 0.4348. However, that jump conflates multiprofile with the introduction of avgpool aggregation, so we cannot yet tell whether aggregation method itself is a meaningful lever. Config_009 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer, concat) changes exactly one factor relative to config_006: aggregation from avgpool to transformer, while keeping the same RNA encoder, image encoder, profile setting, and fusion method. This isolates the effect of aggregation expressiveness. If transformer aggregation matches or exceeds avgpool, it suggests the multiprofile gain is robust to aggregation choice and we can focus on other axes (fusion, encoders). If it underperforms, avgpool is confirmed as the better compressor and we can exploit that. Under a tight budget, this single-factor comparison from the best-known configuration is the most information-dense next step.

The evidence shows a clear progression: rna_only singleprofile (0.411) → multimodal singleprofile concat (0.435) → multimodal multiprofile avgpool concat (0.518), with the multiprofile+avgpool pipeline being the strongest configuration so far. Within this best pipeline (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool), the only untested design dimension is fusion type — all completed multimodal experiments used concat. config_016 is identical to config_006 except it uses weighted fusion instead of concat, providing a clean single-variable comparison that isolates the effect of the fusion strategy. If weighted fusion improves on concat, it identifies a further performance lever; if it does not, it confirms concat is sufficient and redirects exploration toward other dimensions (RNA encoder, image encoder). Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information next step because it exploits the strongest known direction while testing the one remaining unexplored knob within that exact pipeline, without introducing confounding changes.

Evidence: The current best (config_016: scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.542) establishes that multiprofile, avgpool aggregation, and weighted fusion are beneficial. However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (scgpt) across all experiments, leaving the RNA representation axis completely unexplored. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether the specific scgpt architecture is critical or whether a different learned RNA representation (e.g., scvi_n200) would perform comparably or better in the multiprofile + weighted-fusion setting. This experiment (config_033: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) isolates the RNA encoder choice while holding all other settings at their best-known values. If scvi_n200 matches scgpt, it indicates the RNA representation is flexible and we can focus optimization elsewhere; if it is substantially worse, it confirms scgpt's specific value and narrows the search. This is the highest-information experiment because the RNA modality dominates performance (RNA alone 0.41 vs image alone 0.23), so understanding which RNA encoder is most effective is the key remaining design question.

The dominant finding from the history is that switching the RNA encoder from scgpt to scvi_n200 (config_033: 0.706 acc) produced a ~16-point accuracy jump over the prior best (config_016: 0.542 acc), far exceeding any other single design change. However, we have only one data point with scvi_n200, and it is multimodal. The critical open question is whether the image modality (imagenet_vit_l, which alone scores only 0.227) is actually contributing to config_033's strong performance, or whether scvi_n200 RNA features alone are already sufficient. config_028 (rna_only, scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable ablation of config_033—removing only the image branch while keeping the same RNA encoder and profile aggregation. If RNA-only performance is near 0.70, the image adds little and we can simplify; if it drops substantially, the multimodal fusion is genuinely valuable and we should next explore image encoder alternatives (e.g., resnet50 via config_027). Under a limited budget, resolving whether the image modality earns its complexity cost is the highest-information experiment before investing further in fusion or encoder variants.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_033 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) at 0.7062 acc. The RNA-only baseline with the same encoder/profile/aggregation (config_028) achieves 0.6501, leaving a 0.056 gap that conflates two factors: the image modality and the weighted fusion. With scgpt, weighted fusion improved over concat by ~0.024 (config_016 vs config_006), but we have no data on whether this holds for the richer scvi_n200 representations. Question: config_013 changes only fusion (weighted→concat) relative to config_033, isolating the fusion effect under scvi_n200. It also lets us decompose the image contribution: if config_013 is close to 0.6501, the gain is mostly from weighted fusion; if it is substantially above 0.6501, the image modality itself is adding signal. Why best next: This is a single-variable, high-information experiment that simultaneously clarifies (a) whether weighted fusion is critical with scvi_n200 and (b) how much the image encoder contributes. Under a limited budget, resolving whether to invest further in fusion design or image-encoder selection is the most consequential uncertainty remaining.
