The current best configuration (config_013: scvi_n200, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat; acc=0.715) has been validated across multiple runs, but the image encoder dimension remains completely unexplored—only imagenet_vit_l has been tested, and its image-only baseline was very weak (0.227). Config_018 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat) changes only the image encoder relative to config_013, cleanly isolating the effect of image representation while holding the proven-best RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation, and fusion fixed. This is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact design choice left untested: if resnet50 outperforms imagenet_vit_l, it opens a new optimization direction; if it underperforms, it confirms imagenet_vit_l is the right choice and lets us focus remaining budget on other axes (e.g., pca_n2000 or transformer aggregation). Under a limited budget, resolving this binary image-encoder question with a single controlled comparison is more informative than testing a second-order variation (e.g., transformer aggregation) on an already well-characterized axis.

With zero completed experiments, the most critical uncertainty is establishing a performance floor for the RNA modality alone, which serves as the reference against which all multimodal, multiprofile, and learned-encoder choices will be judged. config_022 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest possible RNA baseline: a well-understood linear encoder (PCA), no multi-profile aggregation, no image branch, and no fusion step. This isolates the raw signal quality of the RNA data with minimal confounding from learned representations or architectural complexity. It directly tests whether a basic RNA-only model achieves competitive accuracy, which is essential before investing budget in more complex multimodal or multiprofile variants. Under a limited budget, anchoring the search with a clean, interpretable baseline is the highest-information first step: it calibrates expectations, reveals whether the task is already solvable with simple features, and provides a clear ablation target for every subsequent experiment.

The only completed experiment (config_022) is a minimal RNA-only baseline (pca_n2000, singleprofile, no aggregation) achieving ~48.5% accuracy. The largest unresolved uncertainty is whether adding the image modality provides any benefit at all. Config_002 is the cleanest test of this question: it keeps the RNA encoder (pca_n2000), profile setting (singleprofile), and aggregation (None) identical to config_022, and introduces only the image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) with the simplest fusion (concat). This isolates the effect of adding image information. If accuracy improves substantially, it justifies further investment in multimodal designs and lets us then probe encoder choice, fusion strategy, and profile/aggregation settings. If it does not improve, it strongly suggests the image modality (at least with this RNA representation) is not contributing, redirecting the budget toward RNA-encoder or profile-setting experiments. Under a limited budget, resolving this fundamental modality question before exploring more complex interactions is the highest-information next step.

Evidence: config_022 (RNA-only, PCA, single) achieved 0.485 acc and config_002 (multimodal, PCA, ViT-L, concat, single) achieved 0.535 acc, confirming that adding an image modality with PCA RNA helps. However, we have no information on whether the RNA encoder choice matters—PCA is a simple linear baseline, and a learned representation like scgpt could capture nonlinear biological structure. Question: config_004 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scgpt while holding everything else identical to config_002 (multimodal, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l, concat fusion). This is a clean single-variable A/B comparison that isolates the RNA representation effect. Why best next: With only 2 experiments done, the RNA encoder is the largest untested design axis that could substantially shift performance. A clean comparison to config_002 will tell us whether learned RNA encoders are worth pursuing, directly guiding whether subsequent experiments should focus on scgpt/scvi variants or whether PCA suffices. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_002 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieved the best accuracy (0.5353), substantially outperforming both the RNA-only baseline (config_022, 0.4849) and the scgpt variant (config_004, 0.4348). This strongly suggests pca_n2000 is the superior RNA encoder and that adding the image modality via concat provides a meaningful gain. However, fusion strategy has only been tested as 'concat' so far. Question: config_005 is identical to config_002 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, cleanly isolating the effect of fusion strategy while holding RNA encoder, image encoder, and profile setting constant. Why this is best: With only 3 completed experiments, the evidence base is sparse. This single-variable comparison directly extends our best result and answers whether a more sophisticated fusion (weighted) can further improve on the promising pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l combination. If weighted fusion helps, it opens a high-value direction; if not, we confirm concat is sufficient and can redirect budget toward profile/aggregation questions. It avoids changing multiple factors simultaneously and is the most information-dense next step.

Evidence: Our best result (config_002, acc=0.5353) uses multimodal + pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + concat in singleprofile mode. All four completed experiments are singleprofile, so the effect of multiprofile (and its required aggregation step) is completely unexplored. This is the largest remaining uncertainty in the design space. Question: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation improve performance when all other settings (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat) are held at their known-best values? Why this experiment: config_021 is the minimal, clean extension of our best configuration—changing only the profile setting (and its coupled aggregation), which isolates the multiprofile/aggregation effect. If it outperforms config_002, it validates the added complexity and justifies further exploration of aggregation types (transformer) and other encoders in the multiprofile regime. If it underperforms, it tells us singleprofile is sufficient and we can focus budget on image-encoder or RNA-encoder variations within singleprofile. Either outcome substantially reduces uncertainty about a major design axis under a limited budget.

Evidence: The largest performance jump so far came from moving singleprofile→multiprofile (config_002: 0.535 → config_021: 0.629), and the current best (config_021) uses avgpool aggregation. We have no multiprofile data with transformer aggregation, leaving open whether a more expressive aggregation could further improve over simple averaging. Question: config_038 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) is identical to config_021 except aggregation changes from avgpool to transformer, cleanly isolating the effect of aggregation strategy. Why best next experiment: It is a single-variable ablation on the most promising configuration, directly testing whether the multiprofile gain can be amplified by learned aggregation. If transformer aggregation helps, it opens a rich sub-space (configs 045, 035, 036, etc.); if it does not, it confirms avgpool is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward RNA encoder or image encoder variations in the multiprofile setting. This is more informative than testing fusion (concat≈weighted already shown in singleprofile) or switching encoders (higher risk of confounding).

Evidence: The largest performance jump (0.535→0.629) came from switching to multiprofile+avgpool, and the current best (config_021) is multimodal. However, we have no rna_only multiprofile baseline, so we cannot decompose how much of the 0.629 is driven by multi-profile RNA aggregation versus the image modality. Question: config_032 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) directly isolates the RNA multiprofile contribution. It enables two clean comparisons: (1) vs config_022 (rna_only, singleprofile, 0.485) to measure the multiprofile gain for RNA alone, and (2) vs config_021 (multimodal, multiprofile, 0.629) to quantify the image's marginal contribution in the multiprofile regime. Why best under budget: A single experiment yields two critical decompositions, reducing uncertainty about whether the image encoder is a major performance driver or a minor add-on. This determines whether future budget should prioritize image-encoder variants (e.g., resnet50) or RNA-side improvements (e.g., scvi_n200), making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice.

Evidence: config_021 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.629 acc. In singleprofile, concat (0.535) and weighted (0.532) fusion were nearly equivalent, but we have no multiprofile data on weighted fusion. Question: Does weighted fusion interact differently with multiprofile avgpool aggregation than concat does? This is a single-variable change from the current best, isolating the fusion mechanism. Rationale: Under a limited budget, testing one design axis at a time from the best-known configuration is the most efficient way to determine whether a simple swap can improve performance or confirm that concat is already optimal in this regime. If weighted fusion matches or exceeds concat, it opens a new axis (e.g., combining with alternative RNA encoders); if it underperforms, we can rule out weighted fusion and focus remaining budget on other untested dimensions (e.g., image encoder or RNA encoder in multiprofile).

Evidence: The current best configuration (config_014: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.635) establishes that multiprofile + avgpool + weighted fusion is a strong pipeline. However, the RNA encoder choice remains the largest untested uncertainty: PCA_n2000 works well, scGPT performed poorly (0.435 vs 0.535 in single-profile), but scvi_n200 (a 200-dim VAE latent) is a fundamentally different learned representation that has not been tested. Question: config_030 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 while holding all other settings at their best-known values (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted), providing a clean single-variable comparison against config_014. Why best: Under a limited budget, resolving whether a learned RNA encoder can match or beat PCA in the best-known pipeline is the highest-information next step. If scvi_n200 improves on PCA, it opens a new optimization axis; if it does not, we confirm PCA as the robust choice and can redirect effort toward the image encoder or other dimensions. This avoids the risk of changing multiple variables and directly extends the strongest evidence we have.

The current best (config_030: scvi_n200, vit_l, avgpool, weighted) achieved 0.7062 acc. With pca_n200, avgpool clearly outperformed transformer (0.6352 vs 0.5988, ~3.6 pp gap), but scvi_n200 produces a fundamentally different, richer latent representation that may interact with aggregation differently. Config_007 changes only aggregation (avgpool→transformer) while holding scvi_n200, vit_l, multiprofile, and weighted fusion constant, giving a clean single-variable test of whether transformer aggregation could exploit the richer scvi embeddings. This is the highest-impact remaining uncertainty: if transformer matches or beats avgpool here, it opens a new architectural direction; if not, we can confidently lock in avgpool and redirect budget to other axes (e.g., image encoder). It is a logical exploitation of the best configuration while still resolving a key design question.

With no completed experiments, the priority is to establish a clean, interpretable baseline that anchors all future comparisons. Config_013 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, no aggregation, weighted fusion) uses the simplest reasonable choice in every design dimension: PCA is a standard, computationally cheap RNA representation; Imagenet ViT-L is a strong pretrained image encoder; singleprofile avoids the added complexity of multiprofile aggregation; and weighted fusion is a simple, interpretable combination. This baseline will let subsequent experiments isolate the marginal contribution of each design axis—e.g., swapping to rna_only (config_047) or image_only (config_026) to test modality value, upgrading to multiprofile + aggregation to test whether profile complexity helps, or changing the RNA encoder to scgpt/scvi to test representation quality. Starting from the simplest multimodal configuration rather than a complex one avoids confounding multiple design choices and gives the most informative reference point under a limited budget.

1) Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_013: multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, ViT-L, weighted fusion → 0.532 acc). With a single data point, we have no basis to judge whether the multimodal combination is actually contributing value or whether the image modality alone achieves similar performance. 2) Question: config_026 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is the exact image-only counterpart to config_013, differing only in the removal of the RNA modality. This cleanly isolates whether adding PCA-encoded RNA to ViT-L features provides a meaningful accuracy/F1 gain. 3) Why best next: Under a limited budget, the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact question is whether multimodal fusion is warranted at all. If config_026 matches or exceeds config_013, the search should pivot toward image-encoder quality or profile/aggregation strategies rather than RNA encoder selection. If config_013 clearly wins, we confirm multimodal is productive and can then spend remaining budget isolating RNA encoder or fusion effects. This single-variable comparison maximizes information per experiment.

Evidence: config_013 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, ViT-L, weighted fusion) achieved 0.5318 acc, while config_026 (image_only, ViT-L) achieved only 0.2266 acc, confirming RNA contributes substantially. However, we have no information on whether the weighted fusion strategy is actually beneficial versus a simpler concatenation. Question: config_007 is identical to config_013 except fusion changes from 'weighted' to 'concat', providing a clean single-variable A/B test that isolates the fusion method's effect. Why best next experiment: With only two data points, the most efficient use of the next budget slot is to resolve uncertainty about a design choice (fusion) that applies to every multimodal configuration in the search space. If concat outperforms weighted (or vice versa), the finding generalizes across all remaining multimodal configs, dramatically narrowing the effective search. This follows the principle of isolating one design variable when evidence is sparse, rather than jumping to larger architectural changes (e.g., multiprofile + transformer) that would confound multiple factors.

All three completed experiments are multimodal or image-only; we have no RNA-only baseline. config_026 shows image alone is very weak (acc 0.227), while multimodal configs with pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l reach ~0.53, but we cannot yet quantify how much of that performance comes from RNA vs. the image modality and fusion. config_047 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) changes only the model setting from multimodal to rna_only while keeping the same RNA encoder and profile setting as config_013/007, giving a clean single-variable comparison. If RNA alone approaches ~0.50, the image modality adds little and we should focus budget on RNA encoder/aggregation choices; if it is substantially lower (e.g., ~0.35), the image contribution is large and we should invest in better image encoders and fusion. This baseline is the single most informative missing data point for guiding all subsequent design decisions under a tight budget.

Evidence: Our best result so far is config_007 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat) at 0.5353 acc. RNA alone gives 0.4849 and image alone only 0.2266, so the multimodal gain is modest (~5%). We have zero data on whether multiprofile + aggregation improves over singleprofile — this is the largest untested architectural axis. Question: config_049 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) directly compares multiprofile with simple average-pool aggregation against our best singleprofile baseline, holding RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion method identical. Using avgpool (rather than transformer) keeps the change minimal, isolating the 'multiple profiles' effect from the 'complex aggregation' effect. Why this is the best next experiment: if multiprofile+avgpool helps, it validates the profile/aggregation axis and justifies further investment (e.g., transformer aggregation); if it does not, we can rule out that axis and focus remaining budget on RNA encoder choice (scgpt, scvi_n200) or image encoder. This single experiment resolves a major source of uncertainty with minimal confounding changes.

Evidence: config_049 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.629 acc, a large jump over the best singleprofile config (config_007, 0.535), indicating that multiprofile + aggregation is a critical design axis. However, we do not yet know whether the gain comes from simply having multiple profiles or specifically from the avgpool aggregation. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool when all other settings (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat fusion, multiprofile) are held constant? config_023 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer, directly isolating this variable against the current best. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison against the strongest result, it tests whether a more expressive aggregation is worth the added complexity (important for compute budget), and the answer will determine whether to invest further in aggregation design or pivot to other axes (e.g., RNA encoder choice) in subsequent experiments.

Evidence: The current best result is config_049 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.629 acc, a large jump over singleprofile (~0.535). In singleprofile, concat and weighted fusion were nearly identical (0.535 vs 0.532), but we have no evidence about fusion in the multiprofile+aggregation regime where the dynamics may differ. Question: config_050 changes only the fusion method (weighted vs concat) while holding all other settings identical to config_049, cleanly isolating the fusion effect in the multiprofile+avgpool context. Why best next: It is a minimal one-variable A/B comparison against the current best, directly reducing uncertainty about whether weighted fusion interacts beneficially with multiprofile aggregation. The answer will determine whether to keep concat or switch to weighted for all subsequent multiprofile experiments, making it the highest-information-per-budget choice before exploring RNA encoders or image backbones.

Evidence: The best configuration so far (config_050: pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.6352 acc / 0.6183 F1. All completed experiments used pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, yet RNA is the dominant modality (RNA-only 0.485 vs image-only 0.227), making the RNA representation choice a high-impact, completely unexplored dimension. Question: Does replacing the linear PCA representation with a pretrained nonlinear encoder (scgpt) improve multimodal performance, while holding all other settings (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) at their best-known values? Why this experiment: It changes exactly one variable (RNA encoder) from the current best config, cleanly isolating the representation effect. scgpt is the most expressive RNA encoder in the pool; if it fails to beat PCA, that is strong evidence that the linear representation is already sufficient and further gains must come from other axes (image encoder, aggregation). This maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best config (config_050: multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.635) has been established, and we know multiprofile >> singleprofile and avgpool > transformer for aggregation. However, the image encoder dimension is completely unexplored in the multiprofile setting — all multiprofile experiments used imagenet_vit_l. Question: config_051 changes only the image encoder to resnet50 (keeping pca_n2000, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile), giving a clean single-variable comparison to config_050. This isolates whether the image representation is a critical design choice or whether the pipeline is robust to encoder choice. Why best next: Under limited budget, testing a completely unexplored dimension (image encoder) with a minimal change from the best-known config maximizes information gain. If resnet50 performs similarly, we learn the image encoder is not a bottleneck and can focus remaining experiments on other axes; if it degrades substantially, we confirm imagenet_vit_l is essential and should be locked in. This is more informative than completing the aggregation×fusion 2x2 (config_004), where the avgpool advantage is already strongly suggested.

Evidence: Multi-profile + avgpool + weighted fusion is clearly the best architecture (config_050: 0.6352, config_051: 0.6390). Within this setting, pca_n2000 substantially outperforms scgpt (0.6352 vs 0.5420 in config_009), but scvi_n200 has not yet been tested in the multi-profile regime. Uncertainty: We do not know where a learned deep generative encoder (scvi_n200, 200-dim latent) falls relative to linear PCA (pca_n2000, 2000-dim) — this is a major representation design choice that affects a large portion of the configuration space. Question tested: config_027 (scvi_n200, vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) is a single-variable swap from config_050 (pca_n2000, vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile), cleanly isolating the RNA encoder effect in the best-performing architecture. Why best next experiment: Resolving the RNA encoder ranking (pca vs scvi vs scgpt) in the top configuration is the highest-information experiment remaining — it either confirms PCA as sufficient (letting us focus budget on other axes) or reveals a better representation that could shift the entire search direction. It changes only one variable, making the result interpretable.

With no completed experiments, there is zero evidence about which design dimensions matter. The most important initial uncertainty is whether the core multimodal fusion hypothesis holds at all. Config_001 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, concat) is the cleanest baseline multimodal configuration: it pairs the strongest available RNA encoder (scgpt, a pretrained scRNA-seq foundation model) with the strongest image encoder (ViT-L pretrained on ImageNet), uses the simplest profile setting (singleprofile, so no aggregation is needed), and applies the most straightforward fusion (concat). This isolates the question 'does combining these two strong unimodal representations yield a useful multimodal model?' without confounding from multiprofile aggregation, learned fusion weights, or weaker encoders. If it performs well, the next experiment can be a single-modality baseline (e.g., image-only or RNA-only) to quantify the multimodal benefit. If it underperforms, we can decompose whether the issue is encoder choice, fusion strategy, or the modality combination itself. Starting here gives the most information per experiment under a limited budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, concat; acc≈0.435), the most critical uncertainty is whether the multimodal setup is actually outperforming a unimodal baseline. config_043 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) changes only the model setting relative to config_001 while keeping the same image encoder and profile setting, cleanly isolating the contribution of the RNA modality. If image-only performs comparably to 0.435, the RNA branch or fusion is not adding value and subsequent experiments should target representation or fusion improvements; if it is substantially lower, multimodal fusion is confirmed as beneficial and we can exploit that direction. Establishing this baseline before varying encoders, aggregation, or fusion is the highest-information single experiment under a tight budget, since it determines whether the entire multimodal search space is worth exploring further.

Evidence: config_001 (multimodal, scgpt+imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieves 43.5% acc, while config_043 (image_only, imagenet_vit_l) achieves only 22.7% acc, suggesting RNA contributes substantially. However, we have no RNA-only baseline, so we cannot determine whether the 21-point gain comes from additive modality contributions or synergy. Question: config_031 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) isolates the RNA contribution using the same encoder and profile setting as config_001. Together with the two completed experiments, this trio decomposes the multimodal benefit: if RNA alone is ~35-40%, the multimodal gain is modest; if it is ~20-25%, the combination is synergistic and further multimodal optimization is warranted. Why best next: this is a single-variable change (removing image) from the current best, it resolves a fundamental uncertainty about whether RNA is the primary signal carrier, and it directly informs whether subsequent budget should be spent optimizing fusion/aggregation in the multimodal setting or exploring RNA-only or alternative encoder configurations.

Evidence: config_001 (multimodal, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieves 0.4348 acc, only marginally above RNA-only scgpt (config_031, 0.4106), while image-only is weak (0.2266). This small multimodal gain (~0.024) raises the question of whether the concat fusion is suboptimal and suppressing the image contribution. Question tested: config_032 is identical to config_001 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, isolating the effect of the fusion mechanism on how well the (weaker) image branch contributes. Why best next step: It is the cleanest single-variable comparison available, directly addressing whether the modest multimodal advantage can be amplified by a learned weighting scheme. If weighted fusion meaningfully improves accuracy, it justifies further investment in fusion/aggregation design; if not, it indicates the image modality's contribution is inherently limited and effort should shift to RNA encoder choice or image encoder selection. This is more informative than jumping to multiprofile or changing the RNA encoder, which would conflate multiple variables.

Evidence: RNA (scgpt) alone achieves 0.4106 acc vs image alone at 0.2266, making RNA the dominant signal. Multimodal scgpt+ViT-L with concat (config_001, 0.4348) modestly beats RNA alone, and concat slightly outperforms weighted fusion (config_032, 0.4224). However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (scgpt). Uncertainty: It is unknown whether the learned scgpt representation is essential or whether a simpler PCA-based encoding captures comparable signal, which would drastically affect the complexity/performance tradeoff for all downstream multimodal experiments. This experiment (config_049) changes only the RNA encoder from scgpt to pca_n2000 while holding model_setting=multimodal, profile=singleprofile, image_encoder=imagenet_vit_l, and fusion=concat constant—exactly matching config_001's other settings. This isolates the RNA encoder effect in a clean single-variable comparison. It is the best use of the next budget slot because the RNA encoder is the primary performance driver, and resolving whether scgpt's learned features add meaningful value over PCA before investing in multiprofile/aggregation experiments prevents building on a potentially suboptimal or unnecessary foundation.

The strongest signal from completed experiments is that pca_n2000 dramatically outperforms scgpt as the RNA encoder (0.5353 vs 0.4348 in multimodal concat). However, we do not yet know how much of config_049's performance comes from the image modality versus the RNA encoder alone. With scgpt, image added only ~2.4 points (0.4348 multimodal vs 0.4106 RNA-only), but with pca_n2000 the picture may be very different. config_012 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is a clean single-variable ablation of config_049 that isolates the image contribution. If RNA alone approaches ~0.50+, the image modality is marginal and future budget should focus on RNA encoder/aggregation choices; if RNA alone is ~0.40, image is contributing ~13 points and investing in image encoder, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion becomes critical. This single experiment resolves the most important architectural uncertainty and will efficiently guide all subsequent design decisions under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_049 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + concat) is our best result (acc 0.535), and with scgpt we saw concat (0.435) slightly outperform weighted (0.422), suggesting fusion method may matter. Uncertainty: we have not tested whether the concat > weighted pattern holds with the much stronger pca_n2000 encoder, where the interaction between representation quality and fusion strategy could differ. This experiment (config_002) changes only the fusion method (concat → weighted) relative to config_049, giving a clean single-variable comparison. It is the best next step because it is low-risk, directly extends our strongest result, and will let us lock down the fusion choice before exploring multiprofile/aggregation or alternative image encoders—decisions that would otherwise be confounded if fusion remains unresolved.

Evidence: All 7 completed experiments use imagenet_vit_l as the image encoder, and the best result (config_049, acc=0.5353) pairs pca_n2000 with imagenet_vit_l via concat fusion. We know image adds ~0.05 over RNA-only, but we have no information on whether this contribution is encoder-specific. Uncertainty: resnet50 is completely untested, and it may capture different spatial features than a ViT, potentially changing the magnitude of the image modality's contribution. This experiment (config_010: multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, None, concat) is a clean single-variable swap against config_049, isolating the image encoder effect while holding RNA encoder, fusion, and profile setting at their best-known values. It is the best use of the next budget slot because the image encoder choice will condition every future multimodal experiment, and resolving it now prevents building multiprofile or aggregation experiments on a potentially suboptimal image backbone.

Evidence: All 8 completed experiments are singleprofile with no aggregation. The best configuration (config_049: pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieves 0.5353 acc, with PCA clearly dominating scgpt as RNA encoder and image adding ~5% over RNA-only. The largest unexplored design dimension is whether multiprofile + aggregation improves upon the single-profile baseline. Question: Does adding multiple profiles with average-pool aggregation improve over the best singleprofile setting, holding RNA encoder (pca_n2000), image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), and fusion (concat) constant? Why this experiment: config_048 is the minimal-change extension of config_049—only profile_setting and aggregation differ—so any performance delta cleanly isolates the multiprofile+aggregation effect. Starting with the simplest aggregation (avgpool) before transformer ensures we first learn whether multiprofile itself is beneficial before attributing gains to a more complex aggregation mechanism. This is the highest-information experiment available under the budget constraint.

The strongest evidence so far is config_048 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.6287 accuracy, a large jump over the best singleprofile result (0.5353). This shows multiprofile aggregation is the most impactful design axis. The key remaining uncertainty is whether the simple avgpool aggregation is near-optimal or whether a learned aggregation (transformer) can better capture interactions across profiles. config_039 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding the best RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion constant, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_048. If transformer aggregation yields a meaningful gain, it reveals that cross-profile interactions are exploitable and justifies further investment in richer aggregation; if it does not, avgpool is confirmed as sufficient and the budget is better spent on other axes (e.g., image encoder or fusion). This is the highest-information next step because it directly extends the strongest configuration along the most fundamental untested dimension.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about task difficulty, the value of each modality, or the benefit of added complexity (multiprofile, transformer aggregation, fusion). The most critical unknown is the performance ceiling of a simple, well-understood single-modality model. 2) What this tests: config_002 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the cleanest, most standard baseline in cellular profiling—RNA features reduced by PCA to 2000 dimensions with no image, no multiprofile, no aggregation, no fusion. It establishes the reference accuracy/F1 that every multimodal or multiprofile configuration must beat to justify its added complexity and computational cost. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: With a limited budget, the highest-information first move is a minimal, fast, interpretable baseline. It (a) calibrates the difficulty of the classification task, (b) provides the anchor for isolating the marginal contribution of the image modality, multiprofile aggregation, and fusion strategy in all subsequent comparisons, and (c) is computationally cheap, leaving budget for follow-up experiments. Without this reference, any multimodal result would be uninterpretable.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_002: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), which establishes a weak baseline. The most foundational uncertainty is whether the RNA representation quality (PCA vs. a learned encoder) is a limiting factor, since every downstream multimodal or multiprofile configuration builds on top of the RNA encoder choice. Question: config_008 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_002—only the RNA encoder changes from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. This isolates the effect of a learned, low-dimensional (200-d) RNA representation versus a high-dimensional (2000-d) linear one. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It is the cheapest way to determine whether learned encoders are worth prioritizing in the remaining budget—if scvi_n200 substantially outperforms PCA, I can confidently invest in scvi-based multimodal configs; if they are comparable, the bottleneck lies elsewhere (modality, profile, aggregation) and I should pivot to testing image modality next. (2) It changes exactly one variable relative to the baseline, making the comparison interpretable. (3) scvi_n200 appears in the majority of remaining multimodal configurations, so its standalone performance directly informs which multimodal configs are most promising to test next.

Evidence: We have only two completed experiments, both RNA-only single-profile. scvi_n200 (config_008, acc=0.520) outperforms pca_n2000 (config_002, acc=0.485), establishing scvi_n200 as the stronger RNA encoder. However, we have zero information on whether the image modality contributes any predictive value. Question: config_004 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat) directly tests whether adding a standard image encoder with simple concatenation fusion improves over the best RNA-only baseline (config_008), while keeping the RNA encoder and profile setting identical to isolate the image contribution. Why best: This is the single most critical design decision for a multimodal study—if image adds no value, the entire search space collapses to RNA-only variants. Using the simplest fusion (concat) and a standard encoder (resnet50) avoids confounding the image-contribution question with fusion complexity or encoder capacity. A positive result justifies further exploration of fusion/aggregation; a null result redirects budget to RNA-only multiprofile or encoder comparisons.

Evidence: config_004 (multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.5362 acc, showing that adding image information to the best RNA encoder (scvi_n200, confirmed by config_008 > config_002) provides a modest ~1.6% gain over RNA-only. However, we have only tested one image encoder (resnet50). Uncertainty: whether a stronger pretrained image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) yields meaningfully better image representations than resnet50, which would affect all downstream multimodal configurations. This experiment (config_009) isolates the image encoder effect by keeping RNA encoder (scvi_n200), profile setting (singleprofile), and fusion (concat) identical to config_004, changing only resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l. This is the best use of the next budget slot because it resolves a fundamental representation question that will inform whether to invest in ViT-based or CNN-based image encoders across many future multiprofile/aggregation experiments, and it is a clean single-variable comparison against an already-completed configuration.

Evidence: scvi_n200 outperforms pca_n2000 for RNA encoding (0.5203 vs 0.4849), and adding an image modality (resnet50 or ViT-L) improves over RNA-only by ~1.5-2%. However, all multimodal results so far use concat fusion; we have no evidence on whether weighted fusion is better or worse. Question: config_026 (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + weighted) is a single-variable change from our best config (config_004: concat, 0.5362), isolating the fusion strategy while holding RNA encoder, image encoder, and profile setting constant. Why this is the best next experiment: fusion is a fundamental design axis with zero coverage in the history, and resolving it early (weighted vs concat) will inform whether to invest remaining budget in multiprofile/aggregation variants. A single-variable comparison from the current best is the most efficient way to reduce uncertainty without confounding multiple factors.

All five completed experiments used singleprofile. The current best (config_026: scvi_n200, resnet50, weighted → 0.540 acc) establishes a strong singleprofile baseline, and we have clear evidence that scvi_n200 > pca_n2000, image adds value over rna_only, and weighted fusion slightly edges concat. The largest unexplored design axis is multiprofile + aggregation. config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) keeps RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion identical to the current best, changing only the profile setting and adding the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates the effect of multiprofile with minimal added complexity. If avgpool improves performance, it confirms multiprofile adds signal and motivates testing transformer aggregation next; if it does not, it provides evidence that the additional profile dimension is not the bottleneck, redirecting effort toward other axes (e.g., alternative image encoders or RNA encoders like scgpt). Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information experiment because it tests the single biggest untested architectural decision while keeping the comparison as clean as possible.

The dominant finding is the large jump from singleprofile (best: 0.540, config_026) to multiprofile with avgpool (0.678, config_030), indicating that the profile/aggregation axis is the most impactful design dimension. The key uncertainty now is whether avgpool is sufficient or whether a transformer aggregation that models inter-profile interactions yields further gains. Config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_030, changing only aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding RNA encoder, image encoder, fusion, and profile setting constant. If transformer substantially outperforms avgpool, it signals that inter-profile modeling is a productive direction to exploit; if it is comparable or worse, it confirms that simple pooling captures most of the multiprofile benefit and we can redirect effort to other axes (e.g., image encoder or RNA encoder). Under a limited budget, isolating the aggregation mechanism in the already-promising multiprofile setting is the highest-information next step.

Evidence: The multiprofile+transformer+weighted multimodal setup (config_020, acc=0.713) is the clear best so far, with a large jump over singleprofile (~0.54). In the singleprofile regime, image encoder choice barely mattered (resnet50: 0.536 vs ViT: 0.532 with concat), but that was a low-performance setting where the image signal was a small additive contribution. In the multiprofile+transformer regime, the image features are being combined with aggregated multi-profile information, and the interaction dynamics may differ substantially. Question: Does swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l (config_010) improve or degrade performance in the high-performing multiprofile+transformer+weighted setting? This is a clean single-variable comparison against config_020, isolating the image encoder effect. Why best next: It tests a fundamental representation choice in the regime where gains are largest, and the answer directly determines whether to invest further in ViT-based pipelines or focus on other levers (aggregation, fusion, RNA encoder). A single-variable change from the current best makes the result interpretable and maximally informative under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best configuration (config_010: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1. All completed multiprofile experiments use scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder; scgpt has never been tested in any completed experiment. In singleprofile, scvi_n200 outperformed pca_n2000, but scgpt remains uncharacterized. Question: config_038 changes only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt while holding image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), aggregation (transformer), fusion (weighted), and profile setting (multiprofile) identical to the current best. This isolates the effect of RNA representation in the top-performing regime. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison against the incumbent leader, directly testing whether an alternative learned RNA encoder (scgpt) can improve upon scvi_n200 in the setting that already shows the strongest performance. If scgpt matches or exceeds config_010, it opens a new exploitation direction; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 as the preferred encoder and redirects budget toward other levers (e.g., aggregation or fusion refinements). No other available configuration provides as direct a test of the single largest unexplored variable in the current best configuration.

Evidence: The multiprofile + transformer + weighted pipeline shows a massive jump (~0.71-0.72) over singleprofile (~0.54), and within this regime scvi_n200 (config_010: 0.725) vastly outperforms scgpt (config_038: 0.520), a ~20-point gap. However, pca_n2000 has never been tested in the multiprofile regime. Uncertainty: It is unclear whether the multiprofile + transformer aggregation pipeline is robust to the RNA encoder choice or whether scvi_n200's learned latent representation is specifically required. Config_017 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted) is a clean A/B comparison against config_010, changing only the RNA encoder. This is the best next experiment because the RNA encoder question has the largest unresolved uncertainty (scgpt's dramatic failure suggests encoder quality matters, but pca_n2000's position is unknown), the result would clarify whether we can simplify the RNA pipeline, and it directly informs whether further effort should focus on RNA encoder selection or other design dimensions under the limited budget.

With no prior experiments, the most critical need is to establish a clean, well-defined baseline for the multimodal setting. config_007 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, weighted) uses the most standard and well-understood component at every design dimension: a simple linear RNA encoder (pca_n2000), a widely-used image backbone (resnet50), a single profile (avoiding confounding from multiprofile aggregation), and a simple weighted fusion. This gives a reference performance against which all future experiments can isolate the effect of changing one dimension (e.g., swapping to scgpt, adding multiprofile with avgpool, or trying concat fusion). Starting with this 'control' configuration maximizes the information gained per experiment, because every subsequent result can be interpreted as a delta from a known anchor, reducing uncertainty about which design choices matter.

With only one completed experiment (config_007: multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, weighted fusion → 52.3% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether the multimodal fusion is actually adding value over the image modality alone. config_002 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest possible comparison: it holds the image encoder (resnet50) and profile setting (singleprofile) identical to config_007 while removing the RNA branch entirely. If image-only performance is close to or exceeds 52.3%, the current RNA encoding (pca_n2000) with weighted fusion is not contributing, and future effort should target better RNA representations or fusion strategies. If image-only is substantially lower, multimodal fusion is confirmed as beneficial and we can then efficiently explore fusion type, aggregation, and encoder upgrades. Resolving this fundamental question before varying fusion, aggregation, or encoders avoids wasting budget on secondary design choices while the primary 'does multimodal help?' question remains unanswered.

Evidence: config_007 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, weighted) achieved 0.5232 acc, while config_002 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) achieved only 0.2079 acc. This large gap shows the RNA modality is critical, but we cannot yet decompose whether RNA alone drives most of the signal or whether there is genuine multimodal synergy. Uncertainty: We lack an RNA-only baseline to attribute performance to each modality. This experiment (config_019: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is a clean ablation of config_007 with the image removed, holding RNA encoder and profile setting constant. It will clarify: (a) if RNA alone ≈ 0.5, the image adds little and we should focus on RNA representation; (b) if RNA alone is much lower (~0.2-0.3), there is true multimodal synergy and fusion strategy becomes the key design axis. This is the best use of the next budget slot because it completes the fundamental modality decomposition (image_only / rna_only / multimodal) before investing in more complex configurations (multiprofile, different encoders, aggregation), ensuring subsequent experiments target the right design dimensions.

Evidence: config_007 (multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, weighted) achieves 0.5232 acc, while RNA-only pca_n2000 (config_019) achieves 0.4849 and image-only resnet50 (config_002) only 0.2079. RNA is clearly the dominant signal, and the multimodal gain over RNA-only is modest (+0.038). The only RNA encoder tested so far is pca_n2000, a simple linear projection. Uncertainty: whether a learned, generative RNA representation (scgpt) meaningfully improves the dominant modality's contribution. This experiment (config_034) changes exactly one factor from config_007—RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scgpt—while holding image encoder (resnet50), profile (single), and fusion (weighted) constant. If scgpt substantially outperforms pca_n2000, it tells us to invest in richer RNA representations as the highest-leverage design choice; if not, it confirms pca_n2000 is near-sufficient and redirects budget toward multiprofile or image-encoder improvements. This is the most informative single-factor test under the limited budget because it isolates the effect on the modality that carries most of the signal.

Evidence: config_007 (pca_n2000, resnet50, weighted fusion, singleprofile, multimodal) is our best result at 0.523 acc, but it is only marginally better than rna_only (0.485), and we have only tested weighted fusion so far. The RNA encoder choice (pca_n2000 vs scgpt) showed a large effect, but fusion strategy remains entirely untested. Question: Does concat fusion outperform weighted fusion when all other variables are held constant? config_041 is identical to config_007 except fusion changes from weighted to concat, making it a clean single-variable comparison. Why best next experiment: Fusion is a fundamental design axis for every multimodal configuration; resolving it now prevents us from carrying a suboptimal fusion choice into all subsequent multiprofile or encoder-variation experiments. It is low-risk (worst case confirms weighted is fine) and high-information (a large gap would redirect the entire search), making it the most efficient use of the next budget slot under the principle of isolating one design variable.

Evidence: All five completed experiments are singleprofile. PCA_n2000 clearly outperforms scgpt as RNA encoder (0.523 vs 0.421), and concat fusion marginally beats weighted (0.527 vs 0.523) with pca_n2000+resnet50. RNA dominates over image (0.485 vs 0.208), and multimodal adds ~4 pts over RNA alone. The largest unexplored design axis is multiprofile aggregation—no multiprofile experiment has been run yet. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles (via avgpool) on top of our best singleprofile settings (pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) improve validation accuracy, or does it dilute the signal? Why this experiment: config_008 is the minimal, direct extension of our best result (config_041) by adding only the multiprofile+avgpool aggregation step, isolating that single design choice. Avgpool is the simpler aggregation; if it fails to help, a more complex transformer aggregation is less likely to. This single experiment resolves whether the multiprofile axis is worth further investment under our limited budget.

The strongest evidence so far is that multiprofile with pca_n2000/resnet50/avgpool/concat (config_008, acc 0.619) dramatically outperforms all singleprofile configurations (~0.52–0.53), confirming that multiprofile is the key design lever. However, we have only tested one aggregation strategy (avgpool) in the multiprofile setting. Aggregation determines how multiple profiles are combined before fusion and is arguably the most impactful untested design choice in this regime—transformer aggregation could capture profile-to-profile interactions that a simple average misses. config_006 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, transformer, concat) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding every other factor identical to config_008, giving a clean single-variable comparison. This is the best use of the next budget slot because it isolates the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact design decision in our currently best-performing family, and the result will directly inform whether further investment in multiprofile transformer-based models is warranted.

The best-performing experiment so far is config_008 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat; acc=0.619), which shows that multiprofile + avgpool aggregation + concat fusion is a strong design. However, the image modality's contribution remains uncertain: image_only with resnet50 was very weak (acc=0.208), and we have not yet tested whether a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) can unlock more signal from the image branch. config_043 is identical to config_008 except it swaps resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l, making it a clean single-variable comparison that isolates the image encoder effect in the best-performing setting. This is the highest-value next experiment because (1) it exploits the strongest known configuration, (2) it tests an unexplored and potentially impactful design axis (image encoder quality), (3) a positive result would open a clear exploitation path, while a null result would confirm that the image modality's ceiling is low regardless of encoder, redirecting effort toward RNA-side improvements.

Evidence: config_043 (multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.6287 acc. In singleprofile, concat and weighted fusion are nearly identical (0.5266 vs 0.5232), and in multiprofile with resnet50 we've only tested concat (config_008: 0.6186). We have no multiprofile+ViT data point for weighted fusion. Question: Does weighted fusion match or beat concat in the best-performing multiprofile+ViT+avgpool setup? This isolates the single variable of fusion strategy while holding all other choices at their empirically best values. Rationale: Under a limited budget, a one-variable extension of the top configuration is the most efficient way to either confirm concat's advantage (locking in the design) or discover that weighted fusion is equally good (freeing a design degree for future experiments). It avoids the risk of changing multiple variables (e.g., aggregation + fusion) and directly informs whether the current best can be improved or whether we should pivot to exploring other axes (RNA encoder, aggregation) next.

The current best configuration (config_042: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.6352) establishes that multi-profile + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted fusion is the strongest combination. However, the RNA encoder has only been tested as pca_n2000 in this setting, while scvi_n200 remains completely untested. In single-profile settings, scgpt underperformed pca_n2000 (0.4214 vs 0.5232), but scvi_n200 is a different learned representation that has not been evaluated. Config_047 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 while holding all other hyperparameters at their best-known values, cleanly isolating the effect of the RNA representation. This is the highest-value next experiment because it tests the single most important unexplored design axis in the current best region, and the result will determine whether further investment should go toward learned RNA encoders or toward other dimensions (aggregation, fusion) with PCA fixed.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about which design choices matter. The most critical uncertainty is the overall performance level of a standard multimodal pipeline and whether combining RNA and image modalities is viable at all. 2) What this tests: config_006 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is a 'central' configuration using the most established and commonly expected choices in each dimension: scgpt as a well-validated RNA encoder, resnet50 as a standard pretrained image encoder, avgpool as the simplest aggregation, and concat as the simplest fusion. It establishes a performance anchor for the multimodal approach. 3) Why it is the best first use of budget: Starting from a standard, well-motivated multimodal baseline lets every subsequent experiment isolate a single design change (e.g., swapping avgpool→transformer, concat→weighted, resnet50→ViT-L, scgpt→scvi, or dropping a modality for a single-modality baseline). This maximizes the information gained per experiment under a limited budget, because the reference point is meaningful and comparable across many future variants. A single-modality baseline would be informative but would not directly test the core multimodal hypothesis that motivates this study.

We have only one completed experiment (config_006: multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, concat → acc 0.512, F1 0.477), so the most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality is actually contributing useful signal or is adding noise. Config_044 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is a clean single-variable ablation of config_006: it keeps the identical RNA encoder (scgpt), profile setting (multiprofile), and aggregation (avgpool), and only removes the image branch. If config_044 matches or exceeds config_006, the image is not helping and we should pivot toward RNA-centric or simpler designs; if it falls well short, the image is contributing and we should invest in optimizing fusion/aggregation. Answering this fundamental 'does multimodal help?' question before tuning fusion or aggregation is the highest-information use of the next experiment under a limited budget.

Evidence: config_044 (RNA-only, scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) achieves 0.530 acc / 0.515 F1, outperforming config_006 (multimodal, same RNA/image/aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.512 acc / 0.477 F1. This suggests the image modality, as fused via simple concatenation, is adding noise rather than signal. Question: config_002 is a single-variable change from config_006—only the fusion switches from concat to weighted—keeping scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, and multiprofile identical. This isolates whether the fusion mechanism is the bottleneck: weighted fusion lets the model learn to down-weight unhelpful image features, whereas concat forces equal treatment. Why best next: it is the most direct, minimal-difference follow-up to the key finding (RNA > multimodal), cleanly attributing any performance shift to the fusion choice. If weighted fusion recovers the gap, the image carries useful signal that concat was masking; if it does not, the evidence strengthens that resnet50 image features are not informative under this setup, redirecting budget toward other design axes (encoder, aggregation, or profile setting).

The key finding so far is that RNA-only (config_044, acc 0.5305) outperforms both multimodal configs (config_002 at 0.5251, config_006 at 0.5121), suggesting the image modality with resnet50 is not contributing positively. The most critical uncertainty is whether this is an inherent limitation of the image modality or specific to the resnet50 encoder. Config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) isolates exactly this variable: it is identical to the best multimodal result (config_002) except the image encoder is swapped from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. If imagenet_vit_l also fails to beat RNA-only, we gain strong evidence that the image channel is unhelpful in this task and can focus remaining budget on RNA-side improvements. If it does close or reverse the gap, we identify the image encoder as the bottleneck and have a clear exploitation path. This single-variable comparison is the most information-dense next experiment under a limited budget.

Evidence: config_018 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) achieved the highest accuracy (0.542) but a lower F1 (0.483) than the rna_only baseline config_044 (acc=0.530, F1=0.515), suggesting the multimodal model may be biased toward majority classes. With resnet50, weighted fusion (config_002, acc=0.525) clearly outperformed concat (config_006, acc=0.512), but VIT_L produces fundamentally different patch-level representations where the optimal fusion strategy may differ. Question: Does concat fusion (config_014) outperform or match weighted fusion (config_018) when paired with imagenet_vit_l? This isolates a single variable (fusion method) while holding the best-performing encoder, RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation constant. Why this is the best next experiment: It is the cleanest single-variable comparison to the current best configuration, directly testing whether the fusion strategy that worked for resnet50 also works for VIT_L, and whether concat might improve the F1 gap observed in config_018. This information is critical before investing in more complex changes (e.g., transformer aggregation) that would confound multiple factors.

All five completed experiments use scgpt as the RNA encoder, so we have zero evidence about whether the learned RNA representation is actually critical or whether a simpler linear projection (PCA) would suffice. The best configuration so far is config_018 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc 0.5420). config_007 changes only the RNA encoder from scgpt to pca_n2000 while holding the image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), aggregation (avgpool), fusion (weighted), and profile setting (multiprofile) constant. This gives a clean single-variable comparison that directly tests whether the RNA encoder is a meaningful design decision. If PCA performs comparably, the RNA representation is not a bottleneck and we can simplify the pipeline; if it performs substantially worse, it validates scgpt and focuses future search on other axes (aggregation, profile setting). Under a limited budget, resolving this fundamental representation question is more informative than, e.g., testing transformer aggregation, because the RNA encoder choice affects the entire model family.

The standout result is config_007 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.635), which dramatically outperforms config_018 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.542) with only the RNA encoder changed. This strongly implicates the RNA encoder as the critical design choice. The key uncertainty is whether the pca_n2000 advantage is specific to the imagenet_vit_l image encoder or generalizes. config_004 (pca_n2000 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted) is a single-variable change from config_007 (image encoder swap) and from config_002 (scgpt + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.525; RNA encoder swap). One experiment thus yields two clean comparisons: (a) RNA encoder effect with resnet50 (config_004 vs config_002) and (b) image encoder effect with pca_n2000 (config_004 vs config_007). Under a limited budget, confirming whether the dominant pca_n2000 signal is robust across image encoders is the highest-value uncertainty to resolve before investing further in aggregation or fusion variations.

Evidence: pca_n2000 as RNA encoder dramatically outperforms scgpt (0.635–0.639 vs. 0.512–0.542), making it the dominant design choice. However, with scgpt, rna_only (config_044, acc 0.530) was competitive with or slightly better than multimodal variants (0.512–0.542), suggesting the image branch may not add value. We have no rna_only data point with pca_n2000. Question: Does the image modality actually contribute when paired with the much stronger pca_n2000 encoder? config_042 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is a clean single-variable ablation against config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted), differing only in the presence of the image branch. Why best: The answer fundamentally redirects the remaining budget—if rna_only matches ~0.64, the image modality is dispensable and we can concentrate on RNA encoder/aggregation choices; if it drops substantially, multimodal fusion and image encoder selection become high-priority. This reduces the most consequential uncertainty before committing further experiments to multimodal variants.

Evidence: pca_n2000 as RNA encoder is the dominant factor (0.635–0.639 multimodal vs 0.512–0.542 for scgpt), and config_004 (pca_n2000 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.639) is the current best. The only untested dimension within this strong sub-space is aggregation: all completed experiments used avgpool. Question: Does transformer aggregation improve over avgpool when paired with the proven pca_n2000 + resnet50 + weighted-fusion combination? This is a single-variable change from config_004, isolating the aggregation effect cleanly. Why this is the best next experiment: it directly extends the strongest evidence by probing one untested lever (aggregation) without confounding changes to encoder, profile, or fusion. If transformer helps, it identifies a new optimization axis; if it does not, it confirms avgpool sufficiency and redirects budget toward other untested dimensions (e.g., singleprofile or scvi_n200) with greater confidence.

1) Evidence: The RNA encoder is the single most impactful design choice observed so far — pca_n2000 consistently outperforms scgpt by ~8-10% in accuracy (e.g., config_004 at 0.639 vs config_002 at 0.525 with identical image/aggregation/fusion settings). However, scvi_n2000, a variational autoencoder-based encoder, has not been tested in any completed experiment, leaving a major uncertainty about whether a learned generative representation can match or exceed the simple PCA baseline. 2) Question: config_009 (scvi_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is a clean single-variable swap from the best-performing config_004 (pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted), isolating the effect of the RNA encoder while holding image encoder, aggregation, and fusion constant. 3) Why this is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, resolving whether a more expressive learned encoder can beat PCA is higher-value information than a small fusion-method comparison (config_021) or a profile-setting test that would require changing two variables simultaneously. If scvi_n2000 matches or beats pca_n2000, it opens a new promising direction; if it underperforms, it confirms that simple linear projections are sufficient and lets us focus remaining budget on aggregation/fusion/profile refinements around the PCA-based pipeline.

With no prior experiments, the dominant uncertainty is whether a basic multimodal (RNA + image) pipeline is viable and what level of performance to expect. Config_021 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, aggregation=None, fusion=concat) is the simplest well-motivated multimodal baseline: it uses the most standard and interpretable components on each axis (PCA for RNA, ResNet50 for image, no aggregation needed for a single profile, and plain concatenation for fusion). This establishes a clear reference point with minimal confounding complexity. If it performs well, it confirms multimodality is promising and subsequent experiments can isolate which added complexity (multiprofile, learned encoders, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) actually helps. If it underperforms, we learn early that the basic multimodal signal is weak and should pivot toward unimodal baselines or stronger encoders. Choosing this over a more complex config avoids attributing any (lack of) performance to multiple simultaneous design choices, and choosing it over a unimodal config directly tests the core hypothesis of this multimodal study while still serving as a ceiling for what a unimodal model could achieve with the same image encoder.

With only one completed experiment (config_021: multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat → acc 0.527), the most critical uncertainty is whether the low performance stems from the multimodal fusion, the RNA representation, or the inherent difficulty of the task. Config_028 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean single-variable ablation of config_021: it removes the RNA modality while keeping the image encoder (resnet50) and profile setting (singleprofile) identical. If image-only matches or exceeds 0.527, the PCA-RNA branch is not contributing and we should focus on image encoder quality or multiprofile. If image-only is substantially lower, the multimodal combination is genuinely adding signal and we should explore better RNA encoders or fusion strategies. This baseline is foundational for interpreting all future multimodal results and is the highest-information experiment given the sparse evidence.

Evidence: config_021 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.5266 acc, while config_028 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) achieved only 0.2079 acc. This shows the multimodal setup substantially outperforms image-only, but we cannot yet determine whether RNA alone is the primary driver or whether the fusion of both modalities is essential. Uncertainty: We lack an RNA-only baseline with the same encoder (pca_n2000) and profile setting (singleprofile) to isolate the image's marginal contribution. This experiment (config_009: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the cleanest control for config_021, changing only the model setting from multimodal to rna_only while holding the RNA encoder and profile setting constant. It will clarify whether to prioritize improving the image encoder (if RNA alone is weak, fusion matters) or the RNA encoder/aggregation (if RNA alone is strong, the image is secondary). Under a limited budget, this single-variable comparison maximizes information gain about the most consequential design choice—modality contribution—before investing in more complex multiprofile or aggregation variants.

Evidence: RNA is clearly the dominant signal (RNA-only 0.485 vs image-only 0.208), and the multimodal setup (config_021, 0.527) adds only ~4 points over RNA alone. All three completed experiments used pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder, so we have no information on whether a learned nonlinear representation (scvi_n200) could improve the primary signal. Question: config_008 is identical to config_021 except for swapping pca_n2000 → scvi_n200, cleanly isolating the RNA encoder effect while holding image encoder (resnet50), profile (single), aggregation (None), and fusion (concat) constant. Why this is the best next experiment: Since RNA drives most of the performance, improving its representation has the highest expected impact. A single-variable comparison to config_021 gives a direct, interpretable readout on whether a deep generative encoder helps over linear PCA, reducing uncertainty about the most consequential design axis before investing in more complex multiprofile/aggregation/fusion variations.

All four completed experiments use singleprofile, leaving the single-vs-multiprofile question completely untested. The best singleprofile result is config_008 (scvi_n200, resnet50, concat) at 0.5362 acc. Config_002 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the most controlled extension: it keeps the same RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion strategy, and introduces only the profile change plus the minimal aggregation (avgpool) that multiprofile requires. This isolates whether multiple profiles contribute useful signal beyond a single profile. If multiprofile with simple averaging matches or beats 0.5362, it justifies investing in more complex aggregation (transformer) and other multiprofile variants; if it falls well short, it tells us the extra profiles add noise and we should focus budget on singleprofile refinements (e.g., fusion type, image encoder). This is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact design axis remaining, making it the best use of the next limited experiment.

Evidence: config_002 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.632 acc, a large jump over singleprofile configs (~0.53). In singleprofile, pca_n2000 and scvi_n200 performed similarly (0.527 vs 0.536), but it is unclear whether this equivalence holds under multiprofile+avgpool, where the learned non-linear representation from scvi may interact differently with cross-profile pooling than a linear PCA embedding. Question: Does the RNA encoder choice (scvi_n200 vs pca_n2000) materially affect performance when multiprofile+avgpool aggregation is active? config_003 changes only the RNA encoder from config_002, isolating this variable. Why best next: It is the cleanest single-variable comparison to the current best, and the answer directly determines whether we can simplify the RNA pipeline (pca_n2000 is cheaper and more interpretable) or must retain scvi_n200, which constrains all subsequent multiprofile experiments. Under a limited budget, resolving whether the encoder choice is a free parameter or a critical one is more informative than testing fusion or image-encoder variations, which are secondary to the representation question.

Evidence: The two multiprofile experiments (config_002: scvi_n200+avgpool+concat=0.6315, config_003: pca_n2000+avgpool+concat=0.6186) show a large ~10-point gain over singleprofile, but both use avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. We have zero evidence about whether transformer aggregation could further improve multiprofile performance by modeling inter-profile interactions rather than simple averaging. Question: This experiment isolates the effect of aggregation (avgpool→transformer) while holding all other variables constant at the best-performing config_002 settings (scvi_n200, resnet50, concat). Why this is the best next step: Aggregation is the most architecturally consequential untested dimension in the multiprofile setting—avgpool discards profile-specific information that a transformer could preserve and re-weight. A single-variable change from the current best config cleanly attributes any performance shift to the aggregation mechanism, and the result will determine whether further investment in more complex aggregation (or in fusion) is warranted under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_047 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) is the strongest result at 0.688 acc / 0.659 F1, and the key drivers identified are multiprofile + transformer aggregation. However, fusion strategy has only been tested as 'concat' across all experiments; 'weighted' fusion remains completely unexplored. Question: Does weighted fusion improve over simple concatenation in the multiprofile + transformer regime? This is a single-variable change from config_047 (only fusion: concat → weighted), cleanly isolating the effect of the fusion mechanism. Why best next experiment: Fusion is a fundamental design axis with zero evidence in the high-performing regime. Knowing whether weighted fusion helps or hurts immediately informs all future multimodal configurations and determines whether to invest further in fusion design or pivot to other axes (e.g., image encoder, RNA encoder). It is a low-risk exploitation of the strongest direction while resolving a critical untested design choice.

The current best (config_006: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted; acc=0.713) has established that multiprofile + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion is the strongest design. However, the image encoder has never been varied—all 8 completed experiments use resnet50, leaving a major design dimension completely unexplored. config_020 is identical to config_006 except it swaps resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l, isolating the effect of the image representation while holding all other settings at their best-known values. This is the highest-information single-variable experiment available: if ViT improves performance, it confirms the image encoder is a productive axis to further exploit; if it does not, it tells us resnet50 is already near-sufficient and we should redirect budget toward RNA encoder or other dimensions. No other available configuration tests this critical unexplored axis with a single clean change from the current best.

Evidence: The current best (config_020: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.725 acc. The progression from singleprofile→multiprofile, avgpool→transformer, concat→weighted, and resnet50→ViT has been well-established. However, the RNA encoder choice remains underexplored: only pca_n2000 and scvi_n200 have been tested, and scgpt (a generative-model-based encoder) is entirely untested. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 as the RNA encoder when all other components are held at their best-known settings? config_045 changes only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt relative to config_020, making it a clean single-variable comparison. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly addresses the largest remaining uncertainty in the design space (RNA encoder) within the strongest known configuration, providing a clear exploitation step. If scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, it opens a new promising direction; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 as the preferred encoder and narrows the search, saving budget for other questions.

With no prior experiments, the most critical uncertainty is whether a multimodal model (combining RNA + image) provides meaningful benefit over unimodal baselines, and what a reasonable 'simple multimodal' performance level looks like. Config_018 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, no aggregation, weighted fusion) is the simplest reasonable multimodal configuration: it uses the most straightforward RNA encoder (PCA, no learned parameters), a standard image backbone (ResNet-50), single-profile (no aggregation needed), and weighted fusion. This establishes a central anchor in the design space from which many one-parameter comparisons can be drawn in subsequent experiments: removing RNA (config_004) isolates the image-only baseline, removing image (config_046) isolates the RNA-only baseline, swapping the RNA encoder (config_019 scvi, config_036 scgpt) tests whether learned representations add value over linear dimensionality reduction, swapping the image encoder (config_021 ViT-L) tests backbone quality, and changing fusion (config_009 concat) tests fusion strategy. Starting here maximizes the number of informative follow-up comparisons per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_018: multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, weighted fusion → 52.3% acc). With a single data point, the most critical uncertainty is whether the RNA modality actually contributes to performance or whether the image alone accounts for most of the signal. Question: config_004 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean ablation of config_018 with only the RNA modality removed, isolating the effect of multimodality. Why this is the best next experiment: Without an image-only baseline, we cannot interpret any future multimodal result—improvements could come from better image features, RNA contribution, or fusion interactions. Establishing this reference point first ensures that all subsequent experiments (varying RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, fusion) are interpreted against a meaningful unimodal floor. It is a single-variable change, maximally informative, and essential before investing budget in more complex multimodal variants.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, singleprofile, weighted) achieves 0.523 acc while config_004 (image_only, resnet50, singleprofile) achieves only 0.208 acc, a ~31 pp gap. However, we have no RNA-only data point, so we cannot decompose how much of the multimodal performance comes from the RNA modality versus the image modality or their interaction. Question: config_046 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000, no image, no aggregation, no fusion) isolates the RNA contribution using the same RNA encoder and profile setting as config_018, with no other confounds. Why best next experiment: With only two completed runs, the single most important uncertainty is the per-modality contribution.
