Knowing RNA-only accuracy lets us determine whether the multimodal gain is driven primarily by RNA (suggesting we should invest in better RNA encoders like scgpt/scvi) or by the image+RNA interaction (suggesting we should focus on fusion and image encoder upgrades). This single clean comparison maximally reduces uncertainty before committing further budget to more complex multiprofile or aggregation variants.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000) alone achieves 0.485 acc while image (resnet50) alone is only 0.208, and the multimodal model (config_018) reaches 0.523—only a ~4% gain over RNA alone. This indicates RNA is the dominant signal and the current linear PCA representation may be a bottleneck. Uncertainty: We have only tested a linear RNA encoder (pca_n2000); it is unknown whether a learned encoder (scgpt) captures non-linear biological structure that would substantially improve both the RNA baseline and the multimodal model. This experiment (config_007: multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, resnet50, weighted fusion) changes exactly one variable relative to config_018—the RNA encoder—so the result cleanly isolates the effect of RNA representation quality. If scgpt yields a meaningful accuracy/F1 gain over config_018, it tells us the RNA representation is the primary lever for improvement and justifies further investment in learned encoders; if not, PCA is near-sufficient and we should pivot to image encoder quality or fusion strategy. Under a limited budget, testing the dominant modality's representation first is the highest-information single experiment.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, weighted) achieved 0.523 acc, only modestly above RNA-only pca_n2000 (0.485), while image-only resnet50 was very weak (0.208). This suggests the image branch may be a bottleneck in the multimodal model. Question: Does replacing resnet50 with imagenet_vit_l (a stronger image encoder) improve multimodal performance? config_008 is identical to config_018 except for the image encoder, making it a clean single-variable A/B test that isolates the image representation effect. Why this is the best next step: Under a limited budget, resolving whether the image encoder is the limiting factor is the highest-value uncertainty. If imagenet_vit_l substantially lifts multimodal accuracy, it justifies investing further in image-heavy configurations; if not, we can focus budget on RNA encoder and profile/aggregation choices instead. This avoids the risk of prematurely exploring multiprofile or fusion variants on top of a weak image backbone.

Evidence: config_008 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, weighted) is the current best at 0.532 acc / 0.516 F1, slightly ahead of config_018 (same but resnet50, 0.523). RNA is clearly the dominant modality (0.485 alone vs 0.208 for image), and pca_n2000 substantially outperforms scgpt (0.523 vs 0.421). The only fusion strategy tested so far is 'weighted'; we have no evidence about whether 'concat' could be superior. Question: config_021 is identical to config_008 except fusion changes from weighted to concat, giving a clean single-variable comparison to isolate the effect of fusion strategy with the best-known encoder pair. Why this is the best next experiment: it directly extends the strongest result with a minimal change, reducing uncertainty about whether a different fusion mechanism could push performance higher before we invest budget in more complex multiprofile/aggregation designs. If concat matches or beats weighted, it reshapes the design space; if it underperforms, it confirms weighted as the preferred fusion and lets us focus subsequent experiments on profile setting and aggregation.

Evidence: The best singleprofile configuration is config_021 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat, acc=0.5353), with PCA clearly superior to scgpt for RNA and ViT-L slightly better than ResNet50. However, the multiprofile axis is completely unexplored—zero completed experiments use it. This is the largest remaining source of uncertainty about whether additional profile information (with aggregation) can push performance beyond the current ~0.535 ceiling. Question: Does adding multiple profiles with transformer aggregation, while holding the best-known encoders (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l) and fusion (concat) constant, improve over the singleprofile baseline? Why this experiment: config_042 is the most direct logical extension of config_021, changing only the profile setting and adding transformer aggregation. If it outperforms config_021, we confirm multiprofile is beneficial and can then explore aggregation variants; if it underperforms, we learn that the added complexity does not help and can redirect budget toward other axes (e.g., scvi_n200). Testing transformer first is informative because it is the most expressive aggregation—if even this fails to help, simpler aggregations (avgpool) are unlikely to succeed.

The largest performance jump in the history is from config_021 (singleprofile, no aggregation, concat: 0.535) to config_042 (multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat: 0.599), a ~6-point gain. However, this comparison conflates two changes: (1) switching to multiprofile and (2) introducing transformer aggregation. Config_016 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) changes only the aggregation from transformer to avgpool while holding all other settings identical to config_042. This directly tests whether the transformer's sequential modeling of profiles is the critical driver or whether any aggregation of multiple profiles (even simple averaging) captures most of the gain. If avgpool approaches transformer performance, the multiprofile representation itself is the key factor (and a cheaper model suffices); if it falls well short, transformer aggregation is essential. This single-variable comparison is the most efficient way to reduce uncertainty about the aggregation design choice before committing further budget to the multiprofile+transformer family.

The current best configuration (config_016: pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieves 0.629 acc. We have strong evidence that multiprofile + avgpool + vit_l + pca_n2000 is the dominant design, but the fusion choice at the avgpool level is untested: concat gave 0.629 (config_016) and 0.599 with transformer (config_042), while weighted gave 0.532 in singleprofile (config_008) and 0.599 is untested with avgpool. Config_041 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is a single-variable change from the current best, isolating the fusion effect at the top aggregation level. If weighted outperforms concat here, we identify a new best; if not, we confirm concat is the optimal fusion and can redirect remaining budget toward RNA encoder exploration (e.g., scvi_n200). This is the highest-information, lowest-risk next step under the limited budget.

The current best configuration (config_041: multiprofile, pca_n2000, vit_l, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.6352) establishes a strong baseline. We have clear evidence that PCA outperforms scgpt (0.5232 vs 0.4214 in singleprofile), but scvi_n200 has never been tested in any multimodal setting. Config_049 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 while holding all other settings at their best-known values (multiprofile, vit_l, avgpool, weighted). This single-variable test directly answers whether a learned variational RNA encoder can capture complementary signal beyond PCA's linear dimensionality reduction. If scvi_n200 improves performance, it opens a new promising axis; if it underperforms, it confirms PCA is sufficient and redirects budget toward other unexplored dimensions. This is more informative than completing the aggregation×fusion 2×2 (config_047), where the avgpool>transformer gap (0.6287 vs 0.5988) is already large and the marginal information gain would be small.

With zero completed experiments, the priority is to establish a strong, interpretable baseline that future experiments can be compared against. config_029 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is the most 'standard' multimodal configuration in the space: it uses a well-understood linear RNA encoder (PCA), a strong pretrained image encoder (ImageNet ViT-L), and the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat) options. This makes it a natural reference point. Testing it first lets us (1) gauge whether the multimodal pipeline is viable at all, (2) provide a concrete accuracy/F1 anchor so that subsequent experiments that swap one component (e.g., scgpt vs. PCA, transformer vs. avgpool, weighted vs. concat) can be interpreted as isolated changes from a known baseline, and (3) avoid the risk of over-interpreting a complex configuration before we know what a simple one achieves. It is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under a limited budget because every later design decision can be framed as a controlled deviation from this point.

We have only one completed experiment (config_029: multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat → 0.629 acc), so evidence is extremely sparse and the most fundamental uncertainty is whether the image modality actually contributes. Config_003 (RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is a clean single-variable ablation of config_029: it removes only the image modality while keeping the RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation identical. If RNA-only performs comparably, the image modality is not adding value and the search should pivot toward RNA-encoder and aggregation choices; if it is substantially worse, multimodal fusion is confirmed as worthwhile and we can exploit that direction. Establishing this modality baseline before further multimodal variants is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under a limited budget, because it determines whether the entire fusion/aggregation design space is worth exploring.

Evidence: config_029 (multimodal, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.6287 acc, outperforming the RNA-only baseline config_003 (0.5907 acc) by ~3.8%, confirming that adding the image modality with these encoders is beneficial. However, we have no information on whether the fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted) meaningfully affects performance. Question: config_043 is identical to config_029 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, cleanly isolating the effect of the fusion mechanism while holding RNA encoder, image encoder, profile setting, and aggregation constant. Why this is the best next step: it is a single-variable exploitation of the best-performing configuration, directly tests whether the two modalities contribute unequally (which weighted fusion would capture), and the result will inform whether all future multimodal experiments should use concat or weighted fusion. Under a limited budget, this clean A/B comparison maximizes information per experiment without confounding multiple design changes.

Evidence: config_043 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) is the best result so far (acc=0.635, F1=0.618), and config_003 shows RNA-only with pca_n2000 is notably weaker (acc=0.591), confirming multimodal fusion adds value. However, all three completed experiments use pca_n2000 for RNA, leaving the RNA encoder choice entirely untested. Question: Does a learned RNA representation (scgpt) outperform linear PCA (pca_n2000) when paired with the same image encoder, aggregation, and fusion? config_049 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scgpt while holding imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, and weighted fusion constant, directly isolating the encoder effect. This is the highest-value next experiment because the RNA representation is a fundamental design axis with large uncertainty; if scgpt substantially improves over PCA, it redirects the search toward learned representations, whereas a null result confirms PCA sufficiency and shifts focus to aggregation or image-encoder choices.

Evidence: config_043 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) is the best-performing configuration so far (acc=0.6352, F1=0.6183), and it outperforms its concat-fusion counterpart (config_029, acc=0.6287) and the RNA-only baseline (config_003, acc=0.5907). scGPT as an RNA encoder is clearly inferior to PCA (config_049, acc=0.5420 vs 0.6352). Uncertainty: the effect of aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) has not been tested in the best-known setting. Question: config_034 changes only aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other factors at their best-known values (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, weighted, multiprofile), giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_043. Why this is the best next experiment: it directly extends the current best configuration by isolating one important design axis (aggregation), avoiding confounds from simultaneous changes. The result will tell us whether a more expressive aggregation strategy can further improve the top configuration or whether avgpool is already sufficient, guiding subsequent exploration of image encoder or profile setting.

Evidence: The current best config (config_043: pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.6352) shows that multimodal fusion adds ~4.5 pts over RNA-only (config_003, acc=0.5907), and that avgpool+weighted is the best aggregation/fusion pairing tested. However, the image encoder dimension is completely unexplored—only imagenet_vit_l has been tested. Question: config_015 (pca_n2000 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted) changes exactly one variable (image encoder) relative to the current best, cleanly isolating whether resnet50 contributes more, less, or comparably to imagenet_vit_l. Why this is the best next experiment: With a limited budget, testing the image encoder is the highest-information unexplored axis. It directly informs whether the ViT-L backbone is critical or whether a lighter ResNet-50 suffices, which has major implications for the remaining search space (e.g., whether to invest further in ViT-based or ResNet-based configurations). It also avoids the risk of testing scvi_n200 (a learned RNA encoder) when scgpt already showed a large negative effect (~9 pts), making the RNA encoder question less urgent.

Evidence: pca_n2000 strongly outperforms scgpt (0.6352 vs 0.5420 in config_043 vs config_049), and the current best config_015 (pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.6390. However, scvi_n200 has not been tested at all, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of the RNA encoder design axis. Question: config_011 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) changes only the RNA encoder relative to config_015, cleanly isolating whether scvi_n200 is competitive with pca_n2000 under the best-known image encoder, aggregation, and fusion settings. Why this is the best next experiment: it reduces uncertainty on a key representation choice with a single-variable comparison to the current best, and the result will either confirm pca_n2000 as the dominant RNA encoder (letting us focus budget on other axes) or reveal a promising alternative that could shift the entire search direction.

Evidence: config_011 (scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is the clear best at 0.6776 acc / 0.6464 F1, far ahead of all other configs. The dominant factor appears to be the RNA encoder (scvi_n200 >> pca_n2000 > scgpt). With pca_n2000, resnet50 and imagenet_vit_l performed nearly identically (0.6390 vs 0.6352), so the image encoder's contribution is unresolved. Question: Does pairing the strongest RNA representation (scvi_n200) with the stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) yield further gains, or is resnet50 already sufficient? config_007 changes only the image encoder (resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l) relative to config_011, keeping scvi_n200, avgpool, weighted, and multiprofile fixed. This is the cleanest single-variable test to determine whether the image modality is currently the bottleneck or whether the RNA encoder is the primary driver. Under a limited budget, confirming or refuting the image-encoder interaction with the best RNA encoder is more informative than re-testing aggregation or fusion, for which we already have directional evidence.

Evidence: config_007 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.7062) is the clear best, and scvi_n200 dramatically outperforms pca_n2000 (+7 pts) and scgpt (+16 pts) as the RNA encoder. However, the aggregation choice was only tested with pca_n2000, where transformer was ~5 pts worse than avgpool. Question: Does transformer aggregation interact differently with the learned, lower-dimensional scvi_n200 latent space compared to the high-dimensional PCA space? config_008 is a single-variable change (avgpool→transformer) from the best config, cleanly isolating the aggregation effect on the strongest representation. Why best next experiment: Aggregation is a higher-impact design axis than fusion (5-pt vs <1-pt observed differences), and the scvi_n200 representation is qualitatively different enough that the prior avgpool>transformer ordering may not hold. This either confirms avgpool is optimal (closing the aggregation question) or reveals a new promising direction, making it the most informative use of the next budget slot.

1) Evidence: config_008 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is the current best at 0.7250 acc / 0.6847 F1. The only prior fusion comparison (config_029 concat vs config_043 weighted, both pca_n2000+ViT+avgpool) showed weighted slightly ahead, but that was under avgpool aggregation. The interaction between transformer aggregation and fusion strategy is completely untested. 2) Question: Does the optimal fusion strategy change when the aggregation is a transformer rather than avgpool? A transformer aggregation produces a contextually mixed representation, which may interact differently with concat (preserving modality boundaries) versus weighted (learned scalar combination). 3) Why best next experiment: It is a single-variable change from the current best configuration (fusion: weighted→concat), making it a clean, interpretable comparison. If concat matches or exceeds weighted here, it confirms the fusion choice is aggregation-dependent and opens a new design axis; if weighted remains superior, it solidifies the full best-known recipe and redirects budget toward other unexplored dimensions (e.g., singleprofile or image-encoder interactions). Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information-per-experiment step that directly extends the strongest evidence.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so the most critical unknown is whether multimodal fusion (combining RNA + image) actually provides a meaningful performance gain over a strong unimodal baseline. Without this reference, all multimodal results are uninterpretable. 2) What this tests: config_013 is the simplest possible image-only model (imagenet_vit_l, no aggregation, no fusion, singleprofile). It establishes a clean performance floor for the image modality alone. Any future multimodal configuration that fails to beat this baseline would indicate that the added complexity of RNA fusion is not justified. 3) Why best under limited budget: Starting with the strongest unimodal baseline (ViT-L is the most capable image encoder available) maximizes the information gained per experiment—if multimodal configs must beat a strong baseline, we avoid wasting budget on multimodal variants that merely match what a single modality already achieves. This single result also calibrates expectations for all subsequent comparisons (e.g., rna_only baselines, aggregation/fusion ablations) and directly addresses the principle of not assuming complexity yields gains.

We have only one completed experiment (config_013: image_only, singleprofile, ViT-L → 22.7% acc), which is an extremely sparse evidence base. The most fundamental uncertainty for a multimodal cellular-profiling study is whether adding the RNA modality provides any signal beyond the image alone. config_012 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, aggregation=None, fusion=weighted) matches the baseline on every shared axis—same image encoder (ViT-L), same profile setting (singleprofile), no aggregation—so the only major change is the addition of a pretrained single-cell RNA encoder (scgpt) with a weighted fusion. This gives a clean, near-controlled comparison that isolates the contribution of the RNA modality. If accuracy improves meaningfully over 22.7%, we gain confidence to invest in RNA encoder and fusion choices; if it does not, we learn that the image pathway or the task itself is the bottleneck and can redirect budget toward image-encoder or profile-setting experiments. Under a tight budget, resolving this binary question (does RNA help?) is the highest-information next step before exploring finer-grained design axes.

Evidence: config_013 (image-only, ViT-L, singleprofile) scored 0.227 acc, while config_012 (multimodal, scgpt+ViT-L, weighted, singleprofile) scored 0.422 acc. This ~0.20 gap shows the multimodal combination is strong, but we cannot yet tell how much is driven by the RNA modality versus the image modality or their interaction. Uncertainty: We have no RNA-only baseline, so we don't know whether scgpt alone approaches 0.42 (implying image adds little) or is much lower (implying genuine multimodal synergy). Question tested: config_048 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) is a clean single-variable ablation of config_012—removing only the image modality while keeping the same RNA encoder (scgpt) and profile setting (singleprofile). Why best next: With only two completed experiments, the highest-information move is to establish each modality's individual contribution before investing in fusion/aggregation/profile variants. The result will sharply redirect the search: if RNA alone ≈ 0.40, we should prioritize RNA encoder choices; if RNA alone ≈ 0.25, multimodal fusion is genuinely synergistic and we should explore aggregation and fusion strategies; if RNA alone is very low, image features are critical and we should test alternative image encoders. No other available configuration isolates this question as cleanly.

Evidence: Our three completed experiments show that (1) image-only (ViT-L, singleprofile) is weak (0.227 acc), (2) RNA-only (scgpt, singleprofile) is moderate (0.411 acc), and (3) multimodal (scgpt + ViT-L, singleprofile, weighted) gives a small lift over RNA alone (0.422 vs 0.411). The marginal multimodal gain suggests the current singleprofile representation may be a bottleneck for both modalities. Uncertainty: We have zero data on whether multiprofile with aggregation can unlock additional signal that singleprofile cannot capture. This is the largest unexplored design axis. Question: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with transformer aggregation improve performance, holding encoders (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l) and fusion (weighted) constant? Why this is the best next experiment: config_010 is the minimal, logical extension of our best result (config_012), changing only the profile/aggregation axis. If it helps, we confirm the profile bottleneck and can further optimize aggregation; if it does not, we rule out that axis and redirect budget toward encoder or fusion choices. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most impactful untested design decision under our limited budget.

Evidence: config_010 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer agg, weighted fusion) achieved 0.520 acc, a large jump over config_012 (same but singleprofile, no aggregation) at 0.422. This gain is attributed to the combination of multiprofile + transformer aggregation, but we cannot yet tell whether the transformer is specifically critical or whether any aggregation of multiple profiles would suffice. Question: config_018 changes only the aggregation from transformer to avgpool while holding all other settings identical to config_010, cleanly isolating the aggregation method. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a single-variable comparison against our strongest result, directly testing whether the transformer's learned attention over profiles is the key mechanism or whether simpler pooling captures most of the multiprofile benefit. This mechanistic insight will determine whether subsequent experiments should prioritize transformer-based designs or whether we can redirect budget toward other untested variables (RNA encoder, image encoder, fusion method) with a simpler aggregation.

The best configuration so far (config_018: scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.542 accuracy, and we have strong evidence that multiprofile + avgpool + weighted fusion is a good backbone. However, the RNA encoder has only been tested as scgpt across all top-performing configs, leaving a major design dimension unexplored. Config_003 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) is a controlled comparison that changes only the RNA encoder from scgpt to scvi_n200 while holding image encoder, aggregation, fusion, and profile setting constant. This isolates the effect of the RNA representation: if scvi_n200 performs comparably, the RNA encoder choice is less critical and we can focus budget on other axes (image encoder, fusion); if it performs substantially worse, we confirm scgpt's learned representation is essential; if it performs better, we find a new promising direction. This is the highest-information single change given the current evidence.

Evidence: config_003 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) achieved the best accuracy (0.706), a large jump over config_018 (scgpt, same other settings, 0.542), confirming RNA encoder choice is the dominant factor. With scgpt, avgpool slightly outperformed transformer (0.542 vs 0.520), but scvi_n200 produces a fundamentally different latent representation (VAE-based vs. masked LM), so the optimal aggregation may shift. Question: Does transformer aggregation improve upon avgpool when paired with scvi_n200? config_045 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_003, isolating only the aggregation method. This is the best use of the next budget slot because it directly extends our strongest result, tests a design choice with plausible interaction effects, and avoids changing multiple variables simultaneously.

Evidence: scvi_n200 with multiprofile + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion (config_045) achieves 0.725 acc, far exceeding scgpt-based configs (~0.52-0.54). However, we lack an rna_only baseline for scvi_n200 to determine whether the image modality actually contributes complementary information. With scgpt, image added only ~1% (0.411→0.422), suggesting it may be redundant. Question: config_051 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) directly compares to config_045 with the image encoder and fusion removed, isolating the image's marginal contribution. Why this is best: This is the most fundamental remaining architectural question. If rna_only approaches 0.725, the image is redundant and future budget should focus on RNA representation; if it drops substantially, the multimodal design is justified and fusion/image-encoder optimizations become worthwhile. This single experiment resolves a high-uncertainty design decision that would redirect all subsequent experiments.

Evidence: The best-performing configuration so far is config_045 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc. All top-performing configs use weighted fusion, but we have no evidence on how concat fusion performs in this strong regime—concat was only tested with weaker scgpt encoders. Question: config_007 changes exactly one variable from config_045 (fusion: weighted → concat), cleanly isolating the effect of fusion strategy when the RNA encoder and image encoder are both strong. Why this is the best next experiment: It is the most informative single-variable test available—either it confirms weighted fusion is essential (narrowing the design space) or shows concat is competitive (broadening it). Under a limited budget, this directly informs whether fusion choice is a critical design axis or a minor one, and it avoids simultaneously changing multiple variables as would happen with, e.g., testing a new image encoder and a new fusion at once.

Evidence: The top-performing configurations (config_045: 0.725, config_007: 0.721, config_003: 0.706) all use scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile, with small differences driven by aggregation/fusion. However, the image encoder choice has only been tested as imagenet_vit_l for scvi_n200; we have no data on how resnet50 performs in this regime. Question: config_035 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) is a single-variable change from our current best (config_045), isolating the effect of image encoder while holding RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation, and fusion constant. Why best next experiment: Under a limited budget, knowing whether the ViT-L image encoder is truly necessary or whether a lighter ResNet50 achieves comparable performance is a high-value design decision. If resnet50 matches imagenet_vit_l, it simplifies deployment; if it underperforms significantly, it confirms the ViT-L's learned patch representations are critical for the multimodal fusion. This is more informative than exploring pca_n2000 (likely inferior given scgpt already trails scvi_n200 by ~20 points) or re-testing aggregation/fusion variants that show only ~1-2 point differences.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is no performance baseline. We do not yet know how well a simple single-modality, single-profile model performs, which is essential for judging whether multimodal integration, multiprofile aggregation, or more complex encoders actually add value. 2) What this tests: config_009 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200, no aggregation, no fusion) is the simplest possible pipeline in the search space. It isolates the performance of the scvi_n200 RNA representation on a single profile with no confounding factors from image modality, aggregation, or fusion. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Establishing a clean performance floor is the highest-information first step under a limited budget. Without it, any later multimodal or multiprofile result is ambiguous—we cannot tell if gains come from added complexity or if the baseline was already near ceiling. This single experiment reduces uncertainty about the most fundamental question (does the data support good classification at all?) and provides a reference against which every subsequent design axis (modality, profile, encoder, aggregation, fusion) can be evaluated with controlled comparisons.

With only one completed experiment (config_009: rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200 → acc 0.520), evidence is extremely sparse. The most critical design question for a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether adding the image modality provides any benefit over RNA alone. Config_014 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, no aggregation, concat) is the most direct extension of the baseline: it keeps the RNA encoder (scvi_n200) and profile setting (singleprofile) identical, and adds the simplest image pipeline (resnet50 + concat fusion, no aggregation). This isolates the effect of introducing the image modality with minimal confounding changes. If performance improves, it justifies further exploration of image encoders, aggregation, and fusion; if it does not, it redirects budget toward RNA-side or profile-setting optimizations. No other available config tests the modality question as cleanly while changing the fewest other parameters.

We have two data points: RNA-only (scvi_n200, singleprofile) at 0.5203 and multimodal (scvi_n200 + resnet50, concat, singleprofile) at 0.5362. The ~1.6% gain from adding image is modest and we cannot yet determine whether it reflects genuine cross-modal complementarity or one modality simply dominating. The critical missing baseline is image-only performance with the same resnet50 encoder and singleprofile setting. config_034 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest single-variable complement to config_009 and config_014, isolating the image modality's independent contribution. Resolving this uncertainty is the highest-priority question before investing further budget in multiprofile aggregation, alternative encoders, or fusion strategies, because it tells us whether the multimodal direction is worth pursuing and which modality to prioritize for encoder improvements.

Evidence: Across the three completed experiments, RNA is clearly the dominant signal (rna_only 0.520 vs image_only 0.208), and the only RNA encoder tested so far is scvi_n200. The multimodal gain over RNA-only is modest (+1.6%), suggesting that improving the RNA representation could yield a larger absolute gain than tuning the weak image branch. Question: config_023 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) is a clean single-variable A/B against config_009, changing only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt while holding profile, model setting, and all other hyperparameters fixed. This isolates the effect of the RNA encoder on the dominant modality. Why this is the best next experiment: With only three data points, the largest source of uncertainty is whether the RNA encoder choice materially affects performance. Resolving this early (i) tells us whether to invest further in scvi_n200-based configurations or pivot to scgpt, (ii) avoids confounding the encoder question with aggregation/fusion/multiprofile variables, and (iii) directly informs the design of all subsequent multimodal experiments where the RNA branch is the primary contributor. A simple rna_only, singleprofile design keeps the experiment interpretable and budget-efficient.

All four completed experiments use singleprofile, leaving the multiprofile dimension entirely unexplored. The evidence shows RNA (scvi_n200) is the dominant signal (0.520 acc) while image alone is weak (0.208), and multimodal adds only ~1.6% over RNA-only. The most important open question is whether aggregating multiple profiles (via avgpool) improves representation quality. config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a clean A/B comparison against config_009 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200), changing only the profile setting and adding avgpool aggregation. This isolates the multiprofile effect without confounding it with fusion strategy, image encoder, or model complexity. Under a tight budget, resolving whether multiprofile is beneficial at all—on the modality that carries most signal—is the highest-information next step before committing experiments to more complex multimodal+multi configurations.

The strongest evidence so far is that multiprofile with scvi_n200 and avgpool (config_002, acc 0.650) dramatically outperforms singleprofile RNA-only (config_009, acc 0.520), while adding resnet50 image in the singleprofile setting (config_014) yields only a marginal +0.016 gain. The key uncertainty is whether image contributes meaningfully when combined with the multiprofile gain. config_037 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the minimal extension of config_002: it adds the same resnet50 image encoder and concat fusion already validated in config_014, while keeping aggregation (avgpool) and RNA encoder (scvi_n200) identical. This isolates the image contribution in the multiprofile regime. If it matches or beats 0.650, image is worth retaining; if not, we can focus remaining budget on RNA-only multiprofile refinements (e.g., aggregation method or encoder choice) without the added complexity of a second modality.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved the best accuracy (0.650) so far, while config_037 (same but multimodal with resnet50, avgpool, concat) scored lower (0.632), suggesting the image branch with resnet50 is a weak or even detrimental signal in the multiprofile regime. The aggregation method (avgpool) has only been tested in one configuration, leaving open whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) could further improve the multiprofile representation. Question: config_007 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_002, isolating the effect of aggregation (transformer vs. avgpool) while holding model setting, profile, and encoder constant. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly tests whether the 0.650 ceiling is due to avgpool being suboptimal or whether the multiprofile+scvi_n200 representation is already near its limit. If transformer helps, it informs all future multimodal experiments; if not, we can confidently keep avgpool and redirect budget toward improving the image encoder or fusion strategy. This avoids confounding multiple design choices and reduces uncertainty about a core architectural decision before investing in more complex multimodal variants.

Evidence: Multiprofile + scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest backbone (config_002: 0.650, config_007: 0.653), but adding resnet50 image features in the multimodal multiprofile setting (config_037: 0.632) actually *hurts* relative to RNA-only. Image-only with resnet50 is very weak (0.208), suggesting resnet50 features may be the bottleneck rather than the image modality itself. Uncertainty: We have not tested whether a stronger, pretrained image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) can produce representations that actually complement the RNA profile. Question: config_044 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is a clean single-variable swap of the image encoder from resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l relative to config_037, while matching the aggregation (avgpool) and fusion (concat) of the best RNA-only multiprofile baseline. This isolates the effect of image encoder quality. Why best next experiment: If config_044 exceeds config_037 and approaches or beats config_002, it reveals the image modality has untapped value with a better encoder, justifying further multimodal exploration. If it still lags behind RNA-only, it provides strong evidence that the image channel is not useful for this task, allowing us to focus remaining budget on RNA-only multiprofile refinements (aggregation, encoder variants). Either outcome significantly reduces uncertainty about a core design axis (representation/fusion) with a single clean comparison.

The best configuration so far is config_044 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat, acc 0.715). The two main untested levers on top of this are fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted) and aggregation (avgpool vs. transformer). From the rna_only comparison (config_002 avgpool 0.650 vs. config_007 transformer 0.653), aggregation choice appears to have negligible impact, whereas fusion strategy has been tested only as 'concat' across all multimodal runs, leaving it completely unexplored. Config_008 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted while holding every other variable identical to config_044, giving a clean single-variable test of whether learned or adaptive weighting of the two modalities can improve on simple concatenation. Under a limited budget, resolving this high-uncertainty, high-impact design choice (how to combine the strong image and RNA representations) is more informative than re-testing aggregation, which prior evidence suggests is a minor factor.

Evidence: config_044 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.715 acc. For RNA-only multiprofile, avgpool (0.650) and transformer (0.653) are nearly identical, but the multimodal interaction between a transformer aggregator and the image features is untested. Question: Does transformer aggregation improve over avgpool when both modalities are present, potentially capturing richer cross-profile and cross-modal interactions? This is a clean single-variable change (avgpool → transformer) from the best config, isolating the aggregation effect. Why best next: It directly exploits the strongest evidence (config_044) with a minimal, interpretable perturbation. A positive result yields an immediate performance gain; a null result confirms avgpool suffices and redirects budget toward other dimensions (e.g., standalone image contribution or alternative RNA encoders) without ambiguity.

With no completed experiments, there is zero evidence about which design choices matter. The most informative first step is to establish a clean, interpretable baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) is the simplest possible configuration: one modality, one profile, a well-established RNA encoder, and no aggregation or fusion to confound interpretation. This establishes a performance floor for RNA data and creates a clear anchor for all future comparisons: (a) does multiprofile + aggregation help (compare to config_002)? (b) does adding an image modality help (compare to config_029/034)? (c) does encoder choice matter (compare to config_013 or config_026)? Starting from the simplest configuration ensures that any future performance gains can be attributed to specific design additions rather than being entangled with multiple simultaneous changes. Under a limited budget, this single experiment maximizes the number of informative follow-up comparisons it enables.

Evidence: Only one experiment is complete (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt → acc 0.41, F1 0.38), giving a weak baseline with no information about whether the image modality carries any predictive signal. Question: Does image-only representation (resnet50, singleprofile, no aggregation/fusion) provide meaningful classification signal comparable to or complementary with RNA? Why this is the best next experiment: config_012 mirrors the structural simplicity of config_001 (singleprofile, no aggregation, no fusion) while swapping only the modality from RNA to image. This isolates the effect of modality as the single variable. Answering whether image alone has signal is the most fundamental uncertainty in a multimodal study: if image is weak, the search should focus on RNA encoder/aggregation improvements; if image is strong, multimodal fusion becomes a high-priority direction. This single experiment reduces the largest source of uncertainty in the design space before committing budget to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

Evidence: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) achieves 41.1% accuracy, while config_012 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) achieves only 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. However, we have no information on whether the profile setting (single vs. multi) meaningfully affects performance. Question: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) directly tests whether aggregating multiple profiles improves the RNA signal, keeping the encoder (scgpt) and modality (RNA) identical to our best result. Why this is the best next experiment: With only two completed runs, the profile setting is a fundamental, unexplored design axis that will structure all subsequent multimodal experiments. If multiprofile+avgpool improves on 41%, it justifies investing further in multiprofile configurations and tells us aggregation matters. If it does not, we can safely restrict future search to singleprofile settings, dramatically reducing the effective search space. This is a clean single-dimension comparison (profile setting) from our strongest baseline, making it the most information-dense use of the next experiment under budget constraints.

Evidence: RNA with scgpt improved substantially from singleprofile (0.41) to multiprofile+avgpool (0.53), while image with resnet50 singleprofile is very weak (0.21). We have no data on whether the image modality benefits from multiprofile aggregation. Question: Does multiprofile+avgpool improve the image modality the way it improved RNA? This is a clean single-variable comparison to config_012 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50), directly paralleling the RNA comparison (config_001→config_002). Why this is the best next experiment: The answer determines the strategic direction for all subsequent work—if image improves meaningfully with multiprofile, multimodal fusion becomes a promising avenue to exploit; if it remains near 0.21, the image modality is fundamentally weak with resnet50 and we should prioritize RNA encoder/aggregation improvements or a stronger image encoder instead. This single experiment resolves the largest current uncertainty about whether the image channel carries usable signal, making it the highest-information-use experiment under budget constraints.

Evidence: RNA (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) achieves 0.5305 acc (config_002), far exceeding image-only (resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.3275 (config_042). Multiprofile+avgpool consistently helps both modalities. The critical open question is whether combining the dominant RNA signal with the weaker image signal via fusion actually improves over the RNA-only baseline, or whether image adds noise. Config_034 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) is the minimal single-variable extension of config_002: it keeps the exact same RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation, and only adds the image modality with a weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of multimodal fusion on the best-performing RNA configuration. If it beats 0.53, we confirm image contributes complementary information and can explore better fusion/encoders; if it matches or falls below, we learn image adds little value with resnet50 and should prioritize RNA-side improvements. This is the highest-information experiment under budget constraints because it directly tests the central design question (does multimodal help?) with a clean comparison to an already-established baseline.

Evidence: The multimodal config_034 (scgpt+resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.5251, essentially matching but not clearly beating the RNA-only baseline config_002 (0.5305). Image-only is weak (0.3275), suggesting the resnet50 image representation may be too noisy or uninformative to add value in fusion. Uncertainty: We cannot yet tell whether the multimodal model is bottlenecked by a weak image encoder or by the fusion strategy itself. This experiment (config_006) isolates the image encoder variable by swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l while keeping scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool, and weighted fusion identical to config_034. If ViT-L meaningfully improves the multimodal score over both config_034 and config_002, it confirms that image representation quality is the bottleneck and justifies further investment in image encoders. If it does not, it strongly suggests the image modality is fundamentally limited for this task and future budget should focus on RNA encoder/aggregation improvements or different fusion mechanisms. This single-variable comparison is the most informative next step because it resolves the key question of whether the image signal can ever be useful, which gates many downstream design decisions.

Evidence: The current best configuration is config_006 (multimodal, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.542), which marginally outperforms RNA-only multiprofile (config_002, acc=0.530). However, all experiments so far have used avgpool as the sole aggregation method, and the multiprofile→singleprofile jump was the largest single improvement observed (0.41→0.53 for RNA). This means the aggregation strategy is a critical but unexplored design dimension. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool for combining multiprofile representations in the multimodal setting with the best-performing encoders (scgpt + ViT-L)? Why this experiment: config_027 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer relative to config_006, isolating a single variable while building on the strongest existing configuration. If transformer aggregation improves performance, it reveals a new lever for further gains; if it does not, it confirms avgpool sufficiency and redirects search toward other dimensions (fusion, RNA encoder). This is the highest-information single-variable test available under the limited budget.

Evidence: The best multimodal result (config_006, scgpt+vit_l, avgpool, weighted: acc 0.5420, F1 0.4833) is only marginally better than RNA-only multi-profile scgpt (config_002: acc 0.5305, F1 0.5152), and notably has a lower F1. Multimodal with resnet50 (config_034: 0.5251) is actually worse than RNA-only alone. Image-only with resnet50 (config_042: 0.3275) is far below RNA-only, but we lack the image-only baseline with the stronger vit_l encoder. Uncertainty: We cannot yet determine whether the small multimodal gain over RNA-only is genuinely attributable to the image modality or is within noise, because we don't know how well vit_l performs on images alone in the multi-profile setting. Question: config_004 (image_only, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool) isolates the image encoder's standalone contribution with the stronger backbone, directly comparable to config_042 (resnet50) and config_006 (multimodal vit_l). Why best next: This single-variable experiment (changing only the image encoder from resnet50 to vit_l in the image-only setting) is essential to calibrate whether the image modality is adding real signal in the multimodal configs. If vit_l alone approaches ~0.50, the multimodal gain is minimal and we should refocus on RNA encoder/fusion improvements; if it stays near 0.33, the vit_l contribution in multimodal is more meaningful. This reduces uncertainty about the most fundamental design decision (whether to invest in multimodal fusion at all) before spending further budget on fusion or aggregation variants.

Evidence: All completed experiments use scgpt as the RNA encoder, so we have zero information about whether a simpler representation (pca_n2000) would perform comparably. The best rna_only result is config_002 (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.5305 acc / 0.5152 F1, and the best multimodal result (config_006, scgpt + imagenet_vit_l) is only ~1% higher at 0.5420, suggesting the RNA representation may be the dominant factor. Question: config_017 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_002—only the RNA encoder changes. This directly tests whether the learned scgpt representation is necessary or whether a linear 2000-dim projection suffices. Why best next: Resolving the RNA encoder question is the highest-leverage uncertainty because it affects every downstream decision (whether multimodal fusion is worthwhile, which encoder to pair with, and whether the pipeline can be simplified). If PCA matches scgpt, it invalidates the complexity of the current best configs and redirects the search; if it falls well short, it confirms scgpt's value and lets us focus remaining budget on fusion/aggregation/image-encoder choices with confidence in the RNA backbone.

Evidence: PCA (pca_n2000) as a unimodal RNA encoder (config_017, acc=0.5907) substantially outperforms scGPT (config_002, acc=0.5305) and all multimodal configurations tested so far (best: config_006, scgpt+ViT-L, acc=0.5420). The best multimodal setup uses ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion. However, PCA has never been tested in a multimodal context, leaving a critical uncertainty: does adding image information to the already-strong PCA representation help, or does it dilute the signal? Question: config_051 (pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) directly swaps the RNA encoder in the best multimodal configuration (config_006) while holding image encoder, aggregation, and fusion constant. This isolates the RNA encoder effect in the multimodal setting and tests whether the image modality provides complementary information on top of PCA. Why this is the best next experiment: it resolves the single most important open question—whether the search should exploit the strong PCA unimodal result or whether a PCA-based multimodal model can surpass it—using a minimal, controlled change from the best existing multimodal setup. The outcome will directly guide whether subsequent experiments should focus on PCA+image fusion variants or on further improving the PCA unimodal baseline.

With no prior experiments, the most critical uncertainty is establishing a strong single-modality baseline to judge whether multimodal fusion, multiprofile aggregation, or more complex encoders actually add value. config_011 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) provides a clean, well-established reference: scVI is a standard learned encoder in single-cell genomics, singleprofile avoids confounding from aggregation strategy, and the RNA-only setting isolates the contribution of gene expression without image modality. This baseline lets every subsequent multimodal or multiprofile experiment be interpreted as a delta over a meaningful (not trivially weak) starting point. It is the highest-information first experiment because it anchors the comparison space for modality, profile, and encoder choices simultaneously without introducing multiple untested complexities at once.

We have only one completed experiment (config_011: rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200; acc=0.520, F1=0.498), so the most critical uncertainty is whether adding the image modality provides any benefit at all. config_003 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, no aggregation, concat) is the cleanest direct comparison to config_011: it holds the RNA encoder (scvi_n200), profile setting (singleprofile), and absence of aggregation constant, introducing only the image encoder and a simple concat fusion. This isolates the effect of the image modality with minimal confounds. If accuracy improves meaningfully, it justifies investing further budget in exploring image encoder choice, aggregation, and fusion in the multimodal space. If it does not, we learn that image adds little and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder and profile-setting variations. Under a tight budget, resolving this fundamental question first maximizes information gained per experiment.

Evidence: config_003 (multimodal, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieved 0.532 acc vs config_011 (RNA-only, scvi_n200) at 0.520 acc — a modest ~1.2% gain. This small difference raises uncertainty about whether the image modality is genuinely contributing complementary information or whether the gain is within noise. Question: config_013 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is a clean ablation that isolates the image encoder's standalone contribution using the exact same image encoder and profile setting as config_003, with RNA removed. If image_only performs poorly (<0.45), the multimodal gain is likely a small complementary effect and we should focus budget on RNA-side improvements (e.g., multiprofile, encoder choice). If image_only performs competitively (>0.50), the image is a strong standalone signal and the multimodal combination may be suboptimal, pointing us toward better fusion strategies. Why this is the best next experiment: before spending limited budget on more complex multimodal variants (multiprofile, weighted fusion, transformer aggregation), we must first confirm that the image modality is actually adding meaningful information. This single-variable ablation maximally reduces uncertainty about the most fundamental design decision (whether to include image features at all) and will directly guide whether subsequent experiments should exploit the multimodal direction or pivot to RNA-side optimizations.

Evidence: RNA-only (config_011, scvi_n200, singleprofile) achieves 0.520 acc, while image-only (config_013) is very weak at 0.227, and multimodal (config_003) adds only ~1.2% over RNA-only (0.532). This strongly suggests the RNA representation is the dominant signal and the bottleneck for improvement. All three completed experiments use singleprofile with no aggregation, so the effect of multiprofile is entirely unexplored. Question: Does aggregating multiple RNA profiles (avgpool) improve the RNA signal beyond a single profile, holding the encoder (scvi_n200) and modality (RNA-only) constant? Why this is the best next experiment: config_002 changes exactly one design axis (singleprofile→multiprofile + avgpool) relative to config_011, giving a clean ablation. If it improves, it identifies profile diversity as a key lever and justifies investing further in multiprofile multimodal configs. If it does not, it rules out aggregation as a source of gain and redirects budget toward RNA encoder choice (scgpt, pca_n2000) or fusion strategy. This maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc, a large jump over config_011 (singleprofile, 0.520), showing multiprofile+avgpool is the dominant design lever. Meanwhile, adding image to the singleprofile setting (config_003, 0.532) barely helped over RNA alone (config_011, 0.520), and image alone was very weak (config_013, 0.227). Uncertainty: it is unclear whether image contributes any value on top of the much stronger multiprofile RNA baseline. This experiment (config_042: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) isolates the effect of adding the image modality by keeping the RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation, and fusion strategy identical to the two best singleprofile comparisons (config_002 and config_003). If accuracy stays near 0.650, image adds little even in the multiprofile regime; if it improves meaningfully, it justifies further multimodal investment. This is the highest-information next step because it directly tests the most important open question—whether the image channel is worth the added complexity—while changing only one factor relative to the current best configuration.

Evidence: RNA is the dominant signal (rna_only 0.52 vs image_only 0.23), and multiprofile+avgpool lifts RNA from 0.52→0.65. However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (scvi_n200) across all five experiments, leaving the most fundamental representation choice unexplored. Question: config_036 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_002 (same but scvi_n200), isolating whether the scgpt pre-trained gene-expression representation outperforms the scvi latent embedding. Why this is the best next experiment: RNA encoder quality is the highest-leverage design decision because it determines the primary signal in every multimodal configuration. If scgpt substantially outperforms scvi_n200, the entire multimodal search direction shifts; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 and can confidently build on it. This reduces uncertainty on the most important axis before committing further budget to aggregation or fusion variations on top of a potentially suboptimal RNA representation.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_042 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 acc. We have strong evidence that multiprofile >> singleprofile and multimodal > RNA-only, and that scvi_n200 >> scgpt. However, the only aggregation method tested in multiprofile settings is avgpool. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether a transformer-based aggregation could better model inter-profile interactions than simple averaging, potentially unlocking further gains on top of the already-strong config_042. Question tested: config_048 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other variables (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat fusion, multiprofile) identical to config_042, giving a clean A/B comparison of aggregation strategy. Why best next experiment: It is the most informative single-variable extension of the current best, directly isolating the effect of aggregation—a core design axis for multiprofile models—without confounding other choices. If transformer aggregation helps, it identifies a new productive direction; if not, it confirms avgpool sufficiency and redirects budget toward fusion or encoder choices.

Evidence: The top two configs (config_048: transformer+concat, acc=0.721; config_042: avgpool+concat, acc=0.715) both use concat fusion, and no experiment has yet tested weighted fusion in the multiprofile multimodal setting. The small accuracy/F1 trade-off between transformer and avgpool suggests we are near a plateau for the current fusion strategy. Question: config_027 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) changes only the fusion from concat to weighted relative to config_048, cleanly isolating the fusion mechanism's contribution. Why best next: It is a single-variable extension of the current best configuration, directly testing whether learned modal weighting can improve over simple concatenation. If weighted fusion helps, it identifies a new axis of improvement; if it does not, it confirms concat is sufficient and redirects budget toward other unexplored axes (e.g., image encoder choice). This is more informative than testing a new image encoder or RNA encoder, which would change multiple untested factors simultaneously.

The current best configuration (config_027: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, acc=0.725) has been established through a series of experiments that confirmed multiprofile >> singleprofile, scvi_n200 >> scgpt, and multimodal > rna_only. However, the image encoder choice has never been varied—all multimodal experiments used imagenet_vit_l. config_033 (scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) isolates the effect of the image encoder while holding all other design choices at their best-known settings. This is the highest-uncertainty remaining design decision: if resnet50 performs comparably, the image encoder is not a critical lever and we can focus budget on other dimensions; if it degrades performance, it confirms the ViT's importance and justifies the added complexity. This single-variable comparison to the current best is the most efficient use of the next experiment under a limited budget.

Evidence: In RNA-only multiprofile, scvi_n200 (0.650) substantially outperforms scgpt (0.530), a 0.120 gap. In the multimodal multiprofile setting, our best config (config_027: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) achieves 0.725. However, we have no data on whether the RNA encoder choice still matters when a strong image encoder is present. Question: Does pairing scgpt with the same image encoder, aggregation, and fusion (imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) close the gap to scvi_n200, or does RNA encoder quality remain critical even in multimodal settings? This is a clean single-variable comparison (scgpt vs scvi_n200) with all other factors held at their best-known values. Why best next experiment: Under limited budget, resolving whether the RNA encoder is a dominant or secondary design axis in the multimodal regime directly informs whether further search should focus on RNA encoder variants or on other axes (aggregation, fusion, image encoder). If scgpt+image ≈ scvi_n200+image, it frees the search to explore other dimensions; if the gap persists, it confirms scvi_n200 as the necessary backbone and justifies concentrating remaining budget on tuning around it.

With no prior evidence, the first experiment must establish a performance baseline to anchor all subsequent comparisons. config_001 (image_only, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool) is the cleanest unimodal baseline: it uses the most widely shared image encoder (resnet50) and the simplest aggregation (avgpool), isolating the contribution of the image modality alone. This tells us (1) how well the image channel performs in isolation, (2) how multiprofile + avgpool behaves as a default pipeline, and (3) provides a reference point to later determine whether adding RNA (multimodal) or switching to a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) actually improves over a simple image-only model. Starting simple avoids conflating modality, encoder, and aggregation effects in the first data point, maximizing the interpretability of every future comparison under a tight budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: image_only, resnet50, avgpool → acc 0.328), the most fundamental uncertainty is whether adding the RNA modality provides meaningful signal beyond the image alone. config_008 (multimodal, scgpt, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) keeps the image encoder and aggregation identical to config_001, so any performance difference can be attributed primarily to the addition of RNA via scgpt and the weighted fusion. This directly tests the core hypothesis of the multimodal profiling study. scgpt is a well-established pretrained single-cell RNA encoder, making it a principled first choice for the RNA modality. Establishing whether RNA adds value is the highest-priority design question before investing budget in encoder variants, aggregation strategies, or fusion alternatives. If config_008 substantially outperforms config_001, we can then exploit by testing better encoders/aggregation; if it does not, we learn that the bottleneck lies elsewhere (e.g., image representation or profile setting) and redirect exploration accordingly.

Evidence: config_008 (multimodal, scgpt+resnet50, avgpool, weighted) achieves 0.525 acc, a large jump over config_001 (image_only, resnet50, avgpool) at 0.328 acc. This confirms adding RNA helps, but we cannot yet decompose how much of the gain comes from the RNA signal itself versus the image-RNA fusion. Uncertainty: We do not know the standalone RNA contribution. If scgpt alone (config_009: rna_only, scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) already approaches ~0.50, the image modality adds little and future effort should focus on RNA encoder/aggregation. If it is much lower (~0.30-0.40), the image modality is essential and we should prioritize image encoder and fusion improvements. This is a clean ablation of config_008 (same RNA encoder, profile, aggregation; only the image modality and fusion are removed), making it the single most informative next experiment to reduce fundamental uncertainty about modality contribution before committing budget to narrower questions like fusion type or image encoder choice.

Evidence: RNA-only with scgpt (config_009, acc=0.530, F1=0.515) slightly outperforms multimodal with scgpt+resnet50 weighted fusion (config_008, acc=0.525, F1=0.498), while image-only with resnet50 (config_001) is very weak (acc=0.328). This raises the critical question of whether the image modality has any useful signal or whether resnet50 is simply too weak to contribute. Question: config_007 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is the minimal-change extension of config_008, swapping only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. This isolates the effect of image encoder quality on multimodal performance. Why best next experiment: If imagenet_vit_l substantially improves multimodal accuracy over both config_008 and config_009, it confirms the image modality carries useful information that was being lost by a weak encoder, justifying further investment in multimodal designs. If it does not help, it strongly suggests the image channel is not contributing and the budget should focus on RNA-side improvements (encoder choice, aggregation, profile setting). This single experiment resolves a high-uncertainty, high-impact design decision before spending budget on more complex multimodal variants.

Evidence: config_007 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted fusion) is our best performer (acc 0.542, F1 0.483), but its F1 is notably lower than config_009 (rna_only, scgpt: acc 0.530, F1 0.515), suggesting the weighted fusion with vit_l may be compressing class information. We have only tested 'weighted' fusion so far; 'concat' fusion is completely untested. Question: config_016 changes only the fusion from weighted to concat while keeping scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + multiprofile fixed, directly isolating the fusion strategy's effect on the strongest configuration. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a clean single-variable comparison against our top performer, it addresses the F1 gap that may be fusion-related, and if concat improves F1 without sacrificing accuracy, it identifies a key design lever for subsequent experiments. Testing fusion on a weaker base (e.g., resnet50) would be less informative since that setup already underperforms RNA-only.

Evidence: The best-performing config so far is config_007 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) at 0.5420 acc, which beats rna_only (0.5305) and multimodal with resnet50 (0.5251). All five completed experiments use avgpool aggregation, leaving the aggregation dimension entirely untested. Question: config_023 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while keeping the exact same scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + weighted fusion setup as config_007, cleanly isolating the effect of aggregation. Why best next: It is a single-variable extension of the current best configuration, directly testing whether transformer aggregation can improve upon the 0.5420 baseline. If it helps, we identify a new winning axis; if it doesn't, we confirm avgpool sufficiency and redirect exploration toward profile setting or RNA encoder choices. This is the most information-dense use of the next budget slot given the sparse evidence on aggregation.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_007 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted, acc=0.542), and RNA signal dominates (rna_only scgpt=0.530 vs image_only=0.33). However, all completed experiments use scgpt as the RNA encoder; scvi_n200 and pca_n2000 remain untested in the multimodal setting. Uncertainty: We do not know whether scgpt's learned representation is specifically required or whether another learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200) performs comparably with the same image/fusion/aggregation stack. This experiment (config_019: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) changes only the RNA encoder relative to config_007, giving a clean single-variable comparison. If scvi_n200 matches scgpt, the RNA representation family is flexible and we can focus budget on image/fusion/profile choices; if it falls well short, scgpt is confirmed as the critical RNA encoder and further RNA-encoder exploration is deprioritized. This is the highest-information next step because the RNA encoder is the largest untested design axis and the dominant performance driver.

The dominant finding so far is that the RNA encoder is the primary performance driver: scvi_n200 (config_019, acc=0.706) massively outperforms scgpt (config_007, acc=0.542), while with scgpt the image modality contributed only ~1 point (config_009 rna_only 0.530 vs config_007 multimodal 0.542). The critical open question is whether the image modality adds meaningful value when paired with the superior scvi_n200 encoder. config_031 (rna_only, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a clean single-variable ablation against config_019 (multimodal, scvi_n200, vit_l, avgpool, weighted): the only change is removing the image branch. If rna_only scvi_n200 approaches or matches 0.706, it reveals that image contributes little and we can redirect budget toward RNA-side design (profile setting, aggregation). If it drops substantially, it confirms the image modality is synergistic with scvi_n200 and justifies further image-encoder/fusion exploration. Under a limited budget, resolving whether the image branch is even necessary is the highest-value uncertainty to reduce before investing in image-specific hyperparameter searches.

The current best is config_019 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) at 0.706 acc. With the weaker scgpt encoder, weighted fusion clearly outperformed concat (0.542 vs 0.518, configs 007 vs 016), but scvi_n200 is a fundamentally stronger and different encoder, so the optimal fusion strategy may shift. Config_015 changes only the fusion method (weighted → concat) while holding all other settings at the known-best values, giving a clean single-variable A/B comparison against config_019. If concat matches or exceeds weighted, it reveals an encoder–fusion interaction that could unlock further gains; if weighted remains superior, it confirms weighted fusion is robust across encoder quality and we can redirect the next experiment toward aggregation (transformer) or profile setting. Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information, lowest-risk next step to either exploit the current best or identify a better fusion for the strongest encoder.

The current best configuration is config_015 (scvi_n200, vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.7150 acc / 0.6872 F1. With scgpt, transformer aggregation was clearly worse than avgpool (0.520 vs 0.542, config_023 vs config_007), but scvi_n200 produces qualitatively richer and higher-performing representations, so the aggregation–encoder interaction may differ. Config_011 changes only the aggregation (avgpool → transformer) while holding the best-known RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion method constant, giving a clean single-variable test. If transformer underperforms, we confirm avgpool is optimal and can pivot to testing profile setting or image encoder; if it improves, we gain a direct performance boost on the best pipeline. This is the most informative next step because it isolates one architectural decision on the strongest configuration identified so far, maximizing information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

With no prior experiments completed, the highest-priority question is establishing a clean, interpretable performance baseline. config_005 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest possible configuration: no learned encoder, no aggregation, no fusion. It will (1) provide a reference accuracy/F1 for the task using only transcriptomic data with a standard linear reduction, (2) serve as the anchor against which all future multimodal, multiprofile, or learned-encoder experiments can be compared to isolate the marginal contribution of each added design element, and (3) be fast to train, preserving budget for subsequent experiments. Starting here allows a systematic one-factor-at-a-time exploration: I can next vary the RNA encoder (scvi_n200, scgpt), add image modality, switch to multiprofile, or change aggregation/fusion, each time attributing performance shifts to a single change. This is the most information-efficient first step under a limited budget.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_005: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), establishing a weak RNA-only baseline. The central uncertainty is whether the image modality adds any predictive value, which is the core question of a multimodal study. Question tested: config_023 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat fusion) keeps the profile setting and RNA encoder identical to the baseline and introduces only the image encoder and the necessary fusion step. This isolates the contribution of the image modality with minimal confounding. Why best next step: Under a tight budget, directly comparing a multimodal model to the existing RNA-only baseline (same profile, same RNA encoder) gives the cleanest signal on whether adding a second modality is worthwhile. If config_023 substantially exceeds 0.485, we validate the multimodal direction and can then explore encoder/aggregation/fusion variants; if it does not, we learn early that the image modality or simple concat fusion is not the right lever, redirecting effort toward RNA encoder or profile choices. This is more informative than testing image-only (which would not tell us whether fusion works) or jumping to a complex multiprofile multimodal config (which would change too many variables at once).

Evidence: config_023 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieved 0.535 acc / 0.519 F1, a clear ~5-point improvement over the rna_only baseline (config_005: 0.485/0.464), confirming that the image modality with ViT-L and concat fusion is beneficial. The largest untested design axis is whether moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with aggregation can further improve performance. Question: Does multiprofile + avgpool aggregation, while holding RNA encoder (pca_n2000), image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), and fusion (concat) constant, improve over the singleprofile baseline? Why this experiment: config_003 is the minimal, clean extension of config_023 along the profile/aggregation axis, changing only profile_setting (single→multi) and adding avgpool aggregation. This isolates the multiprofile effect before introducing the more complex transformer aggregation or a different fusion strategy. If multiprofile+avgpool helps, we can then test transformer aggregation (config_017) or weighted fusion; if it does not, we save budget by avoiding more complex aggregation variants. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_003 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) achieved 0.629 acc, a large jump over config_023 (same but singleprofile, 0.535), indicating that multiprofile aggregation is a critical design choice. The specific aggregation method (avgpool) has not been stress-tested. Question: Does transformer-based aggregation outperform simple average pooling for combining multiple profiles, while holding all other variables (pca_n2000, ViT-L, concat fusion) constant? Why this is best: config_017 is a clean single-variable ablation against the current best (config_003), isolating the aggregation effect. If transformer helps, it identifies a further improvement axis; if avgpool is sufficient, it confirms a simpler design and redirects budget toward other dimensions (fusion type, encoder choice). This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

All four completed experiments used concat fusion, so the effect of weighted fusion remains entirely untested. config_003 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.629 acc, and config_022 is identical except for switching fusion from concat to weighted. This isolates a single design variable (fusion strategy) against the strongest known baseline, directly testing whether learned channel weighting improves over simple concatenation. Under a tight budget, this is the highest-information single-variable extension: if weighted fusion helps, it identifies a new lever to exploit across other encoders/aggregations; if it does not, it confirms concat is sufficient and redirects budget toward untested encoders (scvi_n200, scgpt) or image backbones (resnet50).

The current best (config_022: pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.635 acc / 0.618 F1. All completed experiments use PCA as the RNA encoder, leaving the RNA representation choice entirely unexplored. config_046 is a single-variable change from the current best, swapping pca_n2000 for scvi_n200 while holding image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), aggregation (avgpool), fusion (weighted), and profile setting (multiprofile) constant. This directly tests whether a learned nonlinear RNA latent (scVI) captures biological structure that PCA misses, which is a critical design axis given that the RNA modality is the primary biological signal. If scvi_n200 improves performance, it identifies RNA encoder quality as a lever for further gains; if it does not, it confirms PCA sufficiency and redirects budget toward other dimensions (e.g., image encoder or fusion).
