This is the highest-information single experiment available under the limited budget.

The RNA encoder is clearly the most impactful design choice: switching from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 (config_022→config_046, all else identical) yielded the largest single improvement in the study (+7.1% accuracy, 0.635→0.706). However, we have not yet tested the third available learned encoder, scgpt. Config_014 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) is an exact single-variable swap against our current best (config_046), isolating the RNA encoder effect while holding image encoder, aggregation, fusion, and profile setting constant. If scgpt matches or beats scvi_n200, it opens a new promising direction; if it underperforms, it confirms scvi_n200 as the superior learned representation and lets us redirect remaining budget to other dimensions (e.g., aggregation or image encoder). Under a limited budget, resolving uncertainty on the highest-leverage design axis with a clean controlled comparison is the most efficient use of the next experiment.

Evidence: scvi_n200 dramatically outperforms pca_n2000 (+0.071 acc) and scgpt (+0.164 acc) under identical multimodal/multiprofile/vit_l/avgpool/weighted settings (config_046: 0.706 vs config_022: 0.635 vs config_014: 0.542). However, we have no rna_only baseline with scvi_n200 and multiprofile, so we cannot determine how much of the 0.706 performance is driven by the RNA encoder alone versus the image modality. Question: config_012 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) isolates the RNA contribution by removing the image modality while keeping the best-known RNA encoder and profile setting. Why this is the best next experiment: The gap between rna_only/scvi_n200/multiprofile and the current best (config_046) directly quantifies the image modality's marginal contribution. If the gap is small (<0.03), future effort should focus on RNA encoder refinement; if large (>0.08), image encoder choice and fusion strategy become critical levers. This single ablation resolves a major source of uncertainty that would otherwise misdirect subsequent experiments, making it more informative than a marginal aggregation or fusion swap on the already-strong config_046.

Evidence: config_046 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is the best result at 0.706 acc. The only prior evidence on aggregation (avgpool vs. transformer) comes from pca_n2000, where avgpool outperformed transformer (0.629 vs 0.599, configs 003 vs 017). However, scvi_n200 produces a fundamentally different learned, nonlinear, low-dimensional representation, so the aggregation ranking may not transfer. Question: config_006 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while keeping scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, and weighted fusion fixed, directly testing whether transformer aggregation can better model interactions in the scvi latent space. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a single-variable, clean comparison against the current best (config_046), it resolves the most important unresolved design question (aggregation) in the context of the dominant RNA encoder, and it could either confirm that avgpool is robustly superior or uncover a further performance gain—both outcomes are highly informative under a limited budget.

The current best configuration (config_006: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, acc=0.725) has only been tested with imagenet_vit_l as the image encoder. All top-performing multimodal configs use this specific encoder, leaving the image encoder architecture as an unexplored critical design dimension in the high-performing regime. Config_038 makes a single-variable change (imagenet_vit_l → resnet50) from config_006, cleanly isolating the effect of image encoder choice. If resnet50 performs comparably, the image modality contribution is robust to architecture and we can focus optimization on other axes; if it drops significantly, it confirms imagenet_vit_l is essential and the gap informs how much the image representation contributes. This is the best use of the next experiment because it tests the least-resolved design choice in the current best-performing region, provides actionable guidance for practical deployment (lighter encoder), and is a controlled single-variable comparison rather than a multi-factor change.

With zero completed experiments, the priority is to establish a strong anchor configuration that maximizes the number of clean one-at-a-time comparisons available for subsequent experiments. config_001 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) uses the simplest and most standard choices across all variable sub-dimensions: PCA as the baseline RNA encoder, ViT-L as a strong standard image encoder, avgpool as the simplest aggregation, and concat as the simplest fusion. This makes it a natural reference point: config_002 isolates the image encoder (resnet50 vs ViT-L), config_020 isolates fusion (weighted vs concat), config_041 isolates aggregation (transformer vs avgpool), config_050 isolates RNA encoder (scgpt vs PCA), and config_034 isolates RNA encoder (scvi_n200 vs PCA). Starting with this 'simplest full pipeline' also avoids conflating the effect of multimodal fusion with the effect of complex sub-choices, so that if performance is weak, a follow-up unimodal baseline (e.g., config_009 or config_018) can cleanly attribute the gap to fusion vs. individual modality quality. Under a limited budget, this single experiment reduces the most uncertainty about the overall pipeline while preserving the greatest number of informative next steps.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: multimodal, PCA RNA, ViT-L, avgpool, concat → 62.9% acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether the RNA modality actually contributes meaningful signal over the image modality alone. Config_009 (image_only, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool) is a clean ablation: it keeps the image encoder, aggregation, and profile setting identical to config_001 while removing the RNA branch entirely. If image-only performance is close to 62.9%, it suggests PCA-based RNA features add little value and we should redirect budget toward image-side improvements or stronger RNA encoders. If image-only is substantially lower, it confirms multimodal fusion is worthwhile and justifies further investment in optimizing fusion/aggregation. This single experiment resolves the foundational question of whether the multimodal architecture is justified before spending budget on finer-grained fusion or encoder comparisons.

Evidence: config_001 (multimodal, pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) achieves 0.629 acc, while config_009 (image_only, multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool) achieves only 0.332 acc. This large gap suggests RNA is the dominant signal, but we cannot yet quantify how much the image modality actually contributes to the multimodal model. Question: config_018 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is the cleanest single-variable ablation of config_001—it removes only the image modality while keeping the same RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation. This directly isolates the image contribution. Why best: With only two experiments done, the highest-uncertainty design question is whether the image modality adds meaningful value or is largely redundant. The answer determines whether future budget should be spent optimizing image encoders/fusion or RNA encoders/aggregation. Combined with the existing image_only baseline (config_009), this gives both unimodal baselines needed to interpret all future multimodal results. No other single experiment reduces this fundamental uncertainty as efficiently.

Evidence: config_001 (multimodal, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieves 0.629 acc, only +0.038 over RNA-only config_018 (0.591), while image-only config_009 is weak (0.332). This suggests RNA dominates and the image contribution is modest, but it is unclear whether the modest multimodal gain is a ceiling or an artifact of the simple concat fusion. Question: config_020 is identical to config_001 except fusion is changed from concat to weighted, making it a clean single-variable test of whether the fusion strategy is bottlenecking the image signal. Why best next step: it directly isolates the fusion effect without confounding changes to encoder, aggregation, or profile setting. A positive result would justify investing in stronger image encoders or transformer aggregation; a null result would indicate the image contribution is inherently limited with current encoders, redirecting budget toward RNA encoder improvements (scgpt, scvi_n200). Either outcome sharply reduces uncertainty about where to focus remaining experiments.

Evidence: config_020 (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is our best at 0.6352 acc / 0.6183 F1, and weighted fusion clearly beats concat (config_020 vs config_001). RNA dominates (0.5907) while image alone is weak (0.3316), but the multimodal combination adds ~4-5 points over RNA-only. Uncertainty: We have only tested avgpool aggregation; transformer aggregation is completely unexplored and could capture richer cross-profile interactions. Question: Does transformer aggregation improve over avgpool when all other settings (pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion, multiprofile) are held constant? Why this is best: config_022 is a clean single-variable extension of our best-performing config, isolating the aggregation effect. Under a limited budget, testing the most impactful unexplored design axis (aggregation) on top of the strongest known configuration maximizes information gain per experiment and directly builds on the strongest evidence we have.

Evidence: RNA is the dominant modality (rna_only acc=0.5907 vs image_only acc=0.3316), and the best multimodal config (config_020, acc=0.6352) uses pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted. We now know avgpool+weighted is superior to transformer+weighted (0.6352 vs 0.5856) and weighted beats concat (0.6352 vs 0.6287). Uncertainty: We have only tested one RNA encoder (pca_n2000) in the best-performing pipeline. Since RNA drives most of the signal, the RNA encoder choice is the highest-leverage untested design decision. Question: Does a learned variational RNA representation (scvi_n200) outperform a linear PCA reduction (pca_n2000) when all other components (imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) are held at their best-known settings? Why this experiment: config_007 is a clean single-variable swap against config_020 (only rna_encoder changes), isolating the RNA encoder effect. This is more informative than testing the image encoder (resnet50) because RNA contributes far more to performance, so understanding whether a learned encoder can push the RNA signal higher is the key question for improving the overall model under a limited budget.

The strongest finding so far is that scvi_n200 dramatically outperforms pca_n2000 in the multimodal setting (config_007: 0.7062 vs config_020: 0.6352), a ~7-point gap. However, we cannot yet tell whether this gain is intrinsic to the learned RNA representation or arises from a synergy between scvi_n200 and the image modality. Config_040 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_018 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool, acc=0.5907): only the RNA encoder changes. If rna_only+scvi_n200 approaches ~0.68-0.70, the gain is primarily from the RNA representation and the image modality adds little marginal value; if it stays near ~0.60, the multimodal combination is genuinely synergistic and worth further investment. This decomposition is critical for deciding where to spend remaining budget—on improving the RNA encoder, the image encoder, or the fusion—making it the highest-information experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: scvi_n200 is the dominant driver of performance (config_007: 0.7062 vs config_020: 0.6352 with pca_n2000), and the image modality adds ~5.6 pts on top of the RNA-only scvi_n200 baseline (config_040: 0.6501). However, we have only tested one image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) with scvi_n200. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether the image contribution is encoder-specific or whether a lighter backbone like resnet50 captures comparable signal. This experiment (config_014: scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted) is a clean single-variable change from the best-performing config_007, isolating the image encoder effect while holding the RNA encoder, aggregation, fusion, and profile setting at their known-best values. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it either confirms imagenet_vit_l is necessary (justifying its compute cost) or reveals that resnet50 is sufficient (freeing the search to focus on other dimensions), and it directly informs whether the ~5.6-pt image gain is robust to encoder choice.

Evidence: scvi_n200 clearly outperforms pca_n2000 as RNA encoder (rna_only: 0.650 vs 0.591; multimodal+vit_l: 0.706 vs 0.635), and config_007 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) is the current best at 0.706. However, scgpt as an RNA encoder is completely untested across all 8 experiments, leaving a major gap in our understanding of the representation landscape. Question: config_030 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_007, differing only in RNA encoder. This isolates the effect of the scgpt representation while holding the best-known image encoder, aggregation, and fusion fixed. Why best next: Under limited budget, resolving where scgpt sits relative to scvi_n200 and pca_n2000 is critical—it determines whether we should invest further in scgpt-based configurations or concentrate remaining experiments on scvi_n200 variants (e.g., singleprofile, transformer aggregation). A clean A/B test here reduces uncertainty about a fundamental design axis more efficiently than testing a second-order interaction like aggregation choice, which already shows a consistent direction (avgpool > transformer).

All nine completed experiments use multiprofile, so the value of multiprofile versus singleprofile is entirely untested. The strongest configuration so far is config_007 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) at 0.706 acc. config_035 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, singleprofile, weighted) changes only the profile setting relative to config_007 (aggregation becomes None as a natural consequence of single-profile), giving a clean A/B test of whether multiprofile aggregation contributes meaningfully. If singleprofile matches or approaches 0.706, it simplifies the pipeline and redirects future effort; if it falls well short, it confirms multiprofile is a critical design choice and justifies further multiprofile-specific tuning. Under a limited budget, resolving this high-level architectural question is more informative than fine-tuning fusion or aggregation within an already well-supported multiprofile setting.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is no prior information about which modality, encoder, or fusion strategy is effective. The most fundamental uncertainty is whether either single modality alone provides a useful signal, and what performance floor we should expect. 2) What this tests: config_011 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50, no aggregation, no fusion) is the simplest possible configuration in the search space. It isolates the contribution of the image modality with a well-understood encoder and no additional complexity, establishing a clean single-modality baseline. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, establishing a clear performance floor with the fewest confounding design choices is the highest-information first step. It gives a reference point against which every subsequent multimodal or RNA-only experiment can be judged. If image-only performance is already strong, multimodal experiments must clear a high bar; if it is weak, it motivates exploring RNA or fusion. This simple anchor also makes later ablations (e.g., adding RNA, changing encoder, adding aggregation) interpretable because they differ from this baseline in exactly one dimension.

We have only one completed experiment (config_011: image_only, singleprofile, resnet50 → acc 0.208, F1 0.172), which is barely above chance, indicating the task is difficult or the current representation is insufficient. The most critical uncertainty right now is whether the low performance is due to a weak image encoder or a fundamental ceiling of the image modality. Config_039 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_011—only the image encoder changes from ResNet50 to ImageNet-pretrained ViT-L, holding profile setting, aggregation, and fusion constant. If ViT-L substantially outperforms ResNet50, we learn that representation quality is the bottleneck and should prioritize stronger encoders in multimodal settings. If it does not, we gain strong evidence that the image modality alone has a low ceiling and that RNA information (or multiprofile aggregation) is the more important axis to explore next. This experiment maximizes information gain per budget unit by isolating one key design variable without introducing confounds from modality, profile, or fusion changes.

We currently only have two image-only, singleprofile baselines (ResNet50: 0.208, ViT-L: 0.227), which establish that image alone yields modest performance and that ViT-L is the stronger image encoder. The most critical unresolved question is whether the RNA modality carries any predictive signal at all, since no RNA-only or multimodal result exists yet. config_045 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) is the cleanest parallel to our existing image-only singleprofile baselines: it isolates the RNA modality with the same profile setting and uses scgpt, the most expressive RNA encoder that appears in the multimodal configurations. This single experiment tells us (a) whether RNA has usable signal, (b) how it compares in magnitude to the image-only baselines, and (c) whether investing further experiments in multimodal fusion is warranted. It changes only the modality relative to our completed baselines, making the comparison direct and interpretable under a tight budget.

Evidence: RNA-only with scgpt (0.411 acc) substantially outperforms both image-only baselines (ResNet50: 0.208, ViT-L: 0.227), establishing RNA as the dominant modality. However, we have zero multimodal results, so the critical uncertainty is whether adding image information on top of the strong RNA signal provides any benefit. This experiment (config_017: multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion) directly tests that question using the strongest known encoder for each modality while holding profile_setting=singleprofile to isolate the fusion effect. If it exceeds 0.411, multimodal fusion is validated and we can invest in exploring aggregation and multiprofile; if it does not, we know image adds little value and should focus on RNA encoder or profile improvements. This is the highest-information experiment under budget because the answer fundamentally redirects the remaining search.

Evidence: RNA-only with scgpt (config_045) achieves 0.411 acc, and adding image via weighted fusion (config_017) yields only a marginal gain to 0.422, indicating the RNA representation is the dominant performance driver. However, we have only tested one RNA encoder (scgpt), leaving critical uncertainty about whether the specific learned representation (scgpt's pretraining) or any decent RNA encoder would suffice. Question: config_049 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) isolates the RNA encoder variable with a single controlled change from config_045, testing whether a different learned representation (variational autoencoder, 200-dim) matches or diverges from scgpt. Why this is the best next experiment: Before investing budget in multiprofile aggregation, fusion strategy, or image encoder choices, we must understand whether the RNA encoder is a bottleneck or a flexible component. If scvi_n200 performs comparably to scgpt, the design space opens up (cheaper encoders, different fusion options); if it underperforms significantly, scgpt's pretraining is essential and we should focus optimization around it. This single-variable comparison maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_049 (scvi_n200, rna_only) achieved 0.520 acc, far outperforming config_045 (scgpt, rna_only) at 0.411. In multimodal, config_017 (scgpt + vit_l, weighted) gave only a marginal gain over scgpt alone (0.422 vs 0.411). The critical uncertainty is whether the image modality adds value when the RNA encoder is already strong (scvi_n200). This experiment (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, weighted, singleprofile) directly tests that question while keeping fusion and image encoder identical to config_017, isolating the RNA-encoder effect in the multimodal setting. If it substantially exceeds 0.520, multimodal with scvi_n200 is a promising direction to exploit; if it is near or below 0.520, we learn that image adds little and should redirect budget toward RNA-only multiprofile or aggregation experiments. This is the highest-information single step under the limited budget.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_036 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, weighted, singleprofile) at 0.537 acc, showing that scvi_n200 is a strong RNA encoder and weighted multimodal fusion provides a modest but consistent boost over RNA alone (0.520). However, the multiprofile dimension is completely untested—no experiment has yet explored whether aggregating multiple profiles improves performance. This is a high-uncertainty, high-impact design question. Question: config_048 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted, multiprofile) directly extends config_036 by changing only the profile setting from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, isolating the effect of multiprofile while holding the best-known encoder and fusion choices constant. Why this experiment: It is the single most informative next step because (1) it builds on the strongest evidence (scvi_n200 + vit_l + weighted), (2) it tests the largest unexplored design axis, (3) avgpool is a simple, interpretable aggregation that cleanly answers 'does multiprofile help?' before committing budget to more complex aggregations like transformer, and (4) a positive result would open an entire new optimization space, while a null result would efficiently rule out multiprofile as a priority.

The strongest finding so far is the massive multiprofile gain: config_048 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted) reached 0.706 vs config_036 (same but singleprofile) at 0.537, a +0.169 jump. However, it is unclear whether this gain is driven by multiple RNA profiles, multiple image profiles, or the interaction. In the singleprofile setting, the image contributed only ~0.017 (config_036 vs config_049). Config_035 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a clean ablation that removes the image modality while preserving the multiprofile RNA pipeline and avgpool aggregation. If config_035 approaches ~0.70, the image adds little in the multiprofile regime and future effort should focus on RNA aggregation/fusion. If it drops substantially (e.g., below 0.60), the image profiles are a critical contributor and we should prioritize image-side design choices (aggregation, encoder). This single experiment isolates the image's marginal contribution in the multiprofile setting—the most important open question given the limited budget—without changing multiple variables simultaneously.

The strongest evidence so far is that multiprofile + scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l with avgpool/weighted (config_048, acc=0.706) is the best configuration, and the jump from singleprofile to multiprofile was the largest improvement observed (+0.17 over singleprofile multimodal). However, we have only tested avgpool aggregation in the multiprofile setting. The aggregation method is a critical design choice: avgpool treats all profiles symmetrically, while transformer can learn profile-specific attention and interactions. config_029 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer relative to config_048, making it a clean single-variable A/B test. This is the highest-value next experiment because it directly probes whether the current best configuration is bottlenecked by its aggregation strategy, and the result will determine whether further gains should be pursued through richer cross-profile modeling or through other dimensions (fusion, encoder choice).

The current best configuration (config_029: scvi_n200 + vit_l, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) achieves 0.725 accuracy. All top-performing multimodal experiments use 'weighted' fusion, but we have no evidence on whether 'concat' fusion could match or exceed it in this strong setting. Config_007 is identical to config_029 except for fusion (concat vs weighted), making it a clean single-variable A/B test. This is the best use of the next experiment because: (1) the evidence strongly supports the current backbone (scvi_n200, vit_l, multiprofile, transformer), so exploitation is warranted; (2) fusion strategy is the one design axis untested at the top of the performance hierarchy; (3) the result directly informs whether we should continue optimizing within the weighted-fusion family or pivot to concat-based architectures. No other available config isolates this question as cleanly.

With no completed experiments, there is zero evidence to guide exploitation, so the priority is establishing a clean, interpretable baseline. config_006 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50, no aggregation, no fusion) is the simplest and most standard single-modality configuration: it uses the most widely adopted image encoder (ResNet-50), the least complex profile setting, and introduces no confounding aggregation or fusion steps. This gives a clear reference performance for the image modality alone. All subsequent experiments—adding RNA (multimodal), switching to multiprofile, changing the image encoder, or testing fusion strategies—can be directly compared against this anchor. Choosing a more complex multimodal or multiprofile configuration first would conflate multiple design decisions and make it impossible to attribute performance to any single choice, wasting the limited budget.

We have only one completed experiment (config_006: image_only, singleprofile, resnet50 → acc 0.208, F1 0.172), which is barely above chance, giving us very sparse evidence. The most critical uncertainty is whether the image modality has meaningful signal at all or whether ResNet50 is simply too weak a representation. Config_045 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_006—only the image encoder changes—so it isolates the effect of representation quality. If ViT-L substantially improves accuracy, it tells us representation is a bottleneck and motivates investing in stronger encoders and multimodal fusion. If it does not, it strongly suggests the image modality has limited discriminative signal, redirecting the search toward RNA-only or multimodal configurations. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget because it directly addresses the viability of the image modality before committing to more complex multimodal designs.

We have only two completed experiments, both image_only/singleprofile: ResNet50 (acc≈0.208) and ViT-L (acc≈0.227). The core hypothesis of this multimodal cellular profiling study is whether adding RNA information improves on image-only predictions. config_031 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat) is the cleanest test of this hypothesis because it holds the image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) and profile setting (singleprofile) identical to our best baseline (config_045), changing only the addition of an RNA branch (scvi_n200) with the simplest fusion (concat). This isolates the marginal contribution of RNA. If accuracy improves meaningfully over 0.227, RNA adds signal; if it stays flat or drops, RNA is not helpful under this setup and we should focus budget on image-side improvements (e.g., multiprofile aggregation). Choosing scvi_n200 over scgpt or PCA avoids introducing an additional untested variable, and concat is the most interpretable fusion baseline. This is the highest-information single experiment available given the sparse evidence.

Evidence: config_031 (multimodal, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieved 0.532 accuracy, a massive jump over both image-only baselines (~0.21–0.23). However, we have no RNA-only result, so it is unclear whether the RNA encoder alone accounts for most of this gain or whether the image modality contributes meaningfully. Question: config_024 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is a direct ablation of the image modality from config_031, holding the RNA encoder and profile setting identical. It isolates the marginal contribution of the image branch. Why best next: Resolving whether images add real value is the single most consequential design question for the remaining budget. If RNA alone matches ~0.53, subsequent effort should focus on RNA encoder/aggregation choices; if it falls well below, images are essential and we should prioritize fusion strategy and image encoder comparisons. No other single experiment reduces this core uncertainty as cleanly.

Evidence: config_031 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieved 0.532 acc / 0.517 F1, while config_024 (rna_only, scvi_n200, singleprofile) achieved 0.520 acc / 0.498 F1. The multimodal gain over RNA-only is small (+0.012 acc), and we have only tested one RNA encoder (scvi_n200). Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the RNA encoder choice (scvi_n200 vs. scgpt) materially affects performance, which is a fundamental representation decision that will influence all future multimodal experiments. Question tested: config_037 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, concat) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_031, isolating the effect of RNA encoder while holding image encoder, profile setting, and fusion constant. Why best next experiment: Under a limited budget, understanding whether RNA representation quality is a key lever (vs. fusion strategy or profile setting) is the highest-information question. If scgpt significantly outperforms or underperforms scvi_n200, it reshapes the search direction for all subsequent multimodal experiments. If they are similar, we can deprioritize RNA encoder and focus on fusion or multiprofile next.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_031 (multimodal, scvi_n200 + VIT_L, concat) at 0.532 acc, but it only marginally exceeds RNA-only scvi_n200 (config_024, 0.520 acc), suggesting the image contribution is small and the fusion strategy may be a bottleneck. All multimodal results used concat fusion; weighted fusion is untested. Question: config_017 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted while keeping the exact same encoders (scvi_n200 + VIT_L) and singleprofile setting as config_031, giving a clean A/B comparison that isolates the effect of fusion strategy. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It directly extends the top-performing configuration with a single-variable change, maximizing information per experiment. (2) If weighted fusion improves meaningfully over concat, it reveals a lever for further optimization and justifies exploring weighted fusion in multiprofile settings. (3) If it does not improve, it indicates the current encoder pair is near its ceiling with simple fusion, redirecting effort toward multiprofile aggregation or alternative RNA encoders. (4) Under a limited budget, this minimal-change comparison is more informative than jumping to a multiprofile or new-encoder configuration that would confound multiple variables.

Evidence: All 6 completed experiments are singleprofile. The best result is config_017 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion, acc 0.537), with RNA as the dominant signal (rna_only 0.520 vs image_only ~0.22). The untested multiprofile dimension is the largest source of remaining uncertainty. Question: Does aggregating multiple profiles (via avgpool) improve on the best singleprofile result while keeping the same encoders and fusion? Why this experiment: config_005 is the minimal, direct extension of config_017 into the multiprofile setting—same RNA encoder (scvi_n200), same image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), same fusion (weighted)—with only the addition of multiprofile + avgpool aggregation. This isolates the multiprofile effect cleanly. If it beats 0.537, multiprofile is a productive direction and we can then explore transformer aggregation; if it does not, we avoid wasting budget on more complex multiprofile variants. It is the highest-information single experiment under the limited budget.

The strongest finding so far is config_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) at 0.706 acc, a large jump over the best singleprofile multimodal (0.537). This single data point shows multiprofile + avgpool is highly effective, but we have no evidence on whether the aggregation method is a bottleneck or whether a more expressive transformer aggregation could push performance further. Config_032 changes exactly one variable from config_005 (aggregation: avgpool → transformer) while holding all else fixed (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion, multiprofile). This cleanly isolates the aggregation effect in the regime where it matters most. If transformer outperforms avgpool, we identify a new optimization axis; if not, we confirm avgpool suffices and can redirect budget to other variables (e.g., RNA encoder or fusion). Under the limited budget, this is the highest-value single-variable extension of our best result.

Evidence: The largest performance jump in the study is from single-profile to multi-profile in the multimodal setting (0.53→0.725), while RNA-only single-profile (scvi_n200) achieves 0.52 and image-only is negligible (~0.21). We have not yet tested whether the multi-profile + transformer aggregation gain is specific to the multimodal interaction or is a general property of aggregating multiple RNA profiles. Question: config_007 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) directly tests whether multi-profile aggregation alone, without any image modality, can reproduce the large accuracy gain. Why this is the best next experiment: If RNA-only multi-profile also jumps toward ~0.70, the gain is driven by RNA profile aggregation and the image contributes less than assumed, redirecting effort toward better RNA aggregation. If it stays near 0.52, the multi-profile gain is specifically a multimodal interaction effect, confirming that image+RNA synergy is essential and justifying continued investment in multimodal multi-profile configurations. This single experiment resolves a high-uncertainty mechanistic question that would significantly reshape the remaining search strategy, making it more informative than a small incremental fusion-type or encoder swap on the already-strong multimodal multi-profile setting.

The current best configuration is config_032 (scvi_n200, vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc. In single-profile multimodal, weighted vs concat fusion showed a negligible difference (0.537 vs 0.532, config_017 vs config_031), but we have not tested this in the multiprofile+transformer regime where aggregation is more complex. Config_029 (scvi_n200, vit_l, transformer, concat) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_032, isolating the fusion strategy's effect when transformer aggregation is active. If concat performs comparably, it simplifies the design space and confirms fusion type is a low-priority decision; if it underperforms meaningfully, it validates that weighted fusion is specifically important in the multiprofile setting. Under a limited budget, this experiment reduces uncertainty about an important design axis (fusion) at the current performance frontier without changing multiple variables simultaneously.

With no completed experiments, the highest-priority question is establishing a performance floor. config_007 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000, no aggregation, no fusion) is the simplest possible configuration: it requires no trained encoder (PCA is instantaneous), uses a single profile, and has no aggregation or fusion steps. This gives us a clean, fast, low-risk baseline that will serve as the reference point for every subsequent comparison—whether multiprofile helps, whether image modality adds value, whether learned encoders (scgpt, scvi) outperform PCA, and whether aggregation/fusion strategies improve performance. Starting here minimizes implementation risk, is computationally cheap, and maximizes the interpretability of all future deltas. Without this floor, we cannot determine whether any added complexity actually contributes.

We have only one completed experiment (config_007: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA, acc≈0.485), so evidence is extremely sparse and the most critical uncertainty is whether adding the image modality provides any signal at all. config_009 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, no aggregation, concat fusion) is the minimal, clean extension of config_007: it keeps the RNA side identical (same encoder, same profile setting) and adds only a simple ResNet50 image branch with basic concatenation. This isolates the effect of image information without confounding changes to the RNA encoder, profile count, aggregation, or fusion complexity. If accuracy improves, it validates the multimodal premise and justifies investing further in image encoders and fusion strategies; if it does not, it redirects the budget toward RNA representation (scgpt/scvi) or multiprofile aggregation. Under a limited budget, resolving this core question before exploring more complex multimodal or learned-encoder configurations is the highest-information next step.

Evidence: config_007 (rna_only, pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieved 0.485 acc, and config_009 (multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat, singleprofile) improved to 0.527 acc, confirming that adding image modality helps. However, both experiments use pca_n2000—a linear dimensionality reduction—as the RNA encoder. It is unclear whether this linear representation is a bottleneck for the RNA branch in the multimodal setting. Question: config_004 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, resnet50, concat) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_009, changing only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to the learned scgpt representation. This isolates the effect of RNA representation quality while holding image encoder, fusion, and profile setting constant. Why this is the best next experiment: with only two data points, the most impactful uncertainty to resolve is whether a learned RNA encoder provides a meaningful gain over PCA in the multimodal pipeline. If scgpt substantially outperforms pca_n2000, it validates investing in learned representations and opens a high-performing branch for further exploration (multiprofile, aggregation, stronger image encoders). If the gain is marginal, it suggests the current PCA representation is sufficient and budget should shift to testing multiprofile or image encoder upgrades. This single-variable design maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_009 (pca_n2000 + resnet50, concat, singleprofile) is the best so far at 0.527 acc, clearly outperforming both the RNA-only baseline (config_007, 0.485) and the scgpt variant (config_004, 0.427). This establishes pca_n2000 + resnet50 + concat as a strong backbone. Uncertainty: All three completed experiments use singleprofile; we have zero evidence on whether multiprofile + aggregation adds value. Question: config_010 extends the best-known configuration by moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, while keeping the proven RNA encoder (pca_n2000), image encoder (resnet50), and fusion (concat) fixed. This isolates the effect of multiprofile aggregation as the primary new variable. Why best: It is the most natural exploitation of our strongest evidence while exploring the single largest untested design dimension (profile setting). Testing multiprofile now, before investing in further fusion or image-encoder variants, tells us whether the added complexity of multi-profile aggregation is worthwhile, which will shape all subsequent experiments.

Evidence: config_010 (pca_n2000, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) is the strongest result so far at 0.6186 acc, and it clearly outperforms its singleprofile counterpart config_009 (0.5266), establishing multiprofile+avgpool as a key design choice. We also know pca_n2000 > scgpt for RNA (config_009 vs config_004). However, no experiment has yet tested a stronger image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) in the multiprofile setting. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l improve performance when all other components (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) are held at their proven best? Why this is the best next experiment: config_021 changes exactly one variable (image encoder) relative to the current best config_010, cleanly isolating the effect of image representation quality. If imagenet_vit_l helps, it identifies image encoding as a further lever; if it does not, it tells us the bottleneck lies elsewhere (aggregation, fusion, RNA encoder) and we can redirect the remaining budget accordingly. This is the highest-information single-variable test available.

Evidence: The current best is config_021 (acc=0.629, F1=0.599) with multiprofile + pca_n2000 + ViT-L + avgpool + concat. The jump from singleprofile (config_009, 0.527) to multiprofile+avgpool (config_010, 0.619) was the largest gain observed, but aggregation has only been tested as avgpool. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) can further improve over simple average pooling when combining multiple profiles. Question tested: config_045 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other factors constant (pca_n2000, ViT-L, multiprofile, concat), giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_021. Why this is the best next experiment: Aggregation is a fundamental design choice for how multiprofile information is combined, and the potential gain from a learned (transformer) aggregation over a fixed (avgpool) one is a major open question. Isolating this single factor on the current best configuration maximizes information per experiment and directly informs whether to invest further in transformer-based aggregation or confirm avgpool sufficiency.

Evidence: The current best (config_021: pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) achieves 0.629 acc / 0.599 F1. All six completed multiprofile experiments use concat fusion; weighted fusion has never been tested in the multiprofile setting. Aggregation (avgpool > transformer) and image encoder (vit_l ≥ resnet50) effects are partially characterized, but the fusion strategy remains entirely unexplored at the multiprofile level. Question: Does learned weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation when combining RNA and image representations across multiple profiles? config_002 is identical to config_021 in every dimension except fusion (weighted vs concat), making it a clean single-variable comparison. Why best under budget: It directly tests the highest-priority unexplored design axis on the current best configuration. A positive result would identify a new lever for improvement; a null result would efficiently rule out fusion as a factor, narrowing the search to RNA encoder choice (scgpt, scvi) or other dimensions. No other single experiment isolates as important an untested variable with as minimal confounding.

The current best (config_002: pca_n2000, vit_l, avgpool, weighted → 0.635) establishes that multiprofile + vit_l + avgpool + weighted is the strongest pipeline. The RNA encoder is the largest untested design axis in this strong multiprofile setting: scgpt showed a negative signal in singleprofile (0.427 vs 0.527), but that was a fundamentally weaker setting, and scvi_n200 is completely untested anywhere. Config_020 (scvi_n200, vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is a clean single-variable swap against config_002, isolating the effect of a learned variational RNA encoder while holding image encoder, aggregation, and fusion fixed. This maximally reduces uncertainty about whether a learned RNA representation can improve over PCA in the best multiprofile pipeline, which is the most important remaining design question under the limited budget.

The strongest finding is that scvi_n200 dramatically outperforms pca_n2000 (0.706 vs 0.635 in config_020 vs config_002, same image/aggregation/fusion). However, with pca_n2000, transformer aggregation was notably worse than avgpool (0.599 vs 0.635 in config_045 vs config_002). This raises the question: does the richer, more structured scvi_n200 representation benefit from attention-based (transformer) aggregation in a way that the flat pca_n2000 representation did not? Config_028 (scvi_n200, vit_l, transformer, weighted) is a clean single-variable change from the current best (config_020), isolating the aggregation effect. If transformer matches or exceeds avgpool with scvi_n200, it reveals an important interaction between representation quality and aggregation strategy; if it underperforms, it confirms avgpool as the robust choice and narrows the search space. This is the highest-information next step because it directly extends the most promising direction while resolving a key design uncertainty that could guide all subsequent experiments.

The current best (config_028, scvi_n200 + ViT + transformer + weighted, 0.725 acc) suggests scvi_n200 and multimodal fusion are both important, but we have never tested scvi_n200 with multiprofile in an RNA-only setting. The gap between config_007 (pca, RNA-only, singleprofile: 0.485) and config_020 (scvi, multimodal, multiprofile: 0.706) conflates three changes simultaneously (encoder, profile, modality). Config_032 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) cleanly isolates how much of the 0.706 performance comes from the RNA representation and multiprofile aggregation alone versus the image modality. If RNA-only scvi approaches ~0.65+, the image contribution is modest and future effort should focus on RNA representation; if it stays near ~0.50–0.55, the multimodal combination is genuinely additive and justifies further multimodal exploration. This is the highest-information experiment under the limited budget because it resolves a critical uncertainty that will determine whether to exploit the multimodal direction further or pivot toward simpler RNA-centric designs.

With no completed experiments, the most important uncertainty is whether a standard multimodal pipeline (combining RNA and image features) provides a viable and competitive baseline. config_001 uses the most established RNA encoder (scgpt), the strongest pre-trained image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), the simplest profile setting (singleprofile, removing aggregation as a confound), and a simple weighted fusion. This makes it a clean, 'default' multimodal reference point. It is the best first experiment because: (1) it tests the core hypothesis of the study—that multimodal fusion is beneficial—using well-validated components so that any result is not confounded by an unusual encoder choice; (2) it establishes a performance anchor against which all subsequent multimodal variants (multiprofile, different fusion, different encoders) and single-modality baselines (image-only config_017, RNA-only config_011) can be directly compared; and (3) by keeping the design simple (singleprofile, weighted fusion), it isolates the fundamental question of whether the two modalities are complementary before adding complexity. This maximizes the information gained per experiment under the limited budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion → 0.4224 acc), the most critical uncertainty is whether the multimodal fusion actually adds value over a unimodal baseline. config_017 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is the cleanest single-axis comparison: it uses the same image encoder and profile setting as config_001, removing only the RNA modality and fusion step. If image-only achieves comparable accuracy, the RNA contribution (and all downstream RNA-encoder/fusion questions) is deprioritized; if it is substantially lower, multimodal fusion is confirmed as a productive direction and subsequent experiments can focus on optimizing RNA encoder, aggregation, and fusion. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the single most important architectural decision before spending further budget on finer-grained multimodal variants.

With only two completed experiments, the most critical uncertainty is the individual contribution of each modality. We know image-only (config_017, ViT-L) yields acc=0.227, and multimodal (config_001, scgpt+ViT-L, weighted fusion) yields acc=0.422. Testing RNA-only with the same scgpt encoder and singleprofile setting (config_011) directly decomposes the multimodal gain: if RNA-only approaches 0.40, the image adds little and we should focus on RNA encoder/fusion choices; if it is near 0.20–0.25, the image contributes substantially and image encoder improvements become high-value. This single experiment reduces the largest source of uncertainty in the design space and will guide whether subsequent budget is better spent on image-side or RNA-side improvements. It is a clean, single-variable comparison to config_001 (only the modality is removed), making interpretation straightforward under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_001 (multimodal, scgpt+imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion) achieves 0.4224 acc, only marginally above RNA-only config_011 (0.4106 acc), while image-only config_017 is far weaker (0.2266). This suggests the image modality contributes very little, possibly because the weighted fusion strategy is not effectively leveraging it. Question: Does changing fusion from weighted to concat (the only difference in config_006) meaningfully alter the multimodal gain over RNA-only? Why this experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison against our best result, isolating the fusion mechanism. If concat yields a substantially different result, we learn that fusion strategy is a key lever and should be prioritized in all future multimodal runs. If it is similar, we can rule out fusion as the bottleneck and redirect effort toward RNA encoder choice, image encoder, or multiprofile aggregation. Under a limited budget, resolving this binary question with one experiment is the most efficient use of the next slot.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: All four completed experiments use singleprofile with no aggregation. We know RNA (scgpt) dominates (0.4106 rna_only vs 0.2266 image_only), that multimodal concat fusion (config_006, 0.4348) modestly beats weighted (config_001, 0.4224), and that the image modality adds only ~2% over RNA alone. However, the profile-setting axis (single vs. multi) is completely unexplored, representing the largest remaining source of architectural uncertainty. 2) What this tests: config_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) is the minimal-change extension of our best result (config_006) to the multiprofile regime—only the profile setting and the required aggregation (avgpool) change, while keeping the same RNA encoder, image encoder, and concat fusion. This cleanly isolates whether multiple profiles with average-pool aggregation improve over a single profile. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: The profile/aggregation axis is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact design question remaining. Testing it with the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and holding all other variables at their best-known values (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, concat) follows the principle of changing as few factors as possible. A positive result would open the multiprofile design space for further exploitation; a null or negative result would justify concentrating the remaining budget on singleprofile refinements (e.g., RNA encoder choice, image encoder choice). Either outcome substantially reduces uncertainty about a core architectural decision under a tight budget.

The strongest result so far is config_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.5176 accuracy, a large jump over the best singleprofile result (config_006 at 0.4348). This shows that multiprofile with aggregation is highly beneficial. The most important open question is whether the aggregation method matters: avgpool is a simple mean, while a transformer can model inter-profile interactions. config_020 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer, concat) differs from config_005 only in aggregation (transformer vs avgpool), giving a clean, single-variable comparison. If transformer outperforms avgpool, it identifies a new promising direction for further exploration; if avgpool is sufficient or better, it confirms a simpler, more efficient design and redirects effort toward other factors (RNA encoder, image encoder, fusion). This is the highest-information next step because it directly extends the best-performing configuration while isolating one critical design choice under a limited budget.

Evidence: The dominant finding is that multiprofile provides a large gain (~8 pts) over singleprofile (config_005: 0.518 vs config_006: 0.435), and within multiprofile, avgpool+concat with scgpt+imagenet_vit_l is the current best. However, the RNA encoder axis is completely unexplored—we have only tested scgpt. Since RNA is the dominant signal (rna_only 0.411 vs image_only 0.227), the quality of the RNA representation is likely the next most impactful design lever. Question: Does switching the RNA encoder from scgpt to scvi_n200 (another learned, generative-style representation) improve or degrade performance in the multiprofile setting? config_034 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat, multiprofile) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_005, isolating the RNA encoder effect while holding all other design choices constant. Why best next experiment: It tests the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact unexplored axis (RNA representation) in the regime where performance is already highest, with a minimal change that cleanly attributes any performance shift to the encoder choice. The result will determine whether to invest further in learned RNA encoders or pivot to linear (PCA) representations, and will guide all subsequent experiments on the image encoder and fusion axes.

The strongest result so far is config_034 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 acc, driven primarily by the scvi_n200 RNA encoder. The key open question is whether the aggregation method over multiple profiles can further improve performance with this much richer representation. With the weaker scgpt encoder, avgpool marginally beat transformer (0.518 vs 0.507), but that gap was small and may not hold with scvi_n200's higher-dimensional, more structured embeddings where inter-profile interactions might be better captured by a transformer. config_008 changes only the aggregation (avgpool → transformer) while holding all other settings identical to config_034, giving a clean single-variable comparison. This is the best use of the next experiment because it directly exploits the strongest evidence while isolating the effect of aggregation, which is a critical architectural choice for multiprofile models and could unlock further gains or confirm that simple averaging is sufficient.

The two best experiments (config_034: 0.715, config_008: 0.721) both use scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile, showing that the RNA encoder choice is the dominant factor. However, we have no RNA-only baseline with scvi_n200 + multiprofile, so we cannot determine whether the image modality is actually contributing meaningful complementary information or whether the high performance is driven entirely by the RNA encoder. With scgpt, the image added only ~0.02 over RNA-alone (0.411 vs 0.435), suggesting the image contribution may be marginal. Config_025 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) is a clean single-variable ablation of config_034 (removing the image). If RNA alone approaches ~0.70, the image is not adding value and we can simplify the pipeline; if it drops to ~0.50–0.60, the image is providing substantial complementary signal and further image-encoder or fusion experiments become high-priority. Under a limited budget, resolving this fundamental modality-contribution question is more informative than a small fusion-method tweak (e.g., weighted vs concat) that is unlikely to change the ranking of top configurations.

Evidence: The top two configs (config_008: 0.7207, config_034: 0.7150) both use scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile + concat fusion, differing only in aggregation (transformer vs avgpool, a negligible ~0.006 gap). However, we have not yet tested weighted fusion in this high-performing regime—our only fusion comparisons so far were in the weaker scgpt regime (config_001 vs config_006, ~0.01 gap). Question: Does weighted fusion outperform or match concat when the RNA encoder is scvi_n200 and the image encoder is imagenet_vit_l with transformer aggregation? This is a clean single-variable comparison to our current best (config_008), isolating the fusion effect. Why this is the best next experiment: It directly exploits the strongest evidence (scvi_n200 + multiprofile + imagenet_vit_l) while resolving an important, still-uncertain design choice (fusion strategy) in the regime that actually matters. A result here either improves on the current best or confirms concat as the preferred fusion, freeing subsequent budget to test image-encoder alternatives.

With no prior evidence, the most critical uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion actually adds value over a strong unimodal baseline. Config_002 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) is the simplest possible RNA-only configuration—no fusion, no aggregation, single profile—making it a clean reference floor. scvi_n200 is a well-established, robust single-cell RNA encoder, so this experiment isolates the question 'How well can we classify using RNA alone?' without confounding variables. Establishing this baseline first is essential: any subsequent multimodal result can only be interpreted as a gain (or lack thereof) relative to this number. It directly operationalizes the principle of not assuming complex multimodal models will outperform simpler ones, and it reduces the greatest uncertainty in the search space before investing experiments in more complex configurations.

We have only one completed experiment (config_002: rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200 → Acc 0.520), so the most critical uncertainty is whether adding the image modality provides any benefit over the RNA-only baseline. config_051 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat) keeps the RNA encoder and profile setting identical to config_002 and introduces only the image modality with a simple concat fusion, thereby isolating the effect of adding image information. This is the cleanest possible A/B comparison: any performance difference directly attributes to the image channel rather than confounds from a different encoder, profile setting, or aggregation scheme. Under a limited budget, establishing whether multimodality helps at all is the highest-value information to obtain before investing in more complex multiprofile or aggregation variants.

We have RNA-only (config_002: acc 0.520) and multimodal (config_051: acc 0.532) results, but no image-only baseline. The ~1.2% multimodal improvement is small and its source is ambiguous: the image may be contributing genuine signal, or the model may be relying primarily on RNA with the image adding noise. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) directly complements config_002 to complete the single-modality baseline pair, isolating the image encoder's independent predictive power. This is the highest-information experiment under budget because: (1) it clarifies whether the image modality is worth investing further experiments in, (2) it tells us whether the small multimodal gain reflects real complementary information or a marginal effect, and (3) it is a clean single-variable comparison (swap RNA→image) that avoids confounding with profile, aggregation, or fusion changes. Without this baseline, subsequent multiprofile or aggregation experiments would be harder to interpret.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, scvi_n200, singleprofile) achieves 0.5203 acc, and config_051 (multimodal, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, concat) improves to 0.5321 acc / 0.5172 F1, showing a modest but consistent multimodal gain. Image-only (config_010) is very weak (0.2266), confirming RNA dominates. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether the concat fusion in config_051 is optimal or whether a weighted fusion would better calibrate the contribution of the weak image signal. This experiment (config_038) changes only the fusion method (concat → weighted) while holding RNA encoder, image encoder, and profile setting identical to config_051, providing a clean single-variable A/B test. If weighted fusion outperforms concat, it indicates the image branch is noisy and should be downweighted, directly informing all future multimodal designs. If concat remains better, the image signal is additive and the fusion choice is less critical. Under a tight budget, isolating this one design decision from the already-validated baseline is the most informative next step before exploring additional axes (image encoder, multiprofile, RNA encoder).

All four completed experiments are singleprofile, so we have zero evidence on whether multiprofile + aggregation improves performance. The best result so far is config_038 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion, acc=0.537). config_045 is the minimal, controlled extension of that best result: it keeps the same model setting, RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion method, and only changes profile_setting from single to multi with avgpool aggregation (which is inherent to multiprofile). This directly tests whether representing each cell with multiple profiles and aggregating them (vs. a single profile) yields a meaningful gain. If multiprofile helps, it opens a large and promising sub-space; if it does not, we can confidently prune all multiprofile configurations and focus remaining budget on RNA/image encoder and fusion refinements within singleprofile. Under a tight budget, resolving this high-impact binary question with a one-axis change from our current best is the most information-efficient next step.

Evidence: config_045 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is a clear outlier at 0.706 acc, far exceeding the singleprofile multimodal configs (~0.53–0.54). The dominant driver is the multiprofile setting with aggregation. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the simple avgpool aggregation is near-optimal or whether a more expressive transformer aggregation could capture inter-profile interactions and push performance higher. This experiment (config_043) changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding all other parameters identical to config_045 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion, multiprofile). It cleanly isolates the aggregation effect in the multiprofile regime. Under a limited budget, this is the best next step because it directly tests the most impactful potential improvement to our current best configuration; a positive result would justify further aggregation exploration, while a null result would confirm avgpool sufficiency and redirect effort toward encoder or fusion choices.

The current best (config_043: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, multiprofile) achieves 0.725 acc. The single most important untested design variable is the RNA encoder in the multiprofile/transformer setting, since all completed multiprofile experiments used scvi_n200. config_046 swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000 while holding image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), aggregation (transformer), fusion (weighted), and profile setting (multiprofile) constant. This isolates whether a learned nonlinear representation (scvi) is meaningfully better than a linear PCA projection for the RNA modality when profiles are aggregated by a transformer. If pca_n2000 performs comparably, the RNA encoder is not a bottleneck and we can redirect budget to other variables (e.g., image encoder or fusion); if it degrades substantially, scvi's learned representation is confirmed as critical. This single-variable comparison from the current best is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

The largest performance jump in the history (0.537→0.725) came from switching to multiprofile, but we cannot yet tell how much of that gain is driven by the multiprofile aggregation itself versus the multimodal combination. config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) is a clean single-factor ablation of the image modality from the current best config_043. If RNA-only multiprofile approaches ~0.70, the image adds little and future effort should target RNA encoders (e.g., scgpt). If it drops substantially (e.g., below 0.60), the image is essential and we should explore image-encoder variants (resnet50) and fusion strategies. This single experiment resolves a major design uncertainty that will determine the direction of all subsequent experiments, making it the highest-information-use choice under the limited budget.

The current best configuration (config_043: multiprofile, transformer, weighted, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l) achieves 0.725 accuracy, and the single most impactful finding is that multiprofile+transformer aggregation drives most of the gain. However, we have only tested 'weighted' fusion in this critical setting; the single-profile experiments showed weighted marginally beating concat (0.537 vs 0.532), but that gap was tiny and the dynamics may differ when a transformer aggregation produces richer multi-profile representations. Config_047 changes exactly one variable (fusion: weighted→concat) from our best config, cleanly isolating the fusion effect. This is the best use of the next budget slot because it either confirms that weighted fusion is optimal (reducing the search space) or reveals a meaningful gain from concat in the multiprofile+transformer regime, directly informing whether further optimization should focus on fusion architecture or other components.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 acc. We have strong evidence that multiprofile + transformer aggregation + scvi_n200 are critical, and that weighted ≈ concat for fusion. However, the image encoder dimension is essentially unexplored in the multiprofile multimodal regime—we have only tested imagenet_vit_l. Image-only performance is very weak (0.227), yet the image modality adds ~7 points over RNA-only in the multimodal setting, so the specific image architecture may matter. Question: config_018 changes only the image encoder from imagenet_vit_l to resnet50 while holding all other settings at their best-performing values (scvi_n200, transformer, weighted, multiprofile). This isolates the effect of image encoder architecture. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison against the current best, it probes the least-understood design axis (image encoder choice in the multiprofile setting), and the result will tell us whether the ViT-specific features are important or whether a standard CNN backbone is sufficient—information that is critical for both further model search and practical deployment, and that cannot be inferred from any existing experiment.
